Chapter 17

Delhi Sultanate: Slave Dynasty

27 facts · 9 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (64 points)
  • Incumbents of the Delhi Sultanate from 1206 AD to 1290 AD are popularly known as the sultans of the Slave dynasty, whose founder was Qutbuddin Aybak.
  • They were all Turks, and their houses/lines were separate.
  • So it is more appropriate to call them the slave dynasty or Mamluk Sultan of Delhi, instead of calling these sultans as the sultans of the Slave dynasty.
  • The first ruler of the Slave Dynasty in India was Qutbuddin Aybak (1206 - 1210 AD).
  • He was from a Turk tribe called Aybak.
  • In childhood, he was bought by the Qazi of Nishapur Fakhruddin Abdul Aziz Kufi as a slave.
  • From childhood he used to read the Quran in a very melodious tone, which made him famous as the Quran Khwan (the one who recites the Quran).
  • Later, he was brought from Nishapur to Ghazni where Ghori bought him.
  • On the basis of his talent, passion and honesty, he gained the confidence of the Ghori.
  • Ghori promoted him to the post of Amir-i-Akhur. His coronation was held in June 1206 AD, three months after the death of Ghori.
  • Aybak’s capital was Lahore.
  • Aybak never held the title of ‘Sultan’.
  • He kept himself satisfied only with the titles of‘Malik’ and ‘Sipahasalaar’.
  • After obtaining the liberation letter from Ghori’s successor Ghiyasuddin Mahmud, Aybak got rid of slavery in 1208 AD. and ruled as an independent sovereign.
  • Due to his generosity, Qutbuddin Aybak used to donate so much money that he was called by the ‘Lakh Bakhsh’ (Giver of lakhs).
  • Aibak had built mosques known as ‘Quwwat-ul-Islam’ in Delhi and ‘Adhai Din Ka Jhopra’ in Ajmer (in 1192 AD).
  • He started the construction of‘Qutub Minar’ in Delhi, which was completed by Iltutmish.
  • The fourth Storey was damaged by lightning which was rebuilt by Firuz Shah Tughluq, also spelt Feroz Shah Tughluq. He rebuilt the fourth floor of Qutb Minar as well as built the fifth floor.
  • Sultan Qutbuddin Aibak died in 1210 AD when he fell from a horse while playing Chaugan (a game like modern polo).
  • He was buried in Lahore.
  • Iltutmish received the approval as Sultan not from any Ghor ruler, but from the Khalifa.
  • Khalifa recognised the rule of Iltutmish to all those areas which he won and gave him the title of ‘Sultan-e-Azam’.
  • Iltutmish was called ‘Slave of a slave’ [Aybak (who himselfwas a slave), whose slave was Iltutmish].
  • Iltutmish was a Turk of‘Ilbari’tribe.
  • Before becoming Sultan, he was the governor of Budaun.
  • He was with Muhammad Ghori and Aybak during the campaign to suppress the Khokhar tribe rebellion in 1205 - 1206 AD.
  • In the war, Ghori was so influenced by the courage and skill of Iltutmish that he freed him from slavery.
  • Mongol invader Genghis Khan loitered near the Indus river for 3 months but did not cross into India during the reign of Iltutmish. Chasing the ruler of Khwarazmshah Jalaluddin Mengubirni, Genghis Khan reached the bank of Indus river. Jalal-ud-din-Mengubirni sought refuge from Iltutmish. Iltutmish dared not to risk the invasion of a dangerous and furious invader like Genghis. So, he prudently refused to give asylum to the Khwarizm. Jalal-ud-din remained for some time in the north-west; this led to a series of Mongol attacks like seige of Multan around 1224. His departure (~ 1223-24) did not instantly end frontier troubles.
  • Iltutmish defeated Sultan Ghiyas-ud-din Iwaz or Hisamuddin Awaz in mountains of Rajmahal near Teliyagarhi and annexed Bihar Sharifand Barh. Awaz had accepted the subordination to Iltutmish. Iltutmish appointed Malik-Jani as the new Subedar of Bihar.
  • Iltutmish was the first to use the pure Arabic coins during the Sultanate period in India. He introduced two important coins,
  • i.e. silver (Tanka) and copper (Jital) during the Sultanate period and started the tradition of inscribing the name of the Tankshal on the coins.
  • Iltutmish received a certificate of ‘Khilat’ from Caliph of Baghdad in 1229 AD, which made Iltutmish a legitimate Sultan and the Delhi Sultanate an independent state.
  • It is known from the Ibn Battuta’s description that Iltutmish had set up two statues of Lions of marble in front of his palace, which had two bells hanging around their neck which anyone could ring and seek justice from the Sultan.
  • Iltutmish appointed the officials Qazi and Amir-i-dad in all the cities.
  • According to Dr. R. P. Tripathi, the history of Muslim sovereignty in India begins with Iltutmish.
  • According to Dr. Ishwari Prasad, Iltutmish was, undoubtedly, the founder of Slave Dynasty.
  • Raziyya Sultan (1236-40 AD) was the first female ruler of Delhi Sultanate.
  • As an individual, she violated the prevailing gender norms of Islam for the first time in India, and politically, she emphasized the power to be in the hands of the Sultan instead ofdividing it among the Chiefs (Sardars) or the Iqtadars and thus, she tried to exercise real authority which provoked powerful Turkish slave-nobles (Chahalgani).
  • Chahalgani (40 nobles) played an important role in overthrowing Raziyya Begum.
  • Nobles under the leadership of Governor of Bhatinda, Malik Altunia, rebelled against Raziyya and overthrew her.
  • The full name of Sultan Balban was Ghiyasuddin Balban.
  • Balban ruled the Sultanate from 1266 to 1287 AD as Sultan.
  • He was also known as Ulugh Khan.
  • Like Iltutmish, he was also an Ilbari Turk.
  • He laid the foundation of a new dynasty, the Balban Dynasty.
  • Balban was caught by Mongols in his childhood, who sold him at Ghajini to Khwaja Jamaluddin, a resident of Basra.
  • He was brought to Delhi in 1232 AD, where Iltutmish bought him in 1233 AD after Gwalior's victory.
  • Impressed by his abilities, Iltutmish gave him the title of Khasdaar.
  • During the reign of Raziyya, he earned the rank of Amir-i-Shikar.
  • In the conspiracy against Raziyya, he was with the Turkish warlords, consequently Bahramshah became the Sultan, and Balban got the title of ‘Amir-i-Akhur’.
  • Due to the grace of Badruddin Rumi, he got the Jagir of Rewari. Alauddin Masudshah became the Sultan with help of Turkish Amirs in which Balban played an important role, consequently he got the fiefofHansi.
  • Balban married his daughter to Sultan Nasiruddin in 1249 AD. On this occasion, he was given the title of ‘Ulugh Khan’ and the post of ‘Nayab-i-mamlikat’.
  • Balban sat on Delhi’s throne in 1266 AD.
  • It is said about Balban that he adopted a policy of ‘blood and iron’.
  • There were two main characteristics of the rule of Balban - First the divine right of Sultan and second the Sultan had to be autocratic.
  • Balban had created his political ideology inspired by the popular heroes of Persia. The King was considered the God’s representative on earth - ‘Niyabat i-Khudai’.
  • Balban projected kingship as divnely sanctioned.
  • ‘Zille Allah’ or 'Zil-i-Ilahi' means Shadow of God.
  • He was the first Sultan of Delhi, who established the theory of the state/ kingship.
  • He told his son Bughra Khan - “The post of Sultan is a living symbol of autocracy.”
  • Balban started many traditions of the Iranian emperors in his court. He started the rituals of ‘Sijada’ (saluting the Sultan in a prostrate manner) and ‘Paibos’ (kissing the feet of Sultan). In his court, he started the practice of celebrating the Persian festival ‘Nawruz’ with greatjoy every year.
  • Balban established a military department ‘Diwan-i-Arz’ to look after the military organisation of the army.
  • Balban made Imad ul-Mulk his Military minister (Arz-i-Mamalikk), who was a very honest and hardworking person.
  • He kept him free from the financial control of the Wazir so that he did not lack wealth.

Founder of the Slave dynasty → Qutbuddin Aybak (1206 A.D.); dynasty ruled 1206-1290, first of five Sultanate dynasties.

Khalji Dynasty

Key facts from the book (39 points)

Jalaluddin Khalji established the Khalji dynasty in 1290 AD.

  • He was crowned at the Palace of Kilokhari (Kilugarhi), which was built by Qaiqubad.
  • According to Dr. A. L. Srivastava, Jalaluddin Khalji was the first Turkish Sultan of Delhi who believed in the ideal ofbenevolent despotism. When Jalaluddin was the Sultan of Delhi, he offered the post of ‘Amir-i-Tuzuk’ to Alauddin and married his daughter to him.
  • Alauddin Khalji was honoured with the governorship of Kara-Manikpur because of his important role in suppressing the revolt of Malik Chhajju.
  • Alauddin was the first Sultan of Delhi, who established control of the state over religion. He called himself‘Yamin-ul-Khilafat, Nasir-e-Amir-ul-Mumanin’.
  • He remained free from the influence of Ulema class.
  • Alauddin Khalji was an ambitious Sultan.
  • He assumed the title of ‘Sikandar -i- Sani’ (second Alexander) and inscribed it on his coins.
  • Alauddin’s famous commander Zafar Khan who was the best and courageous commander of his time was killed fighting against Mongols.
  • He was an excellent and courageous commander of his time. Mongols were so impressed by the bravery of Zafar Khan and the persistence of Khalji army that they backed down by 30 miles. The original name of Zafar Khan was Malik Hizabruddin.
  • According to Jayasi, Padmini was the wife of Rana Ratan Singh. Queen Padmini committed ‘Jauhar’ due to the death of Rana Ratan Singh during the invasion of Chittor, the capital of Mewar, by Alauddin Khalji. Malik Muhammad Jayasi wrote the famous ‘Padmavat’ which was based on the story of queen Padmini in 1540 AD.
  • Alauddin faced some rebellions at the beginning of his reign. Finding the possible reasons for these rebellions, Alauddin Khalji issued four ordinances to suppress potential rebellions.
  • By the first ordinance, gifts, pensions, land received in donations, etc, were banned, and government officials were ordered to collect more and more taxes.
  • An intelligence (spy) department was set up by the second ordinance.
  • The third ordinance banned intoxicating drinks (alcohol, cannabis, etc.) and gambling.
  • The fourth ordinance banned the marital relations and feasts between the nobles and the Aamirs.
  • Ramchandra Dev was the ruler of Devgiri when Alauddin attacked Devgiri. Ramchandra Dev, the ruler of Devgiri, was demanded the cession of the province of Ellichpur and income from it every year to Alauddin as he was defeated in 1296 AD. But he did not send that tax to Delhi between 1305 AD or 1306 AD.
  • Consequently, Alauddin sent an army led by Malik Kafur to attack Devgiri in 1307 AD.
  • Raja Ramchandra Dev was defeated in the battle and he surrendered. Alauddin treated Ramchandra well and honoured him the title of ‘Rai Rayan’. Six months later he was given one lakh Tankas and the district of Navsari and was sent back to his state.
  • Malik Kafur also led a campaign against Ramchandra’s son Shankerdev in 1313 AD. Alauddin met Malik Kafur during his Gujarat conquest.
  • He was also called ‘Hazar - Dinari’.
  • Alauddin was the first Sultan, who started collecting revenue by measuring the land.
  • Alauddin established a separate department “Diwan-i-Mustakharaj” to implement this system.
  • Alauddin took the authority of tax collection from the traditional tax officers (Khutt, Mukaddam and Chaudhary). All their privileges were abolished.
  • Taxes were collected from their lands and the rest other taxes were also taken, due to which there was little difference between Khut (Zamindar) and Balahar (ordinary farmer).
  • The main objective of Alauddin’s revenue and tax system was to establish a powerful and autocratic state.
  • He took the land from all those people who had been granted land as ‘Milq’ (property, prize, idrarat pensions given by the state) and ‘Waqf’ (charitable land), etc., Consequently, the Khalisa land was developed on a large scale.
  • Alauddin Khalji fixed 50% of the yield as the land tax (Kharaj).
  • Alauddin Khalji was the first Muslim ruler of India who had fixed the revenue on the real income of the land.
  • Alauddin had initiated market control or price control policy. Alauddin appointed officials for the success of his market control policy.
  • According to Barani, the purpose of these market reforms was to support a huge army against the Mongols and to control the idea of rebellion among Hindus.
  • Alauddin Khalji started the state granaries & price controlled sale of grains which was like the Public Distribution System (PDS).
  • There were two new taxes levied by Alauddin Khalji that were ‘Ghari (House) Tax’ which was levied on houses and huts and ‘Grazing (Charai) Tax’ which was imposed on milch animals.
  • The Ravi river was a boundary between the Delhi Sultanate and Mongols during the reign of Alauddin Khalji in 1306 AD.
  • During the reign of Sultan Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, the Mongol army had crossed the Indus under the leadership of Shir Mughal (1325 AD), but he was defeated by Malik Shadi, the Subedar of Samana.
  • Mubarak Khalji declared himself Khalifa and assumed titles such as ‘Al Imam’, ‘Ul-Imam’, ‘Khalifatullah’, of which he was always incapable.
  • Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah (April - September, 1320) was a converted Muslim from Hinduism.
  • He assumed the title of ‘Commander of the Prophet’ (Paigamber -Ka-Senapati).
  • His opponents called him ‘enemy of Islam’ and gave the Slogan of ‘Islam is in danger’.

Chapter 19

Tughluq Dynasty

32 facts · 14 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (66 points)
  • Among the generals of Alauddin, Ghiyasuddin Tughluq or Ghazi Malik became the first ruler of the Tughluq dynasty.
  • He established the Tughluq dynasty.
  • His mother was a Hindu Jat woman and his father was a Qaraunah Turk who was a slave of Balban.
  • Ghiyasuddin Tughluq was the chief of several important campaigns during Alauddin Khalji’s reign and he was appointed as the governor of Dipalpur.
  • He earned the epithet 'Ghazi Malik' for repeated frontier fighting against the Mongols; Barani credits him with 20 routs while Ibn Battuta claims 29 victories.
  • He took control of Delhi’s throne by defeating Khusrau Shah and in 1320 AD, he became Sultan.
  • He was also known as Ghazi Beg Tughluq or Ghazi Tughluq. Because of this, his successors were known as ‘Tughluq’ and his lineage was called Tughluq Dynasty.
  • During the time of Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, tax from farmers
11
to be collected wasorof the yield. In case of famine,
1011
  • land tax was collected with regard to capacity to pay. Tax-free jagirs were granted to the Government employees without giving any share in the revenue.
  • The harsh punishments of the Alauddin's time were abolished, but those who did not pay taxes, the dishonest ones with the government money and the thieves were severely punished.
  • Among all the sultans of Delhi Sultanate, Muhammad-Bin Tughluq (1325-1351 A.D.) was the most learned and educated ruler.
  • He was well versed in many disciplines including astronomy, mathematics, medicine etc.
  • Muhammad-Bin Tughluq established a new department, Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi, for the advancement of agriculture.
  • The main work of this department was to provide more support to the farmers and bring more land under agricultural work.
  • A long piece of land measuring about 30 karohs × 30 karohs was chosen for it.
  • One of the most important experiments of Muhammad Tughluq was to move the capital to Daulatabad (Devgiri) from Delhi.
  • According to Dr. K.A. Nizami, Sultan Qutbuddin Mubarak Khalji named Devgiri as Qutbabad and Muhammad Tughluq named it Daulatabad.
  • Muhammad-Bin Tughluq had inscribed a sentence on his coins, ‘Al Sultan Zilli Allah’ (Sultan is the shadow of God), ‘God is the supporter of Sultan’.
  • Golden coins issued by Muhammad-Bin Tughluq were called ‘Dinar’ by Ibn Battuta.
  • Barani describes five major policies of Muhammad Tughluq-

(1) Tax increase in Doab,

(2) Making Devgiri (Daulatabad) new capital,

(3) Issuing token currency,

(4) Planned expedition to Khurasan and

(5) Qarachil Expedition.

  • Ibn Battuta (1304-77 AD) was an African traveller of Moroccan origin.
  • He came to India during 1333-42 AD. in the reign of Muhammad-Bin Tughluq (1325-51 A.D.).
  • Muhammad-Bin Tughluq appointed him as the Qazi of Delhi. Later in 1342 AD, he was sent to China as an ambassador of the Sultan.
  • Ibn Battuta presented the details of his journey in his book Kitab-ul-Rihla.
  • Details of the postal system were known from Ibn Batuta’s travelogue.
  • Muhammad-Bin Tughluq is accussed by Isami that he was the first sultan of Delhi who used to participate in the festival of Hindus, mainly on Holi.
  • He also appointed non-Turks and Indian Muslims to government posts. Due to this, Barani harshly criticized him for promoting low-born people/low-occupation persons like gardener, weaver, barber, cook, etc.
  • Muhammad-Bin Tughluq died on March 20, 1351. On his death, Badayuni wrote, “The king was freed from his people, and the people from their king”
  • Firuz Shah Tughluq started some welfare programmes for the benefit of common people.
  • After opening an office (employment office) for the appointment of the individual through investigating the qualifications and merit of each individual and giving appointments to as many people as possible - he tried to solve the problem of unemployment.
  • Firuz Shah Tughluq used to donate property to the saints and religious people. He had established a department ‘Diwan-i-Khairat’, which provided financial assistance to the poor Muslims, orphaned women and widows, and arranged marriages for poor Muslim girls.
  • Firuz Tughluq was the first Indian ruler to arrange Hajj at state expenditure. He also established a Khairati hospital called ‘Dar-ul-Shafa/Shifa’ where skilled Haqim were employed.
  • Firuz Shah Tughluq was very fond of the slaves.
  • There were approximately one lakh eighty thousand slaves working under Firuz Tughluq.
  • A separate department (‘Diwan-i-Bandagan’) was formed for caring of them.
  • He established a Public Work Department.
  • It is said that Firuz built 200 new cities. Fatehabad, Hisar, Firozpur, Jaunpur, Firozabad etc. were prominent towns established by him. According to the Firista, Firuz had constructed 40 mosques, 30 schools, 20 palaces, 100 Inns, 200 towns, 100 hospitals, 5 Makabara, 100 public bathrooms, 10 pillars and 150 bridges.
  • His chiefarchitect was Malik Ghazi Shahana.
  • The plan and proposal of each building were presented before ‘Diwan-i-Wajarat’ with its expenditure estimate, and only then the required money could be released.
  • Firuz Tughluq’s reign became famous for constructing the largest network of canals in India.
  • To facilitate irrigation, he constructed five major canals.
  • He was the first Sultan of Delhi who imposed irrigation tax named ‘Haqq-i-Sharb’ after seeking the opinion from the Ulemas.
  • The farmers who used to use the royal canals for irrigation had to give 1/10 portion of their produce to the government.
  • Jizya was imposed on Brahmins by Firuz Tughluq.
  • It is noteworthy that by that time Brahmins were kept free from this tax.
  • Firuz Shah Tughluq planted 1200 new gardens near Delhi due to his interest in horticulture and rehabilitated thirty old orchards of Alauddin period. He also made measures to improve the quality of fruits in his orchards.
  • Two Pillars (Stambh) of Ashoka were brought to Delhi from Meerut and Topra (now in Yamuna Nagar district of Haryana) by Firuz Shah Tughluq.
  • The Topara Pillar (Stambh) was re established near the palace and the mosque of Firozabad.
  • The Pillar (Stambh) of Meerut was re-installed near the current Bara Hindu Rao Hospital of Delhi.
  • Sultan Firuz Tughluq of Delhi had commissioned Sanskrit scholars at his court to translate some sanskrit works into persian, often associated with translation of 300 sanskrit manuscripts collected from Jawalamukhi temple into persian.
  • Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah (1394 - 1412 AD) was the last ruler of the Tughluq dynasty. During his reign, Khwaja Jahan established an independent state of Jaunpur.
  • Another grandson of Firuz, Nusrat Shah challenged Nasiruddin.
  • As a result, Tughluq dynasty was divided into two parts, and both claimants ruled the shrunk kingdom of Delhi simultaneously.
  • Nasiruddin stayed in Delhi and Nusrat Shah in Firozabad. During the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah, Timur, the Great Turk (Turco-Mongol) General of Central Asia, invaded India (1398 AD).
  • This statement was famous with respect to Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah - ‘The sultanate of Shahanshah extends from Delhi to Palam'.
  • Timur’s invasion (1398 AD) destroyed the Delhi and started the fall of the Tughluq dynasty.
  • With the death of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah, the Tughluq dynasty ended in 1412 AD. The warlords of Delhi elected Daulat Khan as Sultan of Delhi in 1413 AD.
  • But he was defeated by Khizr Khan.
  • Khizr Khan was the Subedar of Multan, appointed by Timur and later granted him control over Lahore and Dipalpur.
  • In 1414 AD, he took control of Delhi after the invasion of Timur and laid the foundations of a new lineage Sayyid Dynasty started. He did not assume the title of Sultan.

Chapter 20

Lodi Dynasty

8 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (21 points)
  • Lodi Dynasty was established by Bahlul Khan Lodi in 1451 AD.
  • He sat on the throne of Delhi as ‘Bahlul Shah Ghazi’ and got Khutba proclaimed in his name.
  • His most important victory was over Jaunpur. Bahlul Lodi did not treat Hindus with religious fanaticism. Many reputed Hindu Sardars were in his court; Rai Karan Singh, Rai Pratap Singh, Rai Nar Singh, Rai Trilokchandra and Rai Dadu. He introduced ‘Bahlul coin’ which was the main means of exchange prior to Akbar.
  • Bahlul Lodi appointed his third son, Nizam Khan, as his successor prior to his death, but some of the chiefs opposed him because his mother (Jaiband/Bibi Ambha) was the daughter of a goldsmith.
  • Some powerful warlords joined Nizam Khan and he sat on the throne as Sultan Sikandarshah on 17 July, 1489 AD. He was the greatest ruler of the Lodi dynasty.
  • Sikandar Lodi, in 1504 AD, established a new city called Agra along the Yamuna River to command eastern Rajasthan and routes towards Malwa/Gujarat and made Agra his capital. Sikandar Lodi was a very hard- working, generous but religiously orthodox.
  • He worked for the improvement and advancement of agriculture and trade.
  • The measurement scale used for land ‘Gaj-i-Sikandari’ was started at that time. He arranged free meals for the poor.
  • He prohibited ‘Tazia’ in Muharram and banned Muslim women from visiting ‘Peers’and ‘Mazaars’.
  • During his reign, a list was made of qualified and skilled persons and was presented every six months before him.
  • He was an educated and learned person.
  • He ordered an Ayurvedic treatise to be translated into Persian and named it ‘Farhange Sikandari’.
  • Lajjat-i-Sikandarshahi’, a masterpiece of singing, was composed during his reign.
  • Sikandar Lodi was very fond of hearing Shehnai.
  • He used to write poems under the nickname ‘Gulrukhi’.
  • Sultan Sikandar abolished the octrai duty on grain.
  • There was a battle between Maharana Sanga and Ibrahim Lodi at Khatauli in 1518 AD.
  • Ibrahim Lodi was defeated in this battle.
  • The first battle of Panipat took place between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi on 21 April, 1526 A.D.
  • Ibrahim was defeated and killed on the battle- field.
  • According to Nayamatullah (Niyamatullah), besides Sultan Ibrahim, no other Sultan of India was killed on the battlefield.

Afghan-origin Sultanate dynasty → Lodi (1451-1526 A.D.), last Delhi Sultanate dynasty; ended when Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi at First Panipat (1526).

Chapter 21

Vijayanagara Empire

35 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (53 points)
  • The Vijayanagara Empire was established by Harihara-I and Bukka-I in 1336 AD. Their lineage was called Sangama Dynasty as their father’s name was Sangama.
  • Harihara and Bukka were feudataries of the Kakatiyas of Warangal. After the fall of Warangal at the hands of Delhi Sultans, they shifted to Kampili and become ministers.
  • When Muhammad Tughluq conquered the Kampili, he imprisoned Harihara and Bukka. It is believed that they accepted Islam religion. They were later sent as Tughluq army commanders towards South. Harihara and Bukka came to Kampili with Tughluq's force and suppressed Kampili revolt. Eventually, they became Hindu again, coming under the influence of a Saint Vidyaranya.
  • Harihara and Bukka had taken learning from their teacher(Guru) Vidyaranya and famous mentor of the Vedas, Sayan, to establish Vijayanagara.
  • Four dynasties of this empire - Sangam dynasty (1336 - 1485 A.D.), Saluva dynasty (1485 - 1505 A.D.), Tuluva dynasty (1505 - 1570 A.D.) and Aravidu dynasty (1570-1672 A.D.).
  • The capitals of the Vijayanagara empire were - Anegundi, Vijayanagara, Penukonda, and Chandragiri and later Vellore.
  • In 1365, the Vijayanagar army under Kumara Kampana (son of Bukka I) completed the conquest of Pandyan country (Madhurai region) by about 1370.
  • Kumara Kampana conquered Madurai and merged it into Vijayanagara Empire.
  • His wife Gangadevi has made a living description of her husband’s victory in her book ‘Madhura Vijayam’.
  • Kumara Kampana was the son of Bukka Rai I.
  • After Bukka’s death in 1377 A.D., his son, Harihara II, sat on the throne.
  • He assumed the title of ‘Maharajadhiraja’.
  • He won the states of Kanara, Mysore, Trichinapalli, Kanchi, etc and rulers such as Ceylon are described as sending ambassadors and annual rich presents. The biggest success of Harihara II was to capture Belgaum and Goa of the Bahamani state in the west.
  • He was a worshiper of Virupaksha Shiva.
  • Samant Narasimha Saluva of Chandragiri removed the last ruler of the Sangama dynasty, Praudha Deva Raya, in 1485 A.D. and took control of the throne and established a new dynasty ‘Saluva Dynasty’.
  • Vira Narasimha removed the son of Narasimha Saluva (Immadi Narasimha, the last ruler of the Saluva dynasty) from the throne, took control of the throne and laid the foundation of the Tuluva dynasty. His younger brother Krishnadeva Raya (1509-1529 AD) sat on the throne after the death of Veer Narasimha.
  • Krishnadeva Raya, the ruler of Vijayanagara, fought the battle of Golconda with Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda.
  • The army of Qutb Shahi was defeated.
  • The reign of Krishnadeva Raya is considered to be a classical era of Telugu literature in Vijayanagara.
  • Eight Telugu poets of his court were regarded as eight pillars of his literary assembly and known as Ashtadiggajas.
  • Therefore, his reign was also called the golden age of Telugu literature.
  • Krishnadeva Raya had assumed the title of ‘Andhra Bhoj’.
  • Krishnadeva Raya himselfwas a poet and writer of outstanding ability.
  • His main composition- ‘Amuktamalyada’, is one of the five epics of Telugu language.
  • He established Nagalapuram town.
  • He also constructed temples like ‘Hazara Rama’ and ‘Vitthala (Shree Vijaya Vitthala)’.
  • During his time, the Portuguese traveller 'Domingo Paes’ travelled to the Vijayanagara empire.
  • Babur, in his autobiography, described Krishnadeva Raya as the most powerful ruler of India.
  • Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq came to Vijayanagara during the reign of Devaraya II, the most august ruler of the Sangama dynasty.
  • The translation of Mahabharata in Telugu was started by Nannaya in the 11th century, which was completed by Tikkana in the 13th century and again by the Yerranna in the 14th century.
  • These three are famous as the 'Kavitrayi' of Telugu literature.
  • In the famous Battle of Talikota, the combined forces offour Deccan sultanates (Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar, Golconda) defeated Vijayanagara in January 1565 AD.
  • Barar was not included in that combined Forces. According to the Firista, this battle was fought in Talikota, but the actual area of war was situated between two villages named Rakshasi and Tangadi.
  • During the Battle of Talikota, the ruler of Vijayanagara was Sadashiva Raya but the real power was in the hands of his minister Rama Raya.
  • Hussain Nizamashah killed Rama Raya in this battle.
  • Tirumal after dethroning Sadashiva in Penukonda, sat on the throne and laid the foundation of the Aravidu Dynasty (1570-1672 AD).
  • His successor was Shri Rang-I.
  • Venkata II became the ruler after Rang I.
  • He made Chandragiri his headquarters.
  • It was the last dynasty in the series of great rulers of Vijayanagara.
  • Venkata II a was contemporary of King Wodeyar, who established the kingdom of Mysore in 1612.
  • The main source of revenue in Vijayanagara empire was the taxes on the land/farm. The land was well-surveyed. Normally, the land tax was one-third to one-sixth of the yield. It depends upon land category and crop quality. The tax named ‘Shist’ (Rai-rekha) was the main source of state income.
  • Central Department of Revenue was called ‘Athavane’ (Asthvan or Athvan).
  • The present name of the Dwarasamudra, the capital of the Hoysala Dynasty, is Halebidu, which is in Hassan district of Karnataka.
  • Its reputation is because of its heritage architecture.
  • Among the Halebidu temples, the ancient temple of Hoysaleshwara is very famous.
  • This temple belongs to 12th - 13th century.
  • During the reign of Hoysala ruler Narasimha I, the architect Kedroz constructed the temple under the supervision of Chief Officer of the Public Works Department, Ketamal.
  • Chennakeshava temple, built in Hoysala period, is located in Belur. This temple was built by Vishnuvardhana, the ruler of the Hoysala dynasty.
  • The ruins of Hampi (located in the present Central Karnataka) represent the ancient capital of the Vijayanagara Empire.
  • The Virupaksha Temple was built in the Vijayanagara period in 7th century CE and is located right here.
  • Hampi is also included in the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
  • The Vitthal Temple (Hampi) was built by Krishnadeva Raya (1509 - 1529 A.D.), and continued under Achyuntaraya, one of the great rulers of the Tuluva dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire.

Chapter 22

Delhi Sultanate: Administration

26 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (34 points)
  • Sultans of the Slave Dynasty ruled from 1206 to 1290 AD.
  • Khalji Dynasty ruled from 1290 to 1320 AD.
  • The rulers of the Tughluq Dynasty ruled from 1320 to 1414 AD. Sayyid Dynasty ruled from 1414 to 1451 AD.
  • The rulers of Lodi Dynasty ruled from 1451 to 1526 AD. During Sultanate period, rule of Tughluq dynasty was the longest.
  • Most of the Sultans and Amirs were Turks.
  • Sultan was the head of central government. Similarly, during the Sultanate Period, those often employed in all the influential positions were called the Amir. These Amirs had a great effect when the Sultan was ineligible and weak or under-age.
  • Administrative departments and the rulers who started these departments are as follows –
  • Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (Department of Revenue) - Alauddin Khalji
  • Diwan-i-Riyasat (Department of Market Control) - Alauddin Khalji
  • Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi (Agriculture Department) - Muhammad- Bin Tughluq
  • Diwan-i-Khairat (Charity Department) - Firuz Tughluq
  • Diwan-i-Bandagan - Firuz Tughluq
  • Diwan-i-Arz was related to Army Department
  • Diwan-i-Risalat was related to religious issues and to overseeing foreign affairs.
  • Diwan-i-Insha was related to Government Correspondence
  • Diwan-i-Wizarat was related to financial matters/revenue department.
  • Wizarat was an institution recognized by the Islamic administration. During the reign of Mahmud Ghazni (in Ghaznavid administration), Abbas Fazal - Bin-Ahmad, who was skilled in governing the administration, became the first wazir.
  • The prime minister of the state was called Wazir.
  • Wazir was mainly the chief of revenue department (Diwan-i-Wizarat). From this point of view, he used to take care of Lagaan, tax system, donations and, military expenditures etc.
  • Tughluq period was the golden period of Indian Muslim Wizarat. At the time of Firuz Tughluq, the post of the Wazir reached its peak position.
  • Army organization and the division of posts were done on the basis of the decimal system.
  • The head of the troop of the horsemen was called ‘Sarkhel’.
  • There was a ‘Sipahsalar’ above ten Sarkhels, one ‘Amir’ above ten Sipahsalars, one ‘Malik’ above ten Amirs and one ‘Khan’ over ten Maliks.
  • Sultan was the Chief Commander of the army.
  • Firuz Tughluq levied taxes, keeping the laws of the Islam in mind.
  • He permitted four taxes approved in the Quran - Kharaj, Jizya, Khums and Zakat. Khums was the one-fifth share of looted money.
  • In the war, the enemies of the state were looted by his people. 4/5 part of this loot was distributed among the soldiers, and the remaining 1/5 was deposited in the treasury, but Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq kept 4/5 in the treasury, and the remaining 1/5 was divided among the soldiers. In the Sultanate period, the smallest unit of governance was village and, main village functionaries were Khut, Muqaddam and Patwari, working in close coordination with muqti for revenue collection.
  • Chaudhary was the highest official of land revenue at the village level.
  • The Sultanate period had two major currencies - Jital and Tanka.
  • Iltutmish was the first Turk ruler, who introduced Arabic coins.
  • He introduced the two main coins namely Tanka of silver, and Jital of copper.
  • The ratio of Tanka and Jital was 1: 48.
  • The name of the last Khalifa of Baghdad was first mentioned on the coin of Alauddin Masood Shah (1242 - 46 AD).
  • The last Khalifa of Baghdad was Khalifa-al-Mustasim (1242 - 58 AD ). The name of Khalifa-al-Mustansir was mentioned on coins of Iltutmish. Hadees was an Islamic law, while the Zawabit was related to state law.

  • Iltutmish built Sultangarhi, Hauz-e-Shamsi, Shamsi Eidgaah, Jama Masjid Shamsi (Badayun). Atarkin-ka-Darwaza (Nagaur) etc. Alauddin Khalji built Alai Darwaza near the Qutub Minar. It was built with red sandstones and white marble, and it was completed in 1311 AD.

  • The tomb of Sultan Balban, located in Mehrauli, New Delhi, built by himself, was the first tomb built in a purely Indo-Islamic style in India.
  • Ghiyasuddin Tughluq (1320 - 25 AD), after the foundation of the Tughluq dynasty, established a city in Delhi and named it ‘Tughluqabad’.
  • The Moth Masjid was built during the reign of Sikandar Lodi.
  • Sikandar Lodi’s tomb was built by Sultan Ibrahim Lodi. Kirti Stambha was built by Rana Kumbha after his victory over Malwa. It was built under the supervision of Jaita while Atri and Mahesh were its panegyrists.

Key facts from the book (13 points)
  • Abul Hassan Yaminuddin Khusrau, often called Amir Khusrau, was born in 1253 AD at Patiyali in present-day Kasganj district in Uttar Pradesh. Khusrau was called ‘Tuti- i - Hind’.
  • Some of his famous compositions were Miftah-ul-Futuh, Khazain ul-Futuh (Tarikh-i-Alai), Ashika, Nuh Sipihr and Tughluq namah. He referred to himself as a 'Turkish-Indian'.
  • Amir Khusrau himself said that he knew, Sanskrit and other Indian languages, which are a part of Hindavi.
  • In India, Amir Khusrau was the originator of the early form of the musical genre known as Qawwali.
  • New Persian poetry style, ‘Sabk - i - Hindi’ or Hindustani style, was started by Amir Khusrau.
  • Musical instruments ‘Tabla’ and ‘Sitar’ were made prevalent in the 13th/14th century by Amir Khusrau.
  • The development of Persian literature in India started with the advent of Muslims.
  • After the establishment of Delhi Sultanate, the Persian language was granted the status of official language.
  • Tabakat-i-Nasiri is a treatise of Minhaj-us-Siraj (Minhaj i-Siraj) dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud.
  • Ziauddin Barani composed the ‘Tarik -i-Firozshahi’and ‘Taj-ul-Masir’ was written by Sadruddin Muhammad Hassan Nizami.
  • Yahiya Bin Ahmad Sarhindi wrote ‘Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi’, which is the principal source regarding the history of Sayyid rulers under the patronage of Sayyid Mubarakshah.
  • Rana Kumbha was a patron of music, literature and art. He wrote texts on music, Sangeet Raja (also known as Sangita Mimansa).
  • The Tughluq dynasty ruler Firuz Shah Tughluq wrote his memoir as Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi.

32 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (32 points)
  • Jaunpur was founded by Firuz Shah Tughluq in memory of his cousin Jauna Khan (Muhammad-Bin Tughluq).
  • Jaunpur became an independent state during the reign of Sultan Mahmud Shah II (1394.).
  • It was established by Malik Sarwar, who founded the independent Sharqi Kingdom. Malik Sarwar was a slave of Muhammad Shah II.
  • Sultan gave him the title of Malik-Us Sharq (the Lord of the East) and Khwaja-i-Jahan.
  • Sharqi rulers continued Jaunpur’s independence for nearly 85 years but in 1479 A.D., Bahlul Lodi defeated its last ruler Hussain Shah Sharqi and made Jaunpur a part of Delhi Sultanate again.
  • Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (1402 - 1440 AD) (as per Gazetteer of Jaunpur) was the greatest ruler of the Sharqi Dynasty of Jaunpur.
  • During his reign, a new type of style emerged, which was called ‘Sharqi style’.
  • During this time, the cultural fame of Jaunpur spread all around and the state became famous as the ‘Siraz-i-Hind’(Siraz of India).
  • Vidyapati has beautifully described Jaunpur and Ibrahim Shah in ‘Kirtilata Kavya’.
  • Ali Shah’s brother Shahi Khan sat on the throne of Kashmir as Zain-ul-Abidin in 1420 A.D. He became the greatest ruler of Kashmir.
  • He abolished ‘Jizya’ and banned cow slaughter. He got "Mahabharata" & "Rajtarangini" translated in Persian language.
  • ‘Zaina Lank’ island was built by Zain-ul-Abidin in ‘Wular Lake’. Zain-ul-Abidin (1420-70 AD) is called ‘Akbar of Kashmir’ due to religious tolerance and good deeds.
  • Zafar Khan declared himself Sultan of Gujarat in 1407 AD, adopting the name ‘Sultan Muzaffar Shah’.
  • He defeated the ruler of Malwa, Hoshang Shah and occupied Dhar, but later he returned his kingdom.
  • Later, Fateh Khan sat on the throne in 1458 AD.
  • He took the title of ‘Abul Fateh Mahmood’, but in history he became famous as Mahmud Begada.
  • His main victories were the forts of Champaner and Girnar.
  • Bahmani Kingdom was founded during the Muhammad-bin Tughluq’s reign as a result of the rebellion of Amiran-e-Sadah in Deccan.
  • Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu, 1347 - 1358 AD) a Sardar in 1347 AD, assuming the title of Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, sat on the throne and laid the foundation of the Bahmani kingdom.
  • He made Gulbarga the capital of his newly established kingdom and named it Hasanabad.
  • To govern his empire, he divided it into four provinces of Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar and Bidar.
  • Ibrahim Adilshah II, the ruler of Bijapur, was a skillful administrator, poet and a generous patron of arts.
  • His people used to address him with the title of ‘Jagatguru’ due to his generous and broad (tolerant) approach. He was also called ‘Ablababa’or ‘Friend of the poor’because of his nature of helping the poor.
  • Ibrahim Adil Shah II composed music collection ‘Kitab-i-Nauras’.
  • In the same era, Firishta had completed the work of a famous historic book named ‘Tarikh-i-Firishta’.
  • Ibrahim established a new capital, Naurasapur city.
  • The mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah of Bijapur is known as ‘Gol Gumbaz’. It is one of the largest historic buildings in India and one of the world’s largest domes.
  • Gujari Mahal was built by King Man Singh Tomar between 1486-1516 A.D. century. Currently, Gujari Mahal is converted into Museum.

Chapter 27

Bhakti and Sufi Movement

89 facts · 11 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (102 points)
  • Devotional Worship had a long history of almost a thousand years across the subcontinent. The early medieval Bhakti movement originated in Dravida region and began to spread to the north during the late medieval ages (13th-14th centuries onwards) when north India was under Islamic rule.
  • Some of the earliest Bhakti movements (6th Century) were led by Vaishnava Alvars and Nayanars of South (Shaiva). Bhakti Movement spread with the rise of the great philosopher Adi Shankaracharya in South India in 8th century who propagated pure monism ‘Advaitavada’.
  • Bhakti Movement was reborn in the 15th-16th century A.D. when the Kabir, Nanak, Tulsi, Sur, Meerabai etc. encouraged the movement.
  • In medieval India, the emergence of Sufis helped in promoting harmony in society.
  • They used to do meditation and practised spiritual disciplines such as remembrance and devotional practices like 'Sama' and sometimes breath-focused remembrance.
  • Sufism originated within Islam and later some strands developed theosophical systems adopting tradition such as Neoplatonism and other currents. Some believe that four philosophies influenced the Sufism –

(1) Advaitavada and Vishishta Dvaitavada of Aryans

(2) New Aflatuni theory

(3) Liberal thinking

(4) Deep rooted knowledge of Islam

They took the help of holy songs and music to spread unity and harmony in society and to arouse a state of spiritual ecstasy in their audience.

  • Kamarupa was an ancient Indian state situated roughly in Assam. Vaishnavism in Kamarupa was popularized by Shankaradeva, the founder of Ekasarana sect. They stressed devotion to one deity–krishna (identified with Vishnu). They also opposed both rituals and idolatry. They were known as Chaitanya of Assam.
  • Shuddha Advaitavada is the “purely non-dual” philosophy propounded by Shri Vallabhacharya, the founder and guru of the Vallabha sect. Vallabhacharya was the son of Telugu Brahmin Shri Lakshmana Bhatta of Somyazi clan, who is said to have developed the views of Vishnu Swami into Shuddha Advaita or pure non-dualism.
  • The founder of ‘Dvaitavada’ was Madhvacharya.
  • Nimbarkacharya was the founder of ‘Dvaitadvaitavada (Dvait-Advait Vad)’ and Ramanujacharya was the founder of ‘Vishishtadvaitavad’. Nimbarkacharya is related to the ‘Sanaka’ sect.
  • Ramananda was the promoter of the Bhakti Movement in northern India. He was born in the Kanyakubja Brahmin family of Prayaga (Prayagraj) in 1299 AD.
  • These used to believe in ‘Saguna’ God.
  • He was the first Bhakti saint who promoted his messages in the Hindi language.
  • Kabir (1398 - 1518 AD) was one of the 12 disciples of Ramananda. He was born near Varanasi to a widowed Brahmin and grew up with a weaver couple Neeru and Neema.
  • ‘Bijak’ is a compilation of the works of Saint Kabir. It is a holy book of those who believe in the Kabirpanthi sect.
  • 'Sabad', 'Sakhi' and 'Ramaini' are compositions of Kabir but his dialogues with Dharmadasa are found in the book ‘Amarmul/Anurag Sagar'.
  • Saint Malukdasa was born in the family of Lala Sundar Das Khatri in 1574 AD in Kada (present-day Kaushambi district of Uttar Pradesh).
  • Guru Ghasidas was born on 18 December 1756 AD in Giraudpuri village in Balodabazar-Bhatapara district of Chhattisgarh.

12 Jyotirlingas devoted to lord Shiva are found in different parts of India.

These are - Kedarnath, Vishwanath, Vaidyanath, Mahakaleshwara, Omkareshwara, Nageshwara, Somnath, Trayambakeshwara, Grishneshwara, Bhimashankara, Mallikarjun Swami and Rameshwaram.

  • Guru Nanak was born in Talwandi in Punjab in 1469 AD. Now this place is called ‘Nankana Sahib’.
  • It is located in Nankana Sahib district of western Punjab (now in Pakistan).
  • Guru Nanak died in 1539 AD at Kartarpur (present day in Pakistan).
  • Guru Nanak (1469 - 1539 AD) was the founder of Sikh religion during the reign of Sikandar Lodi (1489 - 1517 AD).
  • Nanak believed in monotheism and emphasized the worship of the one formless God (IK Onkar).
  • Guru Nanak says, "God doesnot ask about social class or birth; you must find your true home."
  • Guru Nanak started the community kitchen known as ‘Guru Ka Langar’. The followers used to eat together without paying any attention to the caste.
  • Mirabai was the only daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore of Merta.
  • She was born in village Kudaki of Merta in 1498 AD. She was married to Prince Bhojraja, the eldest son of famous ruler Rana Sanga of Mewar.
  • Namdev had an important role in popularizing the Bhakti movement in Maharashtra.
  • He was born in Narsi Village (Maharashtra) in 1270 AD. Visoba Khechar was his teacher. He belonged to the Varkari sect.
  • Visoba Khechar had him educated for mystical life and introduced the omnipresent nature of God. Namdev said that “a stone is worshipped, the other is walked upon, if one is God, then the other must also be a God.”
  • The time period of Dadu Dayal was from 1544 AD to 1603 AD.
  • The time period of Tyagraja was from 1767 AD to 1847 AD. He was a devotee poet of Bhakti path and was a great musician of Carnatic music.
  • The famous Saint Mahaprabhu Chaitanya (1486 - 1534 A.D.) of Bhakti Movement was born in Nadia district of Bengal in a Brahmin family.
  • His father’s name was Jagannatha Mishra and his mother’s name was Shachi Devi.
  • Chaitanya’s childhood name was Nimai (Vishwambhar Mishra).
  • Chaitanya was a follower of Lord Krishna.
  • Famous devotee /saint Goswami Tulsidas was contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir.
  • Tulsidas wrote many texts in which Ramcharitmanasa and Vinaya patrika are the major work.
  • ‘Ramcharitmanas’ was composed by Goswami Tulsidas (1532-1623 A.D.) in Awadhi language.
  • Sufism was born in a foreign land within early Islamic asceticism but it was mainly influenced by Indian Vedanta philosophy later.
  • Chishtiya order of Sufi was founded by Abu Ishaq Sami Chishti and his disciple Khwaja Abu Ahmad Abdal in Chishti Sharif of Afghanistan.
  • But, it was primarily promoted by Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti in India.
  • He came to India with Muhammad Ghori’s Army in 1192 AD (12th century).
  • He made his residence in Ajmer (Rajasthan).
  • He died in 1236 AD.
  • Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki was his main disciple. Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti became a disciple of Khwaja Usman Chishti Haruni at Nishapur.
  • Shaikh Fariduddin - Ganj-i-Shakar was a Sufi saint of Chishti order who was popular as Baba Farid.
  • Chishtia order gained more popularity in India due to his efforts.
  • Some of Baba Farid's compositions were included by Guru Arjan in the Adi Granth Sahib. He was the son-in-law of Balban.
  • He was the spiritual teacher of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya.
  • Alauddin Sabir Kaliyari was his other prominent disciple.
  • Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya’s Dargah is located in Delhi.
  • Nizamuddin Auliya died in 1325 AD.
  • He was buried in Ghiyaspur (Delhi)
  • Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya saw the reign of more than seven sultans, who came to power one after the other, but he never went to anyone’s court.
  • When Alauddin asked him to meet, Shaikh replied that 'there are two gates in my house ifSultan comes through one, then I will go out by the other'. Thus, he refused to meet Alauddin.
  • He was popularly known as Mehboob-i-Elahi and ‘Sultan-ul-Mashaikh’ (King of Saints).
  • Shaikh Salim Chishti’s name is notable in the last Sufis of Chishti Branch. His father’s name was Shaikh Bahauddin.
  • He lived in Arabia for several years and was conferred with the title of ‘Shaikh-Ul-Hind’. After that, he returned to India and stayed at a place called Sikri, which was about 37 km from Agra. The place was later developed by Akbar as Fatehpur Sikri.
  • It is said that Jahangir was born with the blessings of Shaikh Salim Chishti.
  • The impact of Chishti order was in Delhi, Rajasthan, and neighbouring areas while the influence of the Suhrawardi order was extended in the region of Sindh and Punjab.
  • Firdausi order traces its origins to Najmuddinkubra and is treated as a collateral line of the Suhrawardiya; it later had close relation with Chishtis in India which had influence in the areas of Bihar.
  • Shaikh Muhiuddin Qadir Jilani of Baghdad was the founder of the Qadiriyya order (Qadiri) and was considered as one of the great saints of Islam.
  • The main titles of Shaikh Abdul Qadir Jailani were - ‘Mehboob-i-Sumani’ (God’s lover), ‘Piran-i Pir’ (Chief of Pirs), ‘Pir-i-Dastagir’ (Helpful Saint) etc. This order was promoted by Shah Niyamatullah in Deccan and Kashmir and Makhdum Jilani in Punjab.
  • Makhdoom Jilani made Uchha as his education centre.
  • Naqshbandi order was established by Khwaja Bahauddin Naqshband in the 14th century.
  • Khwaja Khawand Mahmud was a prominent saint of this branch who came to India and made Kashmir his centre. This order was majorly propagated by Khwaja Baqi Billah (1563-1603), who came from Kabul with the orders of his master.
  • Shaikh Ahmed Sirhindi, also known as ‘Mujaddid’, the reformer of Islam is religion, was his main disciple. He propounded ‘Wahadat-ul-Shuhud’ (positivist philosophy).
  • The Sirhindi/Mujaddadi Naqshbandi branch opposed Sama, but Ferozabadi (Delhi) branch practiced sama.
  • It was the most radical order among Sufis. They opposed Akbar’s liberal policies.
  • Aurangzeb had influence of this Sufi order.
  • Sufi Saint Shah Muhammad Ghaus has accepted Krishna as Wali/Auliya.
  • He was the most famous saint of Sattariyya order.
  • He had close relations with Mughal emperor Humayun and Tansen.
  • The famous composition of Muhammad Gaus is ‘Jawahir-i-Khamsa’ in which he expresses spiritual quest and mystical practices.
  • He has translated the book ‘Amritkund’ of Hatha Yoga by the name of ‘Bahar-al-Hayat’ in persian.
  • The place of residence of Sufi saints is called Khanqah.
  • ‘Sama’ is the name of a Sufi ceremony.
  • The person authorized to teach and guide Sufism was called Shaikh.
  • Scholars of religious laws of Islam are called ‘Ulema’.
  • ‘Premvatika’ was composed by Raskhan This text celebrates Krishna and the ideal of love/devotion.
  • 'Sujan Raskhan' is also famous text by Raskhan.
  • The language of Raskhan is pure Braj.
  • Barahmasa was written by 'Malik Muhammad Jayasi'. The Padmavat has an important place in the Hindi literature written by Jayasi. The other composition of Jayasi are ‘Akharawat’, 'Akhiri Kalam', etc.
  • Dewa Sharif, the Mazar of famous Sufi Saint Haji Waris Ali Shah, is situated in Barabanki, Uttar Pradesh.
  • Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem (south of Jerusalem).
  • Good Friday is celebrated by Christians as as remembrance to sacrificial death of Jesus Christ.
  • According to the Bible, Jesus Christ was crucified on Friday.
  • Saint Francis of Assisi (1181 or 82-1226 A.D.) is a Christian saint who was famous for his love towards birds and animals.
  • Vatican City is a sovereign state located in Europe.
  • Its total area is around 44 hectares, which is the world’s smallest (both population and area) independent country.
  • It is governed by the Bishop of Rome, also called the Pope.
  • It is also known as the capital of the Roman Catholic Church.
  • Medina is a city located in Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia.

Chapter 28

Mughal Dynasty:Babur

20 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (18 points)
  • The Mughal dynasty was of Turkic-Mongol origin and Babur belonged to Chagatai branch of Turks, which derived its name from the second son of Genghis Khan, ruler of central Asia and Turkistan.
  • The Full name of Babur was Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur. He was born on February 14, 1483 AD, to Umar Shaikh Mirza and Qutlugh Nigar Khanum at Ferghana. After the death of his father, he ascended the throne of Ferghana in June 1494 AD as eleven years and four months, old minor.
  • Shaybani Khan invaded Ferghana in 1501 A.D. and defeated Babur at battle of Sar-e-Pul. Babur fled to central-Asia. “Tulughuma” technique of Uzbeks was used by Shaybani Khan in the Battle of Sar-e-Pul in which Babur was defeated.
  • After winning Kabul in 1504 A.D. Babur renounced his ancestral title “Mirza” and assumed a new title, “Padshah”.
  • Alam Khan was the uncle of Ibrahim Lodhi. He invited Babur to invade India, claiming his right to the Delhi throne.
  • In 1524 A.D., during the 4th campaign of Babur, there was a bitter feud between Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi and Daulat Khan, the governor of Punjab. Ibrahim Lodi ordered Daulat Khan to visit his capital but Daulat Khan violated his orders and sent his son Dilawar Khan to Babur with a message to help him to dethrone Ibrahim Lodi and enthrone Alam Khan in place of him. It was a golden opportunity for Babur as he had already received the invitation of Rana Sanga, the king of Mewar. He was quite assured that the opportunity to conquer India had come.
  • The first Battle of Panipat was fought between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi on 21 April 1526 AD. Babur possessed specific military tactics. The vast artillery of Babur was one of the main reasons behind his victory. The army of Ibrahim Lodi lost the battle despite being greater in numbers. Ibrahim Lodi was killed in this battle. As a result, the entire area up to Delhi and Agra came under Babur’s control.
  • Babur declared himselfthe ruler on April 27, 1526 AD and founded the Mughal empire in India. Babur used Tulughma war technique in the first battle of Panipat. Ustad Ali Quli led the artillery and Mustafa commended the battalion ofgunners. Babur's generosity earned him the title of “Qalandar”. Cannons were used for the first time in India in the first Battle of Panipat.
  • Babur declared Jehad in the Battle of Khanwa. The battle of Khanwa was fought on March 16, 1527 AD, between Babur and Rana Sanga. Babur defeated Rana Sanga in this battle and assumed the title of Ghazi. In 1528 AD, Babur took control of Chanderi’s Fort. Medini Rai was killed in the war.
  • The Battle of Ghaghra took place between Babur and Mahmud Lodi in 1529 AD. Babur won the Battle. This was the last battle fought by Babur.
  • He governed through allocation offiefs/jagirs and paraganas, appointing nobles/princess to territorial charges to his vast empire.
  • The governance of Badakhshan was given to Humayun, The governance of Kabul, Qandahar and Multan was given to Kamran. Babur appointed different officers in the Punjab region (e.g. Lahore, Sialkot, Dipalpur had separate governors. Mir Yusuf Ali was appointed to Lahore.
  • The region of Rajasthan was not included in his empire as it was under the control of various Rajput rulers.
  • The founder of Mughal Empire, Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur wrote his autobiography containing various events of his life. It was named Tuzuk-i-Babri or Babur Nama.
  • Babur mentioned two Hindu empires in his autobiography,
  • i.e., Vijayanagara and Mewar (Chittor). The autobiography written by Babur has an important place among autobiographies all over the world. Babur Nama is written in the Chagatai Turkish language.
  • Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan translated Babur Nama in the Persian language by the order of Akbar.
  • The verse compositions written by Babur, are composed in “Diwan” (Diwan-i-Babur) i.e. a collection of his poems. He wrote “Mubaiyan’' in a new verse style i.e. Masnavi, which is a book of Muslim law. The text Risal-i-Usaj (Khat-i-Baburi) written by Babur is considered the most innovative style. The Mughal Emperor Babur’s army chief Mir Baqi built the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya.

Don't confuse Dilawar Khan was Daulat Khan's son, not Alam Khan's.

Key facts from the book (17 points)
  • Kamran, Askari, and Hindal were the sons of Babur and the half-brothers of Humayun. Humayun was the eldest son of Babur, born in Kabul in 1508 AD. His mother, Maham Begum was related to the Shia sect. Gulrukh Begum was the mother of Kamran and Askari whereas Dildar Begam was the mother of Hindal.
  • Humayun invaded Chunar Fort for the first time in 1532. Humayun besieged this fort for four months and, after that, Sher Khan accepted his supremacy. In addition to this, he invaded Kalinjar in 1531 AD and annexed Raisina Fort in 1535 AD.
  • The four significant major battles fought by Humayun are as follows- Devara (Daurah), Chausa, Kannauj and Sirhind. Humayun defeated Afghan rebels on the banks of Gomti at Daurah (Devara) in 1532 AD.
  • Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah in Battle of Chausa on 26 June 1539 AD, in which a water fetcher named Nizam saved his life. This victory against Humayun increased the prestige and power of Sher Shah (Sher Khan).
  • On 17 May 1540 AD Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah again in the Battle of Kannauj (Bilgram) and Humayun fled from one place to the other after this war.
  • Humayun occupied Delhi after the Battle of Sirhind on 22 June, 1555 AD.
  • Farid Khan who later became Sher Shah Suri, got his education from Jaunpur. He left his home in 1494 A.D. and came to Jaunpur for studies which was famous as “Siraj i-Hind” during that time.
  • Haji Begum had commissioned her husband Humayun's Tomb at Delhi (near Deen Panah) in 1565-1572 A.D. It is the first double dome mausoleum of Mughal Architecture. Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son Sayyid Muhammad were the architect of this tomb.
  • Sher Shah Suri had a significant role in Revenue reforms, Administrative reforms, Military Reforms and Currency system reforms. He introduced a different system for Bengal province. He divided the Bengal province into Sarkars (districts) and appointed a military official as Shiqdar to control.
  • A non-military official 'Amir-i-Bangala' was also appointed for assistance. Qazi Fajilat was appointed to this post.
  • Sher Shah introduced pure gold, silver and copper coins. His silver 'Rupee' coins weighed 178 grains, and copper's 'Daam' weighed 308 grains (20 gm). The exchange rate of Rupee and Daam was 1:
  • 64.
  • Sher Shah died on 22 May 1545 AD in Kalinjar. Kalinjar campaign was the last campaign of Sher Shah. Kirat Singh was the king of the Kalinjar at that time. Sher Shah Suri was extremely impressed by chivalry and courage of Rajputs during the battle of Marwar and said, “I would have lost the empire just for a handful of millet”.
  • The tomb of Sher Shah is in the middle of a tank.
  • This tomb is located at Sasaram in Bihar.
  • “Purana Quila” of Delhi is the inner citadel of Din-panah founded by Humayun (1533); Sher Shah renamed it Shergarh and added structures. Here, Qila-i-Kuhna mosque was built by Sher Shah.
  • Sher Shah introduced the system of “Patta” and “Qabuliyat” to help the peasants. The peasants were given “patta” by the central authority, in which the share of government was clearly mentioned. The peasants accepted it through “Qabuliyat”.

Humayun's half-brothers → Kamran, Askari, Hindal (sons of Babur); not Usman; Humayun = Babur's eldest son, born Kabul 1508, mother Maham Begum.

Chapter 30

Akbar

67 facts · 12 Must know

Key facts from the book (38 points)
  • Akbar was born on 15 October 1542 AD, in Amarkot at Raja Veersaal Palace.
  • Akbar was coronated at Kalanaur, present day in Gurdaspur district of Punjab, on 14th February 1556 AD. Akbar was less than 14 years old at that time. Shah Abdul Mali refused to join Akbar’s coronation. Humayun called him “Farjand” (son).
  • Bairam Khan was the guardian and regent of Akbar. Akbar appointed him as his “Wazir” and gave him title of "Khan-i-Khanan”.
  • Akbar had first established marital relations with “Kachhwaha” Rajputs. When Akbar was going to visit the Dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti, his route lay through the Rajput state of Amer. Its ruler, Raja Bihari Mal (Bharmal), with a view of safe guarding his position, offered his submission to Akbar at Sanganer and voluntarily proposed his daughter Princess Harkhabai marriage with him. Akbar accepted the offer and on his returning from Ajmer, married her in 1562. Thus Raja Bharmal was the first Rajput king to accept Akbar’s supremacy of his own accord. Salim (later, Jahangir), heir to the throne, was born of this wedlock on August 30, 1569 AD. at Fatehpur Sikri.
  • Akbar patronised Chishti sect, expressing his faith in Sufism. He frequently visited the Mausoleum of Khwaja Muinuddin Chisti at Ajmer.
  • He abolished Jizya, the pilgrimage tax in 1564 AD and 1563 AD respectively under his liberal religious policy.
  • He ordered that a man should marry only one wife and could marry another only when the first wife became barren.
  • Akbar killed Adham Khan, the son of Maham Anga in 1562 AD as he assassinated Akbar’s Prime Minister, Atgah Khan.
  • Durgavati was the custodian (in the name of her minor son) of the Hindu Kingdom of Gondwana. After the attack of Akbar (1564 A.D.), Durgavati was surrounded by the enemy and then she committed suicide.
  • Rao Chandrasena of Marwar fought against the Mughal army at Bhadrajun in 1565 A.D., but he fled away to Siwana as he was surrounded from all sides. Rao annexed Sojat in 1579 A.D.. Akbar again besieged him, but he fled away on hills and died in 1581 A.D.
  • The main aim of Akbar's fighting the Battle of Haldighati was to subdue Rana Pratap and compel him to accept Mughal Suzerainty. In April 1576 AD, he deputed Man Singh to lead a force of about 5000 soldiers against Maharana Pratap. Man Singh reached through the route of Mandalgarh to Gogundagarh which was fourteen miles away from Haldighati, Rana Pratap also descended from the hills to face the Mughal army. The Battle that took place is famous as the Battle of Haldighati in which Rana was defeated and sought refuge in Aravalli Hills. Mewar did not accept the supremacy of Akbar willingly. Rana Pratap of Mewar continued his struggle against Akbar for a long time. After the death of Rana Pratap, his son Rana Amar Singh signed a treaty with Jahangir in 1615 AD.
  • When Prince Salim started behaving as independent King at Allahabad (Prayagraj) and became rebellious, Akbar called his friend Abul Fazl from Deccan in 1602 A.D. Vir Singh Bundela assassinated Abul Fazl in a plot conspired by Mughal prince Salim while he was returning from Deccan.
  • Akbar was the first Muslim ruler who realised that he could not hope to establish and consolidate the Mughal rule in India without winning the confidence and active support of the majority of the public which is Hindu. He tried to build Hindu-Muslim communities into National unity through 'Sulh-i-Kull' approach, i.e. peace with all.
  • Akbar is credited with consolidating and centralising Mughal administration. His central administration policies and interpretation of the role of the King, his duties and authorities, his provincial administration, his revenue system, his monetary policies, his mansabdari custom, etc. were successful during the period and became the foundation for his successors.
  • Akbar was a great ruler whose empire extended from Bengal to Afghanistan in the north and Kashmir to the Godavari in the South. He followed the religious tolerance policy and the complete authority of the empire was vested in him. Therefore, he is considered as “an enlightened despot” like Queen Elizabeth of England and Frederick the Great, during whose reign all were equal before the law.
  • Under the organised central administrative system in the reign of Akbar, Mir Bakshi was the head of military department but was not the chief commander of the army. Bakshi was responsible for recommending the recruitment and designation of proper rank and assignment of correct pay for soldiers.
  • He followed the practice of Dagh (branding of horses) in 1573-74 A.D.
  • Akbar organised soldiers by Mansabdari System in 1574-75 A.D. The 'Mansab' means rank or position. 'Mansabdar' means the official who had rank or designation in the royal army or government office. The system was based on the decimal system.
  • Diwan is the word of Persian vocabulary and was adopted by Muslims in the period of Caliph Umar. They used that term for the treasury department. Muzaffar Khan Turbati was made Diwan (with Todar Mal as assistant) early in Akbar's reign. Todar Mal and Khwaja Shah Mansur later served in the finance ministry & Akbar sometimes appointed more than one diwan. Diwan was a supreme official of financial affairs and revenue.
  • The Mughal Mansabdari system introduced by Akbar was taken from Central Asia. Genghis Khan's forces used a decimal troop organisation which influenced the Akbar's mansabdari, which was a graded rank system.
  • Mughal Emperor Akbar started the Mansabdari system in the 19th year (1575 A.D.) of his reign. Mansab recipients were divided into three classes Mansabdar from 10 to less than 500, Amir from 500 to 2500 and Amir-i-Azam above 2500.
  • Zabti System was introduced for land revenue in the reign of Akbar, which was measurement based assessment; revenue circles (dasturs) with per-bigha cash rates; Ain-i-Dahsala (ten year average rates). Todarmal achieved fame in the field of land revenue.
  • Ain-i-Dahsala is a land revenue system introduced by Akbar in the 24th year of his reign (1580 A.D.) which is also known as Todarmal Bandobast. This system was instituted by Todarmal under Akbar. That is why it is known as Todarmal settlement. At that time, Todarmal was the finance minister and his main assistant was Khwaja Shah Mansoor. Under this system, the average production of different crops, as well as the average prices prevailing over the last ten years was calculated. One third of the average was fixed as a land revenue for state.
  • Akbar annexed Gujarat in 1572-73 AD and established a city named Fatehpur Sikri. A class of historians believes that Akbar built Buland Darwaza of Sikri as a victory tower to commemorate his win over Gujarat, while Percy Brown states its construction on the occasion of his south victory (1601 A.D.). Akbar launched “Tauhid-i-Ilahi” or “Din-i-Ilahi” in 1582 A.D. Among Hindus, only Birbal accepted Din-i-Ilahi.
  • Jahangir’s contemporary Mohsin Fani stated first Din-i-Ilahi as an independent religion in his text “Dabistan-i-Mazahib”.
  • Akbar had constructed a fort-cum palace around 37 km away from Agra at Fatehpur Sikri. There are several buildings found in this Fort, Jodha Bai Mahal, Panch Mahal, Swarn Mahal or Sunahala Makaan, Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Mariyam Ki Kothi, Birbal Ki Kothi are some of them.
  • The palace of Turkish Sultana is so beautiful that Percy Brown has called it a “Pearl of Architecture”.
  • Panch Mahal was a pyramid-shaped palace, entirely columnar five-storey structure disposed asymmetrically on the pattern of a persian badgir, or wind-catcher-tower. This monument's style is inspired by multi-storey buildings of Nalanda..
  • The tomb of Akbar is located at Sikandra, a small village founded by Sikandar Lodi. Akbar named this place Bahistabad. He commenced its construction plan but it was completed by his son Jahangir in 1613 A.D. This large tomb has five floors. Its speciality is its domeless square apex.
  • Akbar established translation department under the supervision of his poet laureate Abul Fazl. Akbar ordered the translation of the Mahabharata into the Persian language named as Razmnama with a joint effort of Badauni, Naqib Khan, Faizi etc. Besides this, Badauni translated the “Ramayan.” Faizi translated “Leelavati”.
  • Muhammad Husain of Kashmir was one of the famous calligrapher in Akbar’s court who was adorned with the honour of “Zari Qalam” by King Akbar.
  • Hari Vijay Suri was a Jain monk who stayed for a few years in the court of Akbar and was honoured with the title of Jagadguru.
  • Another Jain, scholar who resided in Mughal court was Jin Chandra Suri bestowed with the title of “Yug Pradhan” by Akbar.
  • The Indian ruler, contemporary of Queen Elizabeth-I of England, was Akbar. It is notable that on the occasion of the establishment of East India Company in 1600 A.D., Elizabeth was the Queen of England. India had the reign of Akbar during the period 1556-1605 A.D. The tenure of Elizabeth-I was 1558-1603 A.D.
  • Ralph Fitch (1583-86 A.D.) was the first English merchant who visited Agra and Fatehpur Sikri.
  • Akbar established Ibadat Khana in Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 A.D. the main purpose of which was to facilitate philosophical and theological discussions. He opened the doors of Ibadat Khana for all schools of religion in 1578 A.D.
  • These religious discussions in Ibadat Khana led to the declaration of “Mahzarnama” in 1579 A.D. Mahzarnama was prepared by Shaikh Mubarak (Father of Abul Fazl). Mahzarnama is stated as infallibility decree by Smith and Wolseley Haig. Akbar was titled with Sultan-i-Adil or Imam-i-Adil after the issue of Mahzar.
  • Akbar used to participate in festivals such as Basant, Holi, Diwali etc. According to Stanley Lane-Poole, 'This assimilation of the Hindu chiefs was the most conspicuous feature of Akbar's reign.' According to Dr. R.P. Tripathi, Akbar was both a child and a father of his era.

Akbar enthroned → at Kalanaur, on news of Humayun's death (fell from the stairs of the Dinpanah library).

Chapter 31

Jahangir

24 facts · 9 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (20 points)
  • Jahangir was born on 30 August, 1569 A.D. His first marriage was with the daughter of Bhagwandas who was the king of Amber and the sister of king Man Singh, Man Bai in 1584 AD. Khusrau was the son of Man Bai. The second marriage of Salim was with Jagat Gosain, the daughter of Uday Singh (the Mota Raja). Shahzada Khurram was the son of Jagat Gosain. Jahangir was coronated in the fort of Agra in 1605 A.D. and adopted the title of Nuruddin Muhammad Jahangir Badshah Ghazi. Continuing the tradition of Akbar, Jahangir started his rule generously and when he sat on the throne, he issued various populist orders.
  • “Do-aspa and Sih-aspa” system was introduced by Jahangir. Under this system, Mansabdars had to maintain an excess number of soldiers without an elevation of rank (Zat.)
  • Do-aspa: Mansabdars had to maintain double the number of horses as required for their “Sawar” rank.
  • Sih-aspa: Mansabdars had to maintain three times the number of horses as required for their “Sawar’ rank.
  • Treaty of Chittor was signed between Mughal Emperor Jahangir (authorised Prince Khurram) and Rana Amar Singh of Mewar in 1615 A.D. Rana accepted the suzerainty of Mughal emperor and Jahangir returned Chittor which was annexed by Mughals during the reign of Akbar.
  • Nur Jahan was a cultured, educated, intelligent dominating lady and ambitious wife of Mughal emperor Jahangir. Nur Jahan’s Junta consist of a group of five- herself, her mother Asmat Begum, her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg or Itmad-ud Daula, her brother Asaf Khan and Prince Khurram.
  • Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan) had been allied with Nur Jahan from 1611 to 1622 but when she swung her support to her son-in-law Shaharyar, he left her junta and rebelled.
  • The reign of Jahangir, influenced by Nur Jahan, can be divided into two parts 1611-1622 A.D. and 1622-1627 A.D. Khurram was the member of this group in the first period but not the part of this group in the second period.
  • William Hawkins was the first English by East India Company to visit the court of Jahangir in 1608-1611 A.D.. Jahangir gave Hawkins the title of ''English Khan'' and also pressed him to marry a lady from Armenia.
  • Sir Thomas Roe led the second delegation which visited the court of Jahangir. Sir Thomas Roe arrived in Surat on September, 1615 AD as an ambassador of British King James-I. He attended the court of Jahangir in Ajmer in January 1616 A.D. He got the opportunity to visit Mandu, Ahmedabad and Ajmer with the emperor. He also went for hunting with the emperor. He stayed for one year in Agra.
  • Peter Mundy was a English East India Company factor and traveller who came during the reign of Shah Jahan. Francisco Pelsaert was a Dutch merchant who came to India during Jahangir’s period and left a unique account of the Mughal empire in his text “Jahangir's India: The Remonstrantie of Francisco Pelsaert”.
  • The Mughal painting reached its zenith under the reign of Jahangir. Earlier, the paintings were concerned with the contents of manuscripts, but Jahangir freed it from this bondage.
  • Ustad Mansur and Abul Hasan were excellent painters of Jahangir’s reign. Emperor Jahangir bestowed both Ustad Mansur (Nadir-Ul-Asra) and Abul Hasan (Nadir-Ul-Zaman). Ustad Mansur was specialized in depicting plants and animals while Abul Hasan was a portrait artist.
  • Jahangir was an outstanding author as well as a critic. He wrote his autobiography in Persian language and titled it Tuzuk-i Jahangiri.
  • Jahangir’s eldest son Khusrau revolted against Jahangir just after the coronation but the revolt was suppressed in 1606 A.D.
  • Shahzada Khurram revolted in 1622 A.D. and thereafter suffered defeat at Bilochpur in March 1623 under Mahabat Khan. The conflict ended with submission by 1625 A.D.
  • Mahabat Khan revolted against Jahangir in 1626 A.D.
  • The Mausoleums of Mughal emperors Babur and Jahangir are located in Kabul and Shahdara (Lahore) respectively. Both of them are located in Afghanistan and Pakistan, respectively.
  • The tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula was built by Nur Jahan at Agra between 1622-1628 A.D. after the death of his father. This is the first tomb in India that is entirely made up of white marble. In spite of marble and inlay work, it was for the first time when a new style of ornamentation, Pietra dura, was used.
  • Govind Palace (Bir Singh Palace) is a seven-storey building located in Datia, Madhya Pradesh. It was constructed by Raja Bir Singh Deo with bricks and stones.

Chapter 32

Shah Jahan

20 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (14 points)
  • Shahzada Khurram was born in 1592 A.D. in Lahore. His mother was Jagat Gosain, the daughter of the ruler of Marwar, Mota Raja Uday Singh. Shahzada Khurram married to Arjumand Banu Begum, the daughter of Asaf Khan in 1612 A.D. She was famous in history as Mumtaz Mahal.
  • Shah Jahan adopting the title of ‘Abul Muzaffer Shihabuddin Muhammad Sahib Kiran-i-Sani’ sat on the throne. His coronation took place in Agra. He shifted the capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi).
  • Ahmadnagar was included in the Mughal Empire in 1600 AD. Hussain Nizam Shah III, the ruler of Ahmadnagar was imprisoned in the fort of Gwalior. Nizam Shahi Sardar Shahaji Bhonsle continued the struggle with the Mughals in the name of one child (Murtaza Nizamshah III). Finally, in 1636 AD, Shahaji got surrounded by the Mughals in the Chunar Fort. Shahaji handed over several forts and Murtaza Nizamshah III to the Mughals. Murtaza Nizamshah III was imprisoned in the fort of Gwalior and Shahaji accepted the service of Bijapur State.
  • Aurangzeb was the governor of Deccan first time during 1636 - 44 A.D. in the reign of Shah Jahan and he was the governor of Deccan second time during 1653-1658 A.D. He remained at this designation till the victory in the war of succession and becoming the Mughal emperor.
  • Qandahar was the cause of dispute between Shah of Iran and the Mughal rulers because of strategic and economic grounds and a prestigious issue for Persians and Mughals. The loss of Qandahar was strategically a big blow to the Mughal Empire. The loss of Qandahar exposed the Mughal Kingdom to outside attacks. Finally, Qandahar slipped out from the hands of Mughals during the period of Shah Jahan, weakening Mughals on the North-West frontier.
  • The motive behind Shah Jahan’s Balkh and Badakhshan campaign was to secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakshan which shares its border with Kabul. So, it became a buffer state between the Mughals and the Persians.
  • Shah Jahan's period was considered to be the Golden age of the Mughal period because there had been a substantial development in the field of art, literature and education. In this period, two styles in the Persian language were prevalent, first was Indo-Persian (dominance of India style) and second was Iranian-Persian (native persian). Abul Fazl (Akbar's courtier) was the best promoter of the Indo- Persian style. The scholars of this style were Abdul Hamid Lahori, Muhammad Waris and Chandrabhan Brahmin, etc. Iranian-Persian-style scholars were Ameeni Qazwini and Jalaluddin Tabatabai. Iranian poetry style was quite dominating during that time. Shah Jahan appointed the Persian Poetry style poet Kaleem as court poet. In addition to Kaleem, Persian poets Qudsi, Mir Muhammad Yahya (Kashi), Salim, Masih, Rafi, Farrukh, Munir, Shoda. Chandrabhan Brahmin, Hajiq, Dileri, etc. were among others.
  • Kavindracharya was a dependent poet of Shah Jahan and had the perfect combination of Awadhi and Braj in his language.
  • 'Kavindra Kalplata' was written in praise of Shah Jahan. He requested the emperor for the abolition of pilgrimage tax on pilgrims visiting Benaras (Kashi) and Allahabad and got it abolished.
  • Upanishads were translated into Persian language during the reign of Shah Jahan by his son Dara Shikoh titled as Sirr-i-Akbar. Around 52 Upanishad were translated in this book. Lane pool compares Dara's religions/political posture with Akbar's path. Shah Jahan gave him the title of “Shah Buland Iqbal”. Majma-ul-Bahrain is a masterpiece of Dara Shukoh.
  • Shah Jahan collected designers, engineers, architects, from India, Persia and Central Asia for the construction of Taj Mahal which is the best example of Mughal architecture, blending India, Persian and Islamic styles.
  • Jama Masjid of Delhi was built by Shah Jahan. Buildings built by Shahjahan are Diwan-e-Aam, Diwan-e-Khas, Sheesh Mahal, Moti Masjid (Agra), Khas Mahal, Musamman Burj, Nagina Masjid, Jama Masjid (Delhi), Taj Mahal and Red Fort.
  • Like Akbar’s Fatehpur Sikri’, Shah Jahan established a city named Shahjahanabad in his name in Delhi, and tried to equip it by building many beautiful and magnificent buildings. Among the buildings of Shahjahanabad, Red Fort is the main building. The name of the western entrance of this fort is Lahori Darwaza and the southern gate is Delhi Darwaza. It is unique in beauty and splendour.
  • Among the four sons of Shah Jahan, the eldest, Dara Shikoh was the most educated scholar and writer. He studied many Hindu texts and translated the Hindu texts like Upanishads, Yoga Vashisht, Bhagwat Gita etc into Persian. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan abolished the Iranian Court tradition ‘Sijda’ started by Balban. Elphinstone has written about the period of Shah Jahan that the period of Shah Jahan was the most prosperous period in Indian history. Dr. A.L. Srivastava wrote in his book "Mughalkaleen Bharat", that the regime of Shah Jahan was the golden period in the medieval history of India.

Map of an empire without Golconda → Shah Jahan's; Golconda was captured later, by Aurangzeb in 1687.
