Chapter 33

Aurangzeb

24 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (22 points)
  • Aurangzeb succeeded Shah Jahan to the Mughal throne but not with the rule of primogeniture but by the force of sword. The sword was a symbol of power in the Mughal period. The decision of succession was settled only by the strength of the sword.
  • The coronation of Mughal emperor Aurangzeb was held twice. His first coronation was held on July 21, 1658 in Delhi. His second coronation took place after the success in the battle of ‘Khajwa’ and ‘Deorai’ in Delhi, on June 5, 1659. Assuming the title of ‘Abul Muzaffar Muhiuddin Muhammad Aurangzeb Bahadur Alamgir Padshah 'Ghazi', he sat on the throne as the Mughal emperor.
  • There was a battle between Aurangzeb and Dara's forces commanded by Maharaja Jaswant Singh and Qasim Khan on April 15, 1658, in Dharamat, near Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh. Dara Shikoh was supported by Raja Jaswant Singh of Jodhpur and Aurangzeb was supported by Prince Murad.
  • The Battle of Samugarh took place on May 29, 1658 between Aurangzeb's and Murad‘s joint forces against Dara Shikoh in which Dara Shikoh was defeated.
  • Shahzada Sulaiman Shikoh, son of Dara Shikoh, who was defeated by Aurangzeb in the war of succession and sought refuge from the ruler of Srinagar Garhwal Prithvi Shah. But his successor Medini Shah handed him over to Aurangzeb.
  • Sulaiman Shikoh was imprisoned in Gwalior’s Fort and there he died in prison.
  • In the beginning on 1665 A.D., Aurangzeb sent a large army under the leadership of Raja Jai Singh to suppress Shivaji. Jai Singh was the Kachhwaha ruler who was expert in both the arts of peace and war. He was a clever diplomat and he understood that it was necessary to have a friendship with Shivaji to win Bijapur. Hence, despite the victory of the Mughals on the fort of Purandar and the siege of Raigarh, he made a treaty with Shivaji. The Treaty of Purandar took place in June 1665 A.D.
  • Muhammad Akbar, the rebellious son, revolted against his father in 1681 A.D., weakening Aurangzeb’s position against Rajputs. Akbar was disappointed with the war against the Rajputs. He did not believe in the success of his father’s fanatic policy and he was generous with ideas. On the same occasion, Maharana Raj Singh of Mewar and Durgadas, the Rathore leader of Marwar proposed to him that if he declared himselfthe king of India, the forces of both Mewar and Marwar would help him.

Some contemporaries of Aurangzeb considered him as a ‘Shahi Darvesh’ and Muslims considered him as a ‘Zinda Peer’. When Aurangzeb was appointed the Subedar of the Deccan for the second time, he adopted an aggressive policy against Golconda and Bijapur, perhaps he would have demolished both of these states, but Shah Jahan issued peremptory orders to stop the operations, and the battle was suspended and he had to do treaty in 1656 A.D. with Golconda and in 1657 A.D. with Bijapur.

  • After becoming the emperor, he took his plan to logical conclusion and established control over Bijapur (1686 A.D.) and Golconda (1687 A.D.). During the reign of Aurangzeb, most of the commanders in the Mughal army were Hindus. In Athar Ali's nobility dataset, During his reign, 31.6 percent of the total generals were Hindu, among whom Marathas were more than 50%. During Akbar’s reign proportion was 22.5 percent and 22.4 percent during the reign of Shah Jahan.
  • Akbar abolished Jizya during his reign but Aurangzeb re imposed it on non-muslims in 1679 A.D.
  • The Hindus/Non Muslims were categorised into three classes for the purpose of paying tax according to ability/wealth.

(i) Those with income less than 200 Dirham per annum, had to pay 12 Dirham per annum as tax.

(ii) Those with income 200 to 10,000 Dirham per annum, had to pay 24 Dirham per annum as tax.

(iii) Those with incomes more than 10,000 Dirham per annum had to pay 48 Dirham per annum as tax.

  • Women, slaves, children under 14 years, beggars and unemployed persons were exempted from it. The subordinate Hindu kings and Brahmins were compelled to pay this tax.
  • Aurangzeb was a Sunni Muslim.
  • His religious policy was not influenced by any idea of worldly profit.
  • Aurangzeb tried to enforce the Quranic law, according to which, Muslims needed to carry on Jihad (Holy wars) against non-Muslim lands (Dar ul-Harb) till they were converted to Islam (Dar-ul—lslam). He stopped putting tilak with his hands on the forehead of the Hindu kings as was started by Akbar. Prostitutes were to marry or leave the country. There was a ban on celebrating Basant, Holi, Diwali etc, in the court.
  • Aurangzeb's son Azam Shah (during Aurangzeb's reign) built the mausoleum for his mother Rabia-Ud-Daurani in Aurangabad (now Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar) (Maharastra). It is also known as ‘Bibi Ka Maqbara’. lts architectural style was based on the well-known ‘Taj Mahal’. So, it is also called 'Dakkhani Taj' (Taj of the Deccan). Moti Masjid inside Red Fort in Delhi was built by Aurangzeb.
  • Mehrunissa was the daughter of Aurangzeb while Jahan Ara, Roshan Ara and Gauhar Ara were the daughters of Shah Jahan. The other daughters of Aurangzeb were Jebunissa, Zinat-un-Nissa, Badrunnisa and Jubadtunnisa. Aurangzeb bestowed the title of ‘Sahibat-uz-Zamani’ to Jahan Ara.
  • Samarth Ramdas was the great Saint of Maharashtra. He was born in 1608 A.D. and died in 1681 A.D. He was the contemporary to the Mughal king Aurangzeb.

Aurangzeb (third son) took Shah Jahan's throne by force; no primogeniture rule (Dara was eldest); A true, R false.

Chapter 34

Mughal Administration

29 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (13 points)
  • During the Mughal administration, the district was known as the ‘Sarkar’. Each Suba (province) was divided into several Sarkars (districts) for the convenience of governance. Sarkar was further divided into ‘Pargana’ or ‘Mahal’. The leading officers of each Sarkar were - Faujdar, Amalgujar, Qazi, Kotwal, Bitikchi and Khajandar.
  • Mir Bakhshi was the head of the military department during the reign of Mughals. He also fixed the monthly salary of soldiers by issuing a signed certificate called ‘Sarkhat’. Apart from this, there were Bakhshi'sin the provinces who worked under the control of Mir Bakhshi.
  • In the Mughal regime, head of military department was called the Mir Bakshi and head of land revenue administration was Diwan/Wazir, and Mir Bakshi was responsible for the salary of the military department.
  • Sir Jadunath Sarkar stated Mir Bakshi as Vetanadhikari (Pay Master). The duty of the Pay Master was of Diwaan-i Tan. During the Mughal period, in addition to the soldiers of Mansabdars, there were others two different types of cavalry who were called ‘Ahadi’ and 'Dakhili'. 'Ahadi's have been called gentlemen-troopers, being recruited directly by emperor and having their own muster-master.
  • ‘Dakhili’ soldiers were also recruited by the Emperor although they were kept in the service of Mansabdars.
  • The prostitutes were expelled from the city and settled at some other place named ‘Shaitanpura’.
  • Akbar implemented the dual system of ‘Zat‘ and ‘Sawar’ in the 40th year (1591-95).
  • The word 'Maal' in the Mughal administrative terminology, was related to land revenue.
  • Tobacco was brought to India by the Portuguese After that tobacco became very popular in the public of India. In a few years, the habit of smoking tobacco became so prevalent among people that to avoid this harmful habit, Jahangir prohibited it. He issued an order to ban it in 1617 A.D.
  • The Mughal administration issued grants as Madad-i-Maash for the scholars and also to the religious persons. It was also called ‘Suyurghal’.
  • All the donated lands were inspected by ‘Sadra (Sadr-us-Sudur)’ and the Sadra also had the duty to keep an eye on the donation that they are not misused. These lands were not transferrable and the grantee possessed a right of inheritance over it. During the Mughal period, the mint officer was called Daroga. Gold, silver and copper coins were minted. Akbar issued the coins with figures of Ram and Sita and 'Ram Siya' inscribed on them in Devanagari. The silver coin was called ‘Rupiya’. ‘Daam’ was copper coin largely created by Sher Shah (part of his tri-metallic system) and later continued under the Mughals.
  • Jahangir marked his figure on his coins and named Nur Jahan, along with his name on some coins. Some of the coins were marked with his image holding cup of alcohol in hand.
  • The meaning of word ‘Batai’ during the medieval period was a system of crop sharing in which real produce was distributed between state and peasants.

Chapter 35

Music andPaintingsof Mughal Period

23 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (11 points)
  • War scenes, birds, animals and scenery were illustrated in Mughal paintings. Humayun started the Mughal style of painting. He met two distinguished painters, Khwaja Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali, during the years of his exile in Persia and Afghanistan. From these artists Humayun and his son Akbar learned lessons in drawing and painting.
  • Akbar got a number of texts painted. The first major project was ‘Dastan-i-Amir Hamza’. Almost 100 painters took part in its preparation, first under the supervision of Mir Sayyid Ali and later, under Abdus Samad. There were about 1400 paintings in it. This book mentioned the heroic work of the Persian hero, Amir Hamza (uncle of Prophet Muhammad).
  • The art of Mughal painting reached great heights during Jahangir’s reign. Jahangir was a highly skilled connoisseur of painting. Abul Hasan (the title of Nadiru-z-Zaman), Ustad Mansur (Nadir-ul-Asra), Faruq Begh, Bishan Das, Aqa Reza, Muhammad Nadir, Muhammad Murad, Manohar, Madhav, Govardhan, etc were the main artists of Jahangir's court. Abul Hassan made a painting of Jahangir‘s coronation. This painting is inscribed in the Jahangir’s autobiography ‘Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri’ as frontispiece. Thus, Jahangir’s period was called ‘Golden Age of Mughal Paintings'.
  • ‘Pahari School’, ’Rajput School’, ‘Mughal School’ are different styles of medieval painting.
  • Aurangzeb banned the music as he found it as anti-Islamic, but during the same period, most books on Indian classical music were written in the Persian language. Despite being anti-music. Aurangzeb was a skilled instrumentalist who used to play the Indian instrument called ‘Veena'.
  • ‘Todi’ Raga is used to sing early in the morning. It was sung by Bhats and Charans in the emperor’s court.
  • During the reign of Akbar, Tansen and Swami Haridas were prominent Dhrupad singers. Tansen was a famous musician of Akbar‘s court. Tansen‘s original name was Ramtanu Pandey. He was one of the Akbar’s Navratanas. Before coming to the court of Akbar, Tansen was in the court of King Ramchandra of Rewa from where Akbar summoned him to his court and gave a very high post.
  • Akbar had given Tansen the title of ‘Kanthabharnvanivilas’.
  • Vilas Khan was the musician of Jahangir’s court. The prominent singers of the court of Shah Jahan were Jagannath, Ramdas, Sukhsen, Sursen, Lal Khan, Durrang Khan, etc. Khyal singing became popular in the time of Muhammad Shah ‘Rangila’.
  • The Kishangarh style of Rajasthan is known throughout India for its depiction of courtesan paintings. Raja Sawant Singh was the real inspiration behind the famous Kishangarh School of Painting of Radha-Krishna theme. The main artists of this style, were Amirchand, Chhotu, Bhawanidas, Nihalchand, Sitaram etc.
  • The famous portrait of ‘Bani-Thani’ which is in Kishangarh style, was made by Nihalchand.

Key facts from the book (9 points)
  • The founder of Sikhism and the first Guru of Sikhs was Guru Nanak. There are total of 10 gurus in Sikhism. They are Guru Nanak, Guru Angad, Amar Das, Ramdas, Arjan Dev, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur and Guru Gobind Singh.
  • Guru Angad is considered as the progenitor of‘Gurumukhi script’.
  • Gazetteer of Amritsar district, mentions that the fourth Guru Ramdas obtained from Akbar the grant of a piece of land (around 500 bighas) on the spot where now stands the city of Amritsar, and dug the holy tank, and commenced the erection of a temple in its midst. Some sources also state that it was gifted to Bibi Bhani (wife of Guru Ramdas) by Akbar. Ramdas died in 1581 A.D. and his son and successor, Guru Arjun completed the temple. Some other sources mention that Ramdas purchased land from the zamindars of the villages.
  • Guru Amardas divided the religious empire into 22 parts called Manji. Each Manji was under the authority of a Sikh.
  • Guru Arjan Dev constructed ‘Sri Harmandir Sahib’ in the middle of the Amritsar pond. He established two cities called Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (in Jalandhar Doab). Guru Ram Das organised a network of Sikhs to collect offerings, called Masand. Dasvandh is another practise being following by Sikhs, according to which the Sikhs had to pay one-tenth of their income to Guru.
  • Adi Granth or Guru Granth Sahib was compiled in 1604 A.D. by Arjan Dev, the fifth Sikh guru (1581A.D.- 1606A.D.). It contains preachings of six Sikh Gurus, many Hindu/muslim saints like Kabir, Baba Farid, Namdev and Raidas. Among the earliest compositions in the Adi Granth was written by Vaishnav poet Jaydev and the last compositions added were of Guru Teg Bahadur. Guru Arjan Dev was sentenced to death by Jahangir and Guru Teg Bahadur was sentenced to death by Aurangzeb.
  • The tenth and the last Guru of Sikhs, Guru Gobind Singh, converted Sikhs into a military sect ‘Khalsa Panth’. It was established on 13th April, 1699 in ‘Anandpur Sahib’ on the day of Baisakhi. He called the whole Sikh community as ‘Khalsa’. He ordered Sikhs that each Sikh should have the surname of Singh (male) and Kaur (female) and hold 5 K's-Kesh, Kangha, Kachha, Kripan and Kada.
  • The tenth and the last Sikh Guru Gobind Singh, was assassinated in Nanded, Maharashtra by an Afghan noble in 1708 A.D. Nanded Gurudwara (Huzur Sahib) is situated at his cremation site
  • The another name of Banda Bahadur was Lachman Dev or Lakshan Dev. This name was given to him by Sikh Guru Gobind Singh.

Chapter 39

Maratha State and Confederacy

30 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (28 points)
  • Shivaji was born at the fort of Shivneri in 1627 or 1630 A.D. He adopted the title of Chhatrapati after his coronation in 1674 A.D. He made Raigarh his capital.
  • Pandit Vishweshwar alias ‘Gagabhatta’, a great scholar of that era, declared Shivaji a Kshatriya at his coronation. Shivaji died in 1680 A.D. at the age of 53 or 50 years.
  • The reason for the rise of Maratha power was its residents.
  • The unity of the people on the grounds of regional/collective, consciousness along with religious toleration and integration of social groups, flourished the feeling of nationalism among them. The geographical conditions of Maharashtra were helpful in flourishing the Maratha power.
  • The high leadership quality of Shivaji and other Maratha leaders contributed to the rise of Maratha power.
  • In 1659 A.D., the Sultan of Bijapur Adil Shah II sent his experienced and trusted commander Afzal Khan for suppression of Shivaji, but the diplomat and clever Shivaji killed him.
  • Treaty of Purandar was signed between Shivaji and Mughals under Jai Singh in 1665 A.D. Shivaji was put under house arrest by Aurangzeb in 1666 in Jaipur Bhawan at Agra when he escaped from the custody of Mughals. Aurangzeb imprisoned Shivaji in 1666 A.D. at Agra.
  • ‘Ashtapradhan’ was the Council of Eight Ministers (reaching 8 in no. by 1674) under Shivaji in Maratha administration. The eight ministers were –

(i) Peshwa - Prime Minister of the King.

(ii) Amatya - Finance and Revenue Minister.

(iii) Waqianavis/Mantri - Interior Minister, managing internal affairs, especially intelligence and espionage.

(iv) Sachiv/Surnavis - Responsible for all correspondence.

(v) Sumant/Dabir - Foreign Minister.

(vi) Senapati/Sar-i-Naubat - Maintenance of appointments, organization and food supply of military.

(vii) Pandit Rao - Appointed for religious aid.

(viii) Nyayadhish - Chief Justice.

  • Rajaram led the Marathas as a representative of Shahu from 1689 A.D. to 1700 A.D. After the death of Rajaram, his widow Tarabai continued the struggle with the Mughals placing his four year old son Shivaji-II on the throne. At the time of Aurangzeb’s death, the Maratha leadership was in the hands of Tarabai.
  • Under Shahu, the power of Maratha kingdom came in the hands of Balaji Vishwanath who made the administration easy and convenient.
  • Maratha Chhatrapati Shahu appointed Balaji to the post of Peshwa. November 1713 was an important day not only for Balaji but also for the whole Marathas as the power gradually shifted from Chhatrapati to the Peshwa.
  • Balaji Vishwanath served as Peshwa from 1713 A.D. to 1720 A.D.
  • Shahu appointed the elder son of Balaji Vishwanath, Bajirao - I as Peshwa whose tenure was from 1720 A.D. to 1740 A.D.
  • Balaji Bajirao served as Peshwa from 1740 A.D. to 1761 A.D. after the death of Bajirao. Madhavrao’s tenure was from 1761 A.D. to 1772 A.D.
  • After the death of Madhavrao in 1772 A.D., his brother Narayanrao became a victim of the conspiracy of his uncle Raghunathrao, who himself wanted to become Peshwa.
  • By the time of Balaji Bajirao, the Post of Peshwa became hereditary. Previously the power was in the hands of the Chhatrapati, but now the centre of power shifted into the hands of Peshwas. By the treaty of Sangola in 1750 A.D., Peshwa emerged as the real and effective head of Maratha confederacy.
  • Saranzami system was related to Feudal-military land grant system in Maratha period. The land given under Saranzami system was provided for the livelihood of Maratha Jagirdar (for maintenance of forts/troops for Public Service) during the Maratha period.
  • In January, 1757 A.D., Ahmad Shah Abdali entered Delhi and looted up to Agra and Mathura. Before returning to his motherland, he confirmed Alamgir II as Emperor, Imadulmulk as prime minister and Rohilla leader Najib-Ud-Daulah as his chief agent and Mir Bakshi of the Empire.
  • The third battle of Panipat was fought between Maratha Sadashivrao Bhau and Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali on 14th January 1761. Marathas were badly defeated by Afghans in this battle. According to Kashiraj Pandit, a historian who was eyewitness of this battle 'Third battle of Panipat proved catastrophic for Marathas.' “Two pearls have been dissolved, 22 gold coins have been lost and of the silver and copper the total cannot be cast up” that was the message which was sent to Balaji Bajirao by a merchant after this agonising defeat of Marathas. The immediate reason for the battle of Panipat was the Ahmad Shah Abdali’s desire to avenge Marathas as they expelled his Viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore.
  • Ahilyabai was a Maratha ruler from Holkar dynasty. Holkars belong to Indore and under Ahilyabai, the capital was moved to Maheshwar.

Rise of the Marathas → religious consciousness, geographical security, political awakening and high-quality leadership (all of the above).

Key facts from the book (15 points)
  • After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 A.D. his 63-year-old son Muazzam (Shah Alam) ascended the throne adopting the name of ‘Bahadur Shah I’. He ruled during the period from 1707-1712 A.D.
  • He was given the title of ‘Shah-e-Bekhabar’ by Khafi Khan.
  • Jahandar Shah was the first emperor in the Mughal dynasty, who proved to be weak and highly disqualified for governance. He ascended the throne with the help of Zulfiqar Khan. He was defeated and later executed by his nephew Farrukh Siyar in a battle in 1713 A.D.
  • Farrukh Siyar issued a decree (farman) in which he granted duty - free trading concessions to the British in Bengal in 1717 A.D. It was mentioned in the contract that the East India Company could trade without duty (charge) after paying the annual tax of Rs. 3000
  • Muhammad Shah (1719 - 1748 A.D.) was the last Mughal emperor to sit on Peacock throne (built by Shah Jahan). During his reign, Nadir Shah attacked India in 1739 A.D. and defeated Mughals in the battle of Karnal. The contemporary historian Anand Ram Mukhlis wrote, "Nadir Shah took sixty thousand rupees, many thousands of gold coins, gold of one crore rupees, jewels of fifty crores, Kohinoor and peacock throne with him to Iran." and remarked that "the accumulated wealth of 348 years changed owners in a moment."
  • Muhammad Shah (1719-1748 A.D.) spent most of his time in watching animal fight. People called him Rangeela due to his obsession towards wine and beauty and apathy towards administration. A group of eunuchs and ladies dominated in Mughal Darbar during the regime of Muhammad Shah.
  • The tenure of Shah Alam-II was from 1759 to 1806 A.D. His real name was Ali Gauhar. English captured Delhi in 1803 A.D. during his tenure.
  • The last Mughal emperor was Bahadur Shah Zafar / Bahadur Shah II (reigned 1837 -1857 A.D.). His father’s name was Akbar -II (1806 -1837 A.D.). He was called as the "Emperor without Empire".
  • Ibrahim Zauq and Asad Ullah Khan Ghalib taught poetry to Bahadur Shah Zafar. Hasan Askari was sufi saint and Pir to Zafar.
  • Bahadur Shah Zafar got Rs 1 lakh per month from the East India Company as pension, which consisted of Rs. 99000 given in Delhi and one thousand rupees for regular family expenses in Lucknow. He died in 1862 A.D.
  • Chin Qilich Khan aka Nizam-ul-Mulk founded the independent Kingdom of Hyderabad in 1724. Nizam became the real king after the death of the Mughal governor Mubariz Khan in the battle of Sakhar - Kheda of Deccan, 1724 A.D..
  • Sawai Jai Singh (Jai Singh II) (1688 - 1743 A.D.) of Amber was a Rajput king of the 18th century.
  • He established ‘Jaipur’ city and made it the centre of science and art.
  • He built well equipped observatories in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi. He patronised the translation of‘‘Euclid's Geometry” in Sanskrit.
  • He organized two Ashvamedh sacrifices during his reign.

Chapter 41

The Advent of European Companies

52 facts · 9 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (34 points)
  • According to one theory, Vasco da Gama reached India with the help of an Arab navigator Ahmad Ibn Majid, but according to historical & authentic evidence, the person who helped Vasco da Gama reach Indian port of Calicut was a Gujarati sailor. Vasco da Gama sailed to the Western Coast of India, at the port of Calicut on May 20, 1498. He had successfully discovered a new and alternative sea route to India from Europe. Zamorin (Zamorin was the ancestral title of the rulers of Calicut), then the ruler of Calicut, welcomed Vasco da Gama. The arrival of Vasco da Gama in India started a new era of trade between Portuguese and Indians. Vasco da Gama returned with the cargo having 60 times more profit than the expedition cost, in the business of Black Pepper which was enough to lure other merchants to India.
  • In 1505 A.D., Francisco de Almeida arrived in India as first Portuguese Viceroy. In the light of Portuguese trade interests and to establish Portuguese authority in the Indian Ocean, Almeida rendered the Blue Water Policy.
  • Afonso de Albuquerque came as the Governor of the Portuguese region in India 1509 A.D. after Almeida. In 1510 A.D., he snatched Goa from Adil-Shahi Sultanate, the rulers of Bijapur, and established his authority there. He is known as the real founder of the Portuguese power in India.
  • Albuquerque in 1511 A.D. captured Malacca, an important South-East Asian Market and, in 1515, captured Hormuz situated at the mouth of Persian Gulf.
  • Nuno da Cunha assumed the Governor office after Lopo Vaz de Sampaio in 1529 A.D. and remained the Governor until the end of 1538 A.D.
  • A new sea route to India was discovered by Portuguese traveller Vasco da Gama whereas Columbus, a traveller originally from Italy and financed by Spain discovered America, and Tasman of Holland discovered Van Diemen's Land (currently Tasmania) and New Zealand. The first European to reach Australia was English Navigator Willem Janszoon (1712-1780), while the British Navigator Captain Cook arrived at Australia in 1770 A.D. (about 164 years later, when Willem Janszoon reached to Australia). Captain Cook is credited with surveying Australia’s east coast and laying foundation of British rule there.
  • In 1503, at Cochin, first Portuguese Fort (first European Fort in India) was constructed by Afonso de Albuquerque (during his first visit to India in 1503 A.D.). The fort was named as ‘Emmanuel Fort’.
  • The sequence of Arrival of European Companies to India is:
  • Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danish and French.
  • Portuguese were the first to arrive in 1498 A.D. and were last to leave India in 1961 (de Jure transfer took place in August 1962).
  • In 1961 the Portuguese Governor-General of Goa was Manuel Antonio Vassalo e Silva (1958-61 A.D.).
  • Jose Ferreira Bossa was the Governor- General of Goa when India gained Independence in 1947.
  • Among all European powers, Portuguese were the first to establish Sea trading centers in India.
  • Portuguese in 1500 A.D. established their first factory at Calicut.
  • In 1535 A.D. Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah, the ruler of Bengal, promised the Portuguese to establish the forts in Chittagong and Satgaon, in return for their assistance of the ruler during the Sher Shah Suri’s invasion of Bengal.
  • Hooghly was used as a base by Portuguese for plundering activities in the Bay of Bengal.
  • In 1632 A.D., Mughal king Shahjahan, ordered Bengal Subedar Qasim Khan to destroy the establishments of Portuguese in Hooghly and imprison thousands of Portuguese residents.
  • Job Charnock, head of the factory of Qasim Bazar, selected Sutanuti instead at Hooghly for English Trading Center. This is how he established Calcutta as a Base of Englishmen.
  • In 1602 A.D., Dutch (Holland) States General Chartered the establishment of a United East India Company. It had a Capital of6,500,000 Guilders. This company had a monopoly to do trade and to attack and win territories in India and eastern countries. Its eastern centre was situated in Batavia (currently Jakarta). Eastern Empire of Dutch was operated and administered by this company. Its partners worked as a private group. Dutch constructed William Fort at Modern Kochi in 1663 A.D. after defeating Portuguese. Kochi in 1814 AD was included in British settlements under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814.
  • In 1600 A.D., a trading company English East India Company or 'The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies' was founded in England.
  • Akbar was the King of India during establishment.
  • The Levant Company (1592) was granted a monopoly to trade with Ottoman Empire (The Levant) and its eastern areas (including India). They traded in Silk, spices etc. After the ‘Royal Charter’ of Queen Elizabeth I, the East India company was provided with exclusive 15-year monopoly on English trade with all countries east of Cape of Good Hope, which included India.
  • During the Reign of Jahangir, in 1611 A.D., East India Company established its first temporary factory at Masulipatnam. In 1613 A.D., English established their first permanent factory at Surat.
  • Dutch established their factory at Surat in 1616 A.D. followed by French in 1668 A.D.
  • Thomas Best was the English officer who defeated Portuguese at a place named Swally.
  • In 1662 A.D., King of Britain Charles II married Portuguese Princess Catherine and received Mumbai as a gift which was leased to East India Company on payment of 10 Pound annually (under the Marriage Treaty of 1961).
  • A British official John Child, in 1688 A.D., surrounded Mughal ports in Bombay and other Mughal ports on the western coast and tried to imprison Hajj travellers going to Mecca as a result of which Aurangzeb expelled him from India.
  • First Carnatic War (1746-48 A.D.) was just an extension of the War of Succession in Austria which started in 1740.
  • In 1746 English and French started war without the consent of their home nations in India. English Navy under the leadership of Commodore Bernett seized French Ships, this was the immediate reason for war. During the first Carnatic War, the Nawab of Carnatic, Anwaruddin, sent an Army of 10,000 men under the leadership of Mahfooz Khan to attack French. Under the leadership of Captain Paradise, the French defeated the Force of Nawab at a place called St. Thome on the bank of Adyar River. With the end of the war in Europe, the war in India also ended with the Treaty of Aix - la - Chapelle (1748 A.D.). Austrian Succession war ended and Madras was again granted to English.
  • Dupleix for the first time used tactics that guided the future campaigns of English men. It was Dupleix who appointed European forces into Indian Courts on Indian expense and interfered in the internal conflicts of kingdoms in the light of European interests and sown the seeds of European rule in India.
  • Colbert, a minister of Louis XIV, founded French East India Company in 1664 A.D. which is also known as Compagnie Francaise Pour le Commerce des Indes Orientales (or Compagnie francaise des Indes orientales) in 1667 A.D. Francois Caron headed an expedition to India setting up a factory in Surat in 1668 A.D. Marcara, a Persian who accompanied Caron founded another French factory in Masulipatnam in 1669 A.D. after obtaining permission from the Sultan of Golconda.

Chapter 42

East India Company and Nawabs of Bengal

16 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (13 points)
  • Murshid Quli Khan was the last Governor of Bengal who was independently appointed by Mughal King.
  • Murshid Quli Khan shifted his Capital to Maksudabad from Dhaka and named it Murshidabad. He started Izara System in the land settlement.
  • Alivardi Khan (1740-1756 A.D.) comparing Europeans with the Honeybees, said that ifthey are left undisturbed, they will give you honey, and if try to disturb them they will bite you till death.
  • After the death of Alivardi Khan, his grandson Siraj-ud-Daula succeeded to the throne of Bengal. The Black Hole tragedy took place during his reign on 20th June 1756 A.D. According to one of the 23 survivors, J.Z. Holwell, 146 English prisoners were put in a cell with a dimension of18 feet in length and 14 feet 10 inches in breadth. 123 of them died due to suffocation and only 23 survived. This incident is known as Black Hole tragedy. Contemporary Muslim historian Ghulam Hussain in his book ‘Siyar-ul Mutakherin’ has not mentioned this incident.
  • Robert Clive is known as the founder of the English Empire in India who defeated the forces of Bengal’s Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula in the Battle of Plassey (presently known as Palasi) on 23rd June, 1757 A.D. and sown the seeds of British rule in India. The Battlefield of Plassey is situated on the Banks of Bhagirathi River in Nadia district of West Bengal. Robert Clive was the Governor in 1758- 60 A.D. and 1765-67 A.D. in India. During this period he signed Allahabad Treaty with Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II During his governorship White Mutiny broke out among English soldiers.
  • Plundering of resources of Bengal by the British Company was started during Clive’s governorship.
  • Mir Qasim (1760-63 A.D.) was the ablest among the successors of Alivardi Khan. As a ‘Faujdar’ of Poornia and Rangpur, Mir Qasim had already proven his ability. To save his courtiers from repeated conspiracies by Britishers and to avoid interference from Englishmen, Mir Qasim shifted his Capital to Munger from Murshidabad so as to stay away from Calcutta. He consolidated his army using European methods. He made arrangements in Munger for the manufacturing of Matchlock guns. Mir Qasim also took some brave steps so as to improve the economic conditions in Bengal. The officers involved in embezzlement were fined heavily, some new taxes were introduced
  • The Combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), and Mughal King Shah Alam II were defeated by Britishers in the Battle of Buxar on 22/23 October, 1764 AD. English army was led by Hector Munro. Henry Vansittart was the then Governor of Bengal. This victory of Britishers made the English a great power in northern India and contenders for supremacy over the whole country. The area up to Allahabad was now under the British and the door of Delhi was now open for British. Battle of Buxar changed the course of Indian History. During this battle, Mir Jafar was Nawab of Bengal and Delhi was ruled by Shah Alam II. By the treaties of Allahabad (August, 1765) Shah Alam II agreed to reside at Allahabad, under the company’s protection. Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula surrendered Allahabad and Kora to Emperor Shah Alam II.
  • Shah Alam II issued a decree granting Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the East India Company.
  • Robert Clive became the governor of Bengal and started Dual government system in Bengal.
  • The Company appointed two deputy Diwans, Mohammad Raza Khan for Bengal and Raja Shitab Roy for Bihar to exercise Diwani functions. Rohilla Sardar Ghulam Qadir annexed Delhi in July 1788, and August 1788, he ousted Shah Alam II and made him blind. During the time of Shah Alam II in 1803, Delhi fell completely to East India Company. Shah Alam II and his two successors Akbar II (1806-37 AD) and Bahadur Shah II (1837-57 AD) were mere pensioners of the East India Company.
  • The British came to Sylhet (then Sylhet was part of Bengal Presidency) in 1765 AD after acquiring the Diwani right of Bengal. After the War of Burma, David Scott tried to connect Assam (Brahmaputra Valley) with Sylhet through roads to Jaintia and Garo Hill areas, but faced a very tough resistance from the Khasi tribes who lived in these areas under the leadership of Tirot Sing.
  • K.M. Panikar said that from 1757 to 1773 AD the Company made Bengal a ‘State of Robbers’.

  • Ranjit Singh was born to the chief of Sukerchakia Misl on 13th November, 1780 A.D. Ranjit Singh captured Multan in 1818 A.D., Kashmir in 1819 and Peshawar and North-West frontier (Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) in 1834 A.D..
  • In 1798 AD, Zaman Shah attacked Punjab. While returning, his cannons accidentally fell into the Jhelam River (some sources refer for Chenab River but Jhelam River is authenticated by many historians). These cannons were sent back to Jaman Shah by Ranjit Singh. Happy with this gesture of Ranjit Singh, Jaman Shah allowed Ranjit Singh to rule Lahore. As a result, in 1799 A.D., Ranjit Singh took control of Lahore and made it his Capital. Zaman Shah gave him the title of Raja (in return of his service and providing tanks and artileries) and appointed him as the Subedar of Lahore. He also captured Amritsar from Bhangi Misl in 1802. Now, both the political capital ‘Lahore’ and religious capital ‘Amritsar’ were under the control of Ranjit Singh.
  • Ranjit Singh was an able ruler. He once said, “God wants me to see all the religions as one, so he took the light of my other eye”.

  • His son Kharak Singh succeeded Ranjit Singh after the laters death in 1839. He was an opium addict. During his reign two opposite groups, one consisting of Dogra Brothers - Dhyan Singh, Ghulab Singh and Suchet Singh other included Sandhawaliya Sardar (an aid of Chait Singh) Atar Singh, Lahna Singh and his nephew Ajeet Singh, and Dogras (Dhyan Singh, Gulab Singh and Suchet Singh) were the main reason of growing chaos in Punjab.
  • Battle of Chillianwala was fought on 13th January 1849 A.D. between English forces led by Lord Gough and Sikh forces led by Sher Singh. The war ended undecided. Lord Dalhousie was the Governor-General of India during this war.
  • Maharaja Duleep Singh was the last ruler of Sikh Empire. He ruled from 1843 to 1849 AD. He converted to Christianity and travelled to Russia. Later in 1886 A.D. he again accepted Sikhism. He died in Paris in 1893 AD. His funeral took place in England. In 1849 AD, after the Anglo-Sikh war, Punjab was annexed by Britishers and Duleep Singh was sent to Britain on a pension in 1854 A.D. After the annexation of Punjab, in 1849 A.D. Lord Dalhousie made a three-member body consisting of Sir Henry Lawrence as Board’s President and, John Lawrence and Charles Grenville Mansel as members to administer Punjab.
  • The First Anglo-Mysore war in 1767-69 A.D. made Haidar Ali victorious. The war ended in April, 1769 AD with the Treaty of Madras. During this the Governor of Bengal was Harry Verelst (1734-85).
  • The Second Anglo Mysore War (1780-84 AD) - During this war, Haidar Ali made an alliance with Nizam and Marathas against Britishers. In July 1780 A.D. Haidar attacked Carnatic and on 10 September 1780 AD, colonel Baillie was defeated by the combined forces of Haidar Ali and Tipu in the battle of Pollilur (other name Perambakam). In 1781 A.D. Haidar Ali faced Sir Eyre Coote who defeated Haidar Ali at Porto Novo (July, 1781 A.D.), Pollilur (In this war, Haider Ali was out rightly defeated but his army faced heavy loss during this) and Sholingur.
  • Tipu Sultan made Srirangapattnam his Capital where he established Jacobin Club and became its member. He planted the tree of liberty in his capital as a sign of friendship between Mysore and France.
  • Tipu sent ambassadors to contemporary foreign states and also established their embassies to maintain friendly relations and to gather help from them against the Britishers. These foreign states included - Iran, Istanbul, Afghanistan, France.
  • The Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92 A.D.) ended with the Treaty of Srirangapattna (March 1792 A.D.). The treaty fo Seringapatam (Srirangapatna) was signed in March 1792 A.D. between Tipu Sultan of Mysore and Lord Cornwallis on behalf of British East India Company. The agreement also included representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and Maratha Empire, requiring Tipu to cede halfofhis Kingdom. Tipu Sultan died fighting in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799 A.D.). All the members of his family were imprisoned in Vellore. British Commanders like Arthur Wellesley (brother of Governor General of Bengal Lord Wellesley), Stuart and General Harris led this war from the English side. In the happiness of this victory, the Lord Society of Ireland conferred the title of Marquess to Wellesley. After the war, a minor Krishnaraja Wodeyar III (Mummadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar) from Wodeyar dynasty was placed on the Mysore throne and the British took possession of Kanara, Coimbatore, and Srirangapattnam.
  • Begum Samru (1750-1836 A.D.) constructed a very famous church at Sardhana near Meerut (Some sources mention the birth year of Begum Samru is 1753 A.D.). Walter Reinhardt Sombre, a European, was her husband who served many kingdoms. Sombre was granted Jagir of Sardhana as a gift for his service to the Mughal king Shah Alam II in defeating Zabita Khan (induced by NajafKhan). Begum Samru became ruler of Sardhana after the death of her husband.

Chapter 44

Governor/Governor General/ Viceroy

98 facts · 24 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (38 points)
  • Both Civilian and Military reforms took place during the period of Robert Clive. Under the civilian reform, a ban was imposed on the gift to officials and controlled private trade (Clive imposed conditioned ban on accepting gifts; i.e. for accepting gifts above Rs. 1000 of value, a pre-permission of governor is necessary). Under the Military reforms, he ended ‘double batta’ for European officers and from January 1, 1766 AD this allowance was only granted to soldiers who served outside the boundaries of Bengal and Bihar (except Allahabad).
  • Under administrative reforms, Warren Hastings in 1772 A.D. ended the dual government system of Bengal by order of the Court of Directors. He transferred the State’s treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Warren Hastings believed that the whole land belonged to the ruler. To reform in Revenue field, he chose trial and error method. Warren Hastings in 1774 A.D. was made Governor-General of Bengal by the Regulating Act 1773. The act provides for Governor-General and four consellors (“Council of four”), total five (including Governor-general). The Governor General was head of the government and had casting vote if equally divided. It was established to look after the affairs of Bengal. The Chairman of the Executive Council was called Governor-General. Several types of reforms in Police, Judiciary, Taxation, Faujdari related Acts etc. took place during the time of Cornwallis.
  • Asiatic Society of Bengal was established on 15th January, 1784 A.D. in the tenure of Governor General Warren Hastings.
  • Warren Hastings and Wellesley were related to the Ring-Fence theory.
  • Impeachment proceedings were initiated on Hastings for injustices and atrocities committed by him but in the light of his service, proceedings which took place between the years 1788 A.D. and 1795 A.D. (until he was acquitted in April 1795) The following were the policies of Britishers towards Indian States (Princely States):-

1- Company’s struggle for equality with Indian provinces (1740-1765 AD)

2- Policy of Ring Fence (1765-1813 AD)

3- Policy of Subordinate Isolation (1813-1857 AD)

4- Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1935 AD)

5- Policy of Equal Federation (1935-1947 AD)

  • Britishers developed a new system forjustice delivery through hierarchical institutions consisting of Diwani and Faujdari Courts. This system was started by Warren Hastings but Cornwallis made it more rigid. He concentrated all powers in the hands of Collector. In 1787 A.D. the District Collector was made the Diwani Judge of Diwani Courts and was granted some Faujdari Powers to deliver Justice in some Faujdari cases too.
  • In 1790-92 AD, District Faujdari Courts with Indian Judges were abolished and in their place four Circuit Courts, three for Bengal and one for Bihar, were appointed. These Courts were headed by European officials and the Justice was delivered with the help of Indian Kazis and Muftis. Cornwallis initiated his rule of specification of law, it was a set of regulations that codified administrative, revenue and judicial reforms of East India Company in Bengal.
  • ‘Cornwallis Code’ is the collection of judicial reforms by Cornwallis in 1793 A.D. This reform was based on the law of ‘Separation of Powers’. He separated Revenue and Judicial administration. The judicial and faujdari power of collector was taken back and he was entrusted with powers related to taxation only.
  • A new hierarchy of officers was created for jobs in the District Diwani Courts. District Judges were given works of Faujdari and Police too. The modern Indian Civil Services was reorganised and professionalised by Cornwallis (1793). He forbade private trade and gifts, raised salaries, separated functions and gave legal form to civil service rules; he was regarded as the reformer of civil service. Lord Cornwallis was the Governor General of Bengal from 1786 to 1793 and from 30th July, 1805 A.D. to 5th October, 1805 A.D. He died at Ghazipur (Uttar Pradesh) on 5th October 1805 A.D. His grave is present in Ghazipur.
  • Treaty of Bassein (December, 1802) was made between Peshwa Bajirao II and Britishers. Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the Peshwa Bajirao II becoming the first Maratha chief to do so. According to subsidiary alliance, Peshwa accepted the offer of protection of English. As per the treaty, Britishers provided 6 thousands soldiers to reinstate Peshwa at Poona and the Peshwa promised lands are having revenues worth 26 lakhs annually as a payback.
  • Lord Wellesley (1798-1805 A.D.) cleverly used subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces as puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his Army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First such instances can be traced as 1765 treaty in Oudh/ Awadh (can be marked as the precursor of subsidiary alliance) where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Oudh on a fixed payment to the Company.
  • The evolved version of the Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad (1798 A.D. and 1800 A.D.), Mysore (1799 A.D.), Tanjore (October 1799 A.D.), Awadh (November 1801 A.D.), Peshwa (December 1802 A.D.), Bhonsle of Nagpur/ Berar (December 1803 A.D.). Sindhiya Bharatpur (1803-05) (February 1804 A.D.), Some other alliances include Jodhpur (1818), Udaipur/ Mewar (1818), Bundi (Feb., 1818), Bikaner (March, 1818) and Jaipur (April, 1818).
  • Lord William Bentinck in July 1828 A.D. assumed the office of Governor-General of Bengal. He took some bold steps to eliminate evil social practices such as Sati system, Female Infanticide etc. On the will of Court of Directors, he tried to adopt neutral policies towards the Princely Indian States wherever possible. Mismanagement in Jaipur one time grew so high that the British Resident was attacked there but William Bentinck did not interfere. Similarly, he did not interfere in the internal matters of Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota and Bhopal when he had enough reasons to do so. Deviating from this policy, he placed Mysore (in 1831 A.D.) and provinces of Kurg (1834 A.D.) and Kachhar (in 1832 A.D.) under British Empire because of extreme mismanagement prevailing there.
  • During the seven- year rule of William Bentinck (1828-35 A.D.) the old policies of war and annexation were abandoned or reduced. William Bentinck is remembered for his contributions in the field of Administrative and Social Reforms.
  • By the Charter Act of 1833 an attempt was made towards totally centralised Administration. Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India through this Act. Captain Sleeman was appointed by the William Bentinck to tackle the Thug Activities. He arrested 1562 thugs between 1826 to 1835 A.D. Many of them hanged and the rest of them were exiled. By 1839 A.D., the organiZed nature of Thugi ended.
  • By the declaration of 1789 A.D. the export of slaves from Bengal was stopped. Acts related to slaves were formulated in 1811 A.D. and 1823 A.D. The Charter Act of 1833 A.D. emphasized on formulating law by the Governor to end slavery as soon as possible. By 1843 A.D. slavery was declared illegal in most part of British India (it removed the enforceability of slave property in civil courts). In 1860 A.D., Indian Penal Code declared slavery as a crime. (IPC was repealed and Bhartiya Nyay Samhita came into force in 2024).
  • Anglo-Nepal War (1814-16 A.D.) took place during the time of Governor-General Lord Hastings (1813-23 A.D.) which ended with Sugauli’s Treaty.
  • In 1854 James Outram was made British resident of Oudh replacing Sleeman. He said the administration of Oudh is very polluted and the condition of the people was miserable. This report of Outram emerged as the base for the annexation of Awadh. Lord Dalhousie (1848-56 A.D.) blamed Nawab of Awadh Wajid Ali Shah for maladministration and, in February 1856 A.D., Awadh was annexed by Britishers. The States that were annexed through the policy of Doctrine of Lapse are - Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) etc.
  • Lord Dalhousie formulated the first comprehensive Railway Policy for India in 1853 and strongly promoted railway expansion, though the earliest railway proposals predated his tenure (like early plan of 1832 and Lord Hardinge 1844 plan etc.). The first railway line was laid between Bombay to Thane in 1853 A.D. The Great Indian Peninsula Railway started the train travel in India.
  • Main Reason for the development of railways was to export raw materials from the inner parts of the country to different Ports of India and also open Indian markets to British manufactured goods. Its second objective was the swift movement of Army in remote and distant areas to easily suppress any kind of revolt taking place in any part of the country.
  • Railway expansion in India accelerated particulary between 1880 and 1900, while Lord Curzon’s contribution was mainly administrative such as the establishment of the ‘Railway Board’ in 1905.
  • During Dalhousie a separate Public Work Department was established and a significant amount was spent on public work through this body.
  • With the efforts of Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar, Lord Canning in 1856 A.D., passed Hindu Widow Remarriage Act. According to Act XV (15) of 1856, widow remarriage and the Child born to that marriage was legalized. Dhondo Keshav Karve and Vishnu Shashtri were two propagators of widow remarriage. Dhondo Keshav in 1896 A.D. established a widow Ashram in Poona. On August 2, 1858 the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act 1858, transferring British power over India from East India Company. The act legally abolished the company and created the secretary of State. This act led to Queen’s Proclamation.
  • Queen’s Proclamation of 1858 was the most important result of the 1857 revolt. This proclamation was announced on 1st November, 1858 AD by Lord Canning at a Court held in Allahabad. The 1858 Act ended the Company rule and put the affairs of India under the direct control of the British Crown. Lord Canning was made first Viceroy of India. Queen Victoria was made the ruler of India in 1858 AD. A Grand Delhi Darbar organized in January 1877 AD. This Grand Durbar was organised by Lord Lytton, following the ‘Royal Titles Act 1876. During this, Queen Victoria was proclaimed ‘Empress/Sovereign of India’ & conferred with the title Kaiser-e-Hind (Qaiser-i-Hind).
  • Under Governor-General Auckland, first Anglo-Afghan war took place in 1839-1842 A.D. Lord Lytton was the Governor-General when second Anglo-Afghan war broke in 1878-1880 A.D. By Act-V of 1843 Slavery was abolished (removed legal enforce ability) by Governor-General of India Lord Ellenborough. During his tenure (1842-44 AD) in March 1843 AD Sindh was fully merged into British Empire. The policy of Masterly Inactivity in Anglo-Afghan relations was started during Lord Ellenborough and continued till Lord North Brooke. This period is called the Period of Masterly Inactivity. This policy is often recognized with John Lawrence because during his time at the office, he got full chance to follow this policy and evolution of this policy took place in his time only. Masterly Inactivity word is taken from an Article published by J.W.S. Wiley.
  • First Census took place in 1872 A.D. during Lord Mayo (1869-72 A.D.). Proper census took place in 1881 A.D. during Lord Rippon. Lord Mayo (1869-72 A.D.) was killed during an excursion in Andaman and Nicobar Islands group by a prisoner named Sher Ali Afridi. Mayo was the Viceroy who was killed while holding the office.
  • In 1876 A.D., Lytton became Viceroy and changed his policies towards Afghanistan.
  • Vernacular Press Act of 1878 A.D. was passed during Lord Lytton. This Act is also called the Gagging Act. (some historians also called this as silencing act due to its strict censorship). Sir Erskine Perry termed this act as a dangerous step towards India’s right to expression. Sri S.N. Banerjee termed this act as lightning from the sky.
  • Sir C.P. Ilbert who was the law member of Viceroy executive council, on 2nd February, 1883 in Legislative council presented a bill known as Ilbert Bill. This Bill was aimed at equalizing both European and Indian Judges so that Indian judges can hereby try a cases involving British subjects in various criminal cases changing the decade-old provision of barring Indian civil servants from doing so. This Bill was aimed at ending any judicial disqualification based on races. The Bill faced a severe opposition by Britishers as they perceived this as an attack on their privileges.
  • Lord Ripon is believed to be most pro Indian Viceroy of British India. He made some lenient laws in favour of children employed in factories numbering 100 or more, this was called as First Factory Act, 1881. According to this act, a ban was imposed on the employment of children below 7 years in factories and the working hours of children aged 7 to 12 years were reduced to 9 hours daily and they got 4 holidays in a month. Second Factory Act, 1891 made week holidays possible. Lord Ripon is known as the father of the local government. Charles Metcalfe removed the restrictions on the press, he is also known as the liberator of Indian Press. In 1784 A.D., Sir William Jones founded Asiatic Society in Calcutta and steps were taken towards Archaeological Survey of India. Alexander Cunningham was appointed as the Archaeological Surveyor in 1861. In 1871, Archaeological Survey was made a separate body and Cunningham was made its Director General.
  • During the tenure of Lord Curzon (1899-1905 A.D.) in 1901 The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) became centralized and the post of DG was restored and in 1902, John Marshall (who was appointed in 1901) assumed office of the Director General (DG) of this body. The Ancient Monument Preservation Act, 1904 allocated about 50,000 Pound for the protection and maintenance of the historical monuments of India.
  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale compared the rule of Curzon with Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb.
  • In November, 1905 Lord Minto replaced Lord Curzon and John Morley was made Secretary of State for India. They both proposed Morley-Minto Reforms (1909 A.D.) which granted separate electorate to Muslims. During the tenure of Lord Hardinge-II (Charles Hardinge) Capital of India was shifted to Delhi from Calcutta. He invited Queen Mary and George V in a Grand Darbar organized at Delhi which is known as third Delhi Darbar (1911 A.D.). In this Darbar, the partition of Bengal was abolished and the announcement was made for the transfer of Capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

1 paper question

Chapter 45

Economic Impact of British Rule on India

36 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (20 points)
  • The Indian administration was in British hands and was conducted in a manner subserving the interests of England.
  • Home charges refer to the expenditure incurred in England by the Secretary of State for India on behalfofIndia. It includes dividends to the shareholders of the East India Company, interest on public debt raised abroad, Civil and Military charges, store purchases in England etc.
  • Interest and profit on private foreign capital were another important leakage from the National Income System.
  • For banking, insurance and shipping services India had to make huge payments.
  • In British India, a term Imperial Preference was often used for the empire-wide preferential tariffarrangement (Concession given to British Imports in India). Under these arrangements, Britain pledged to maintain free entry for most colonial goods while imposing tariffs on foreign imports. This resulted in, almost no charge levied on British Imports but Indian Exports were charged heavily in Britain.
  • Strong preference to invest in land property by the rich class of India during British Rule proved detrimental for the development of Industries as they were low on Capital Investments.
  • In 1793 A.D. Cornwallis started Permanent Settlement of Land Revenue. Permanent Settlement was called by different names such as Istimrari, Malgujari and Bishwedari. This system was launched in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi of U.P. etc. Around 19% of British India was under Permanent Settlement. A new section of Zamindars was announced as landowners who were to provide 10/11 of the total revenue to Company and were paid the rest 1/11 of the total revenue for their duties. In the Permanent Settlement, Zamindars were small capitalist.
  • Ryotwari System was generated by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read. Alexander Read first implemented this land system in Baramahal district of Tamil Nadu. Later on, this system spread to Madras, some parts of Bombay, Assam and Coorg (a part of modern Karnataka) etc.
  • According to this system, the Ryots were given the ownership and rights to occupy the lands and they were required to pay the revenue directly to the government. By this system, the farmer was the owner of his land. A total of around 51% British India area was covered under this settlement. The rate of land taxes in this system was very high and the recovery of agricultural rent was handled very strictly.
  • Under Mahalwari System the unit for revenue settlement is the village or the mahal. The village land belongs to the village community. The community was jointly responsible for the payment of the land revenue.
  • This system prevailed in around 30% of British India covering United Provinces, Central Provinces and Punjab (with some changes).
  • The constant flow of wealth from India to England for which India did not receive any adequate economic, commercial or material return has been described by national leaders and economists as ‘drain’ of wealth from India. Before 1813 AD company had a recurring surplus which accrued from (a) profits from oppressive land revenue policy (b) profits from its trade resulting from monopolistic control over Indian markets and
  • (c) exactions made by the company’s officials. The surplus was used by the Company as an “investment”, i.e. for making a purchase ofexportable items in India and elsewhere. Against the exports of goods made out of this investment, India did not receive anything in return. This system was brought to an end by the charter act of 1813.
  • From 1813 AD onwards economic drain took the form of ‘unrequited’ exports. Dadabhai Naoroji described the drain of wealth as the “evil of all evils” and the main cause of Indian poverty.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji was one of the earliest and most prominent propounder of the Drain of Wealth theory. He with his articles and books ‘England’s Duties to India’ (paper), ‘Poverty and Un-British Rule in India’, ‘The wants and means of India’ and ‘On the commerce of India’ propounded his Drain of wealth theory.
  • Romesh Chunder Dutt also emphasized the drain of wealth theory. In his Article ‘The Economic History of India’ He proposed that half of the net revenues of India is being outflowed every year.
  • Indian National Congress in 1896 A.D. accepted the Drain Theory in Calcutta session and announced that the real cause for frequent famines and the poverty of Indian nationals is the ongoing Drain of Wealth for the previous years.
  • Syed Ahmad Khan was loyal towards British Rule and he believed that the development of Muslim Community could take place with British government only.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji (1825-1917 A.D.) along with W.C. Bonnerjee established London Indian Society in 1865 A.D. which popularized the severe exploitation and the pain of Indian nationals.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons on the ticket of the Liberal Party in 1892 A.D.

Chapter 46

Revolt of 1857

72 facts · 11 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (30 points)
  • In December 1856, the East India Company decided to replace the old iron made Brown Bess (standardised musket) with new and advanced Enfield Rifle (musket). Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot were decided the place for the training and trials of the new Gun. The Rifle required the biting of the upper part of the cartridge by mouth the rumours was that catridges were deliberately greased. In January 1857, rumours spread that the cartridge contained fats of cow and pig. The soldiers believed this new Rifle is an attempt to destroy their religions by the British. It became the immediate reason for the Revolt of 1857. The first sepoys to refuse catridged related practice were at Berhampore in late February 1857. Later, the refusal spread to other places. On 29th March, 1857 soldiers of Barrakpore refused to use the fat-containing cartridges and, Mangal Pandey attacked and Shot and wounded two of their officers, they were sergeant Major James Thorton Hewson and Lieutenant and Adjutant Bebpde Henry Baugh, at Barrackpore. One of the reasons for the Revolt of 1857 was the exploitative policies of Britishers and it was the outflow of all the dissents and grievances of Indians all of a sudden as an explosion in Volcano.
  • Anglo-Indian historians believed the Soldier’s discontentment and the fat-containing cartridges were the main and important reason for the Revolt of 1857. But modern historians proved this as only a reason followed by several other reasons. The fat-containing cartridges were just a spark which started the explosions of the explosives which were accumulated due to political, social, religious and economic discontent of Indians against the exploitative policies of British Rule.
  • Revolt of1857 started on 10th May, 1857 from Meerut, where the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry regiment (85 out of90 cavalries) refused to receive the new cartridges and openly rebelled against the authorities. They fired on their officers released their imprisoned comrades from jail and marched towards Delhi. Major General William Hewitt had 2200 European soldiers but he didn’t try to stop this storm. Rebels captured Delhi on 12th May, 1857 AD. During the revolt of 1857, the message was conveyed by circulation of Chappatis (Bread) and lotus flowers, which is marked as the symbol of revolt.
  • Khan Bahadur Khan from Rohilkhand, led the Revolt from Bareilly. He was appointed as the Viceroy in Rohilkhand by Mughal King Bahadur Shah II.
  • Rani Lakshmi Bai (Manikarnika) was born on C. 19th November 1828 at Kashi/Benaras (now Varanasi). At the age of 14 Laxmibai was married to Maharaja Gangadhar Rao who died in Gwalior. Rani Laxmi Bai was the widow of Maratha king Maharaja Gangadhar Rao. When Gangadhar Rao died by leaving his adopted son (Damodar Rao) as his heir, but the British did not recognise the adoption and imposed Doctrine of Lapse. Dalhousie by Doctrine of lapse, annexed Jhansi to British Empire in 1854.
  • In June, 1857, the revolt began in Jhansi under the leadership of Rani Laxmi Bai (the revolt in Jhansi was outbreaked/began by sepoys Laxmibai Later assumed control and led resistance). She died on 17/18 June, 1858 A.D. fighting General Hugh Henry Rose. On her death, Hugh Rose said, “Among the Indian revolutionaries the women lying here is the only man.”
  • Revolt in Lucknow began under the leadership of Begum Hazrat Mahal on 30th May, 1857 A.D. She declared her minor son Birjis Qadr as Nawab and took to all affairs of the Lucknow into herself. On 21st March, 1858 A.D., Campbell with the help of Gurkha Regiment regained Lucknow.
  • On 5 June 1857, the rebel repoys halted at Kalyanpur; on 6 June they returned to Kanpur, where Nana Saheb (Nana Dhondhu Pant) assumed their leadership. He was later proclaimed/declared Peshwa at Kanpur (on June 30, 1857 as recorded by R.C. Majumdar) and the war of Independence spread in Kanpur.

He was helped a lot by Commander-in-Chief (his General Military Advisor) Tatya Tope, The original name of Tatya Tope was Ramchandra Pandurang Tope. After being betrayed by a close friend Man Singh, he was captured when he was camping in a forest. Tope was captured on 7 April 1859, after a hurried trial the military court gave the verdict on 15th April 1859 punishing him with death by hanging and he was hanged on 18th April 1859 at Sipri/Shivpuri.

  • Kunwar Singh led the revolt from Jagdishpur (currently Bhojpur district), Bihar. He was from Shahabad region of Bihar.
  • Maniram Dutt Deewan in Assam declared Kandarpeswar Singha, the grandson of the last king as the king and planned an armed insurrection conspiracy. But soon after Maniram Deewan was caught and hanged for his promotional activities regarding the revolt.
  • Thakur Kushal Singh of Auwa defeated the combined army of English and Jodhpur.
  • Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah provided leadership to the revolt from Faizabad (Ayodhya) in 1857 A.D. He was a determined opponent of British rule. He was native to Chinapattan of Madras, but he migrated to Faizabad. He asked all the different religious believers to stand as one against these English foreigners and to wipe them out from India. About him, Britishers said a man of great abilities, of undaunted courage of stern determination; and best soldier among the rebels. A bounty of Rs. 50,000 was placed on his arrest (dead or alive).
  • Mirza Ghalib saw the revolt of1857 A.D. with his own eyes. He was born on 27 December, 1797 AD in Agra and died in Delhi on 15 February, 1869.
  • Shindhiyas of Gwalior helped the Britishers in the suppression of the Revolt.
  • Minister of Gwalior Sir Dinkar Rao was praised by European historians for his loyalty to English. Minister of Hyderabad Salar Jung was praised in the same way for his loyalty.
  • The revolt of 1857 was spread over a wide area and was substantially supported by the public. But still, this Revolt was unable to bring whole of India together. This revolt did not become an all-India revolt; South India remained largely quiet, while Bengal and Punjab were only marginally affected though parts of eastern and western India were involved.
  • Scindia of Gwalior, Holkar of Indore, Nizam of Hyderabad, King of Jodhpur, Nawab of Bhopal, Sikh rulers of Patiala, Nabha and Jind and other Sikh Sardar of Punjab, Maharaja of Kashmir and other kings were actively helping the Britishers in suppressing the revolts. To these rulers, Governor-General Canning said, that these rulers acted as barriers against the high and fast-moving wave of seas, in the absence of which we would have washed out from India completely. The Educated Class didn’t show any interest in the Revolt of 1857 they generally remained neutral or sided with the British, viewing the rebellion as a regressive, reactionary and anti-modern movement; which was one of the major causes of the failure of this Revolt.
  • Lord Canning (1856-62 A.D.) was the Governor-General during the revolt of1857. During the Revolt, he made Allahabad as an emergency headquarter. Lord Canning was the last Governor-General appointed by the Company and was the first Viceroy appointed by the British Crown.
  • Under the judicial reforms, Indian High Court Act, 1861 established High Courts at Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. After enabling 1861 Act, the courts were formally established by the ‘Letters Patent of 1862 under Lord Canning. Under the social reforms Canning passed Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, 1856. The Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 is known as First War of Independence in India and as an Indian Mutiny in England.
  • Sir Syed Ahmed Khan wrote Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind which was written/ submitted in 1858 and published in 1859 A.D.
  • R.C Majumdar was appointed by Government of India to write on the Revolt of 1857, but due to differences with the government committee he rejected this proposal, and he published his book “The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857” on his own in 1957 (although his original proposal was turned down in first instance, later he became member of ‘Board of Editors’ for history of the freedom movement but later discontinued with this service & wrote independently).
  • R.C. Majumdar said, “ It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the so-called First National War of Independence of 1857 is neither First, nor National, nor a war of Independence”.
  • Most important outcome of 1857 was the Queen’s Proclamation of 1858. It was declared on 1st November, 1858 in Allahabad by Lord Canning ending the Company Rule and putting the Realm of British India under the direct control of Crown. This declaration included no extension of British India’s then present territorial possessions no further interference in the religious matters of people, equal protection of law to be available to all. British stopped all further annexation of native states and kings were allowed to adopt.
  • Approximately after the Suppression of 1857 Revolt, ‘Peel Commission’ was constituted for the reorganization of Indian Army by British Government. The Commission divided the army on the basis of caste, religion, race, community, etc. The number of European soldiers was increased from 45,000 in 1857 A.D. to 65,000 by 1863 A.D. Indian troops were reduced from 2,38,000 to 1,40,000.The ratio of Europeans to Indian soldiers in Bengal was 1:2 whereas in Madras and Bombay it was 1:3. After the Revolt the soldiers the recruitment of Gorkha, Sikh and Punjab is increased
  • John Bennet Hearsey was the commanding officer of Barrakpore when Revolt of 1857 broke out there.
  • Viscount Palmerston was the then Prime Minister of United Kingdom. His tenure as Prime Minister was from 1855 to 1858 and 1859 to 1865.
  • The Revolt was poorly organized with least coordination or nominal central leadership. The rebels lacked a clear understanding of Colonial Rule, they have a myopic views of forward-looking programme, a coherent ideology, a political perspective or societal alternatives. Although official sources record substantial Hindu-Muslim and inter-regional unity among many rebels, but many central leaderships lack unity and which proved to be detrimental to this revolt. Modern Nationalism was not known to them at that time, which led to everyone fighting for their own interests and not for the nation. Except with the common shared hatred for alien rule in their own land.
  • Brigadier General John Nicholson died on 23rd September, 1857, Who was wounded nine days before while leading his men to capture Delhi. The Delhi was captured by British on September 20-21, 1857. Sir Henry Montgomery Lawrence Chief Commissioner of Oudh (‘Lawrence of Lucknow’), mortally wounded on July 2, died on July 4, 1857 in Lucknow in the 1857 revolt while protecting British residency. Brigadier General James George Smith Neill died in September 1857 while attempting to reach the Residency during the siege. Major-General Sir Henry Havelock was died on dysentery in November 1857 a few days after the siege was lifted. Sir James Outram and W. Taylor termed the Revolt of1857 as a result of a conspiracy of Hindu and Muslim. Outram said that this was a Muslim conspiracy in which the Hindus concerns were used for the Revolt. It was only a Sepoy Mutiny, according to John Lawrence and Seeley. According to T.R. Holmes, it was a war between Barbarism and Civilization. V. D. Savarkar in his book “The Indian War of Independence 1857”, termed this Revolt as an organized struggle for Independence. He said it was the First War of Independence.
  • Surendra Nath Sen whose book ‘Eighteen Fifty-Seven’ was published in 1957 was commissioned by Indian government to write history of 1857 and was the first Director of the National Archives of India.
