Chapter 47

Other Civil Uprisings

67 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (34 points)
  • The revolt of 1857 causes other civil uprising because it gave confidence to fight against British. The immediate revolt was Indigo revolt. The Indigo Revolt (1859-60 A.D.) took place in Bengal immediately after the revolt of1857. Sanyasi Rebellion occurred in 1763-1800 A.D., Santhal Rebellion occurred in 1855-56 A.D., and Pabna uprising took place in 1873-76 A.D.
  • Indigo revolt was started in Govindpur village of Nadia district in West Bengal. Farmers there stopped the Indigo cultivation under the leadership of two workers Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas who had once worked for an Indigo cultivator. By 1860, Indigo movement had spread to Nadia, Pabna, Khulna, Dhaka, Malda, Dinajpur etc. The intelligentsia of Bengal through public meetings, journals and articles in newspaper popularized the movement. Harishchandra Mukherjee, the editor of ‘Hindu Patriot’, played a major role in this. Through ‘Neel Darpan’, Dinabandhu Mitra openly visualised the atrocities of Indigo plantation owners on the farmers there. ‘Vande Mataram’ song is derived from the famous Novel Anandamath written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee. The plot of this novel is based on Sanyasi Revolt. ‘Vande Mataram’ was sung for the first time in Congress session of Calcutta in 1896.
  • Wahabi Movement which continued from the 4th to 7th decade of the 19th century provided an organized and stiff resistance to Britishers. Syed Ahmad Barelvi of Rae Bareli was the proponent of this movement. He was inspired by Abdul Wahab of Arabia but, in India, the movement was majorly inspired by Shah Waliullah of Delhi. By the efforts of Syed Ahmad Barelvi, this ideology soon spread to Northwest frontier provinces, Bengal, Bihar, Kabul and Central provinces. He captured Peshawar for some time in 1830 but he was killed in the battle of Balakot (1831). He introduced coins with his name in Peshawar. After the death of Syed Ahmad Barelvi, Patna became centre of this movement. During this period the leadership was provided by Maullavi Qasim, Vilayat Ali, Inayat Ali, Ahmadullah etc. After Patna, the branches of this movement were established in Hyderabad, Madras, Bengal, U.P. and Bombay.

The Namdhar Movement, popularly known as the Kuka Movement, was a socio-religious reform movement among Sikhs in Punjab in the mid 19th century. The movement was initiated by Bhagat Jawahar Mal (Sai Sahib) and Baba Balak Singh, who emphasised devotion to one God, spiritual purity and revival of Sikh religious values. It later developed into a powerful reform movement under Baba Ram Singh (1816- 1885), who organised the Namdhari sect and expanded its influence among Sikh masses. The movement was called “Kuka” because followers used to shout ecstatic cries called “Kuk” during religious devotion. Baba Ram Singh preached monotheism, prayer, meditation (Naam Simran) and strict moral discipline among followers. He opposed social evils such as caste system, female infanticide, early marriage, and the practice of exchanging daughters in marriage. He also popularised simple and inexpensive Anand marriages, promoting social reform and equality. The movement gradually acquired political overtones and resistance against British rule, which made British authorities suspicious of its growing popularity. The 1872 Kuka uprising in Punjab against cow slaughter and British authority was severely suppressed by the British administration. He died in 1885 while in exile as a state prisoner in Mergui, Burma (now Myanmar), where he had been held by the British since 1872.

  • Pagal Panth was a semi-religious group founded by Karim/ Karam Shah. Tribal peasants organised themselves under Karim/Karam Shah’s son, Tipu Shah, to fight the oppression of Zamindars. Tipu Shah (1852) was the leader of the Pagal Panthi movement after the death of his father Karim Shah in 1813. Under him, the movement changed from a religious group into a peasant rebellion against oppressive zamindars and indirectly against the English East India Company. The main cause of the revolt was the heavy oppression and extra taxes imposed on raiyats (peasants). After the division of the Sherpur zamindari in 1820, litigation and Company financial pressures led zamindars to increase tax burdens further. Tipu Shah declared that land belonged equally to all human beings as God’s creation and that an oppressive ruler had no moral right to rule. Under Tipu Shah and his mother Chandi Bibi (Pir-Mata), the rebels fought several clashes and established an independent administration in the Sherpur area for over two years. Gar-jaripa, a mud fort north of Sherpur, became his capital. Tipu Shah was arrested multiple times between December 1824 and January 1825, then tried and imprisoned. Even after his arrest, leaders like Janku Pathor and Dubraj Pathor continued the movement for some time.
  • The Faraizis were the followers of a Muslim sect founded by Haji Shariatullah of Faridpur in Eastern Bengal. They advocated radical religious, social and political changes. Shariatullah’s son Dudu Miyan organised his followers with the aim oforganising the oppressed peasantry against oppressive landlords and Indigo planters. This revolt continued from 1818 to 1862 A.D. and further, at the end, the followers of this sect got merged into Wahabi Movement.
  • Wellesley in 1805 compelled Maharaja of Travancore (Kerala) to accept the subsidiary alliance. Maharaja was very unhappy with this alliance and was hesitating towards completing some of its terms. The behaviour of the English resident was rude and was full of hatred as a result of this Diwan Velu Thampi with the support of Nair Battalion revolted against them.
  • Vasudev Balwant Phadke (1845-83 A.D.) was one of the leading earliest Indian revolutionaries who organized the Ramoshi tribes and trained them into a fighting force. He founded Ramoshi farmers group.
  • Gadakaris were the hereditary workers on the Maratha forts. Gadakaris were hereditary fort-servants/garrison men/fort-keepers attached to Maratha forts, especially in the Kolhapur region. They were dismissed/disbanded from their traditional fort service under British-controlled administrative changes, which caused resentment. Their lands were brought under the control/supervision of the Mamlatdar (mamlatdar/ mamlatdars). These situations made them to revolt in 1844-45 A.D. at Kolhapur.
  • The Khonds tribes spread in the hills of Orissa/Odisha and neighbouring districts, they were virtually independent. They rebelled against the British from 1846 to 1855 AD. Chakra Bisoi, a young king, led the Khonds who were joined by the Ghumsar, Kalahandi and other tribals to oppose the abolition of human sacrifices (Mariah), the introduction of new taxes and the entry of Zamindars into their areas. Khonds opposed the establishment of Mariah Agency.
  • Kol Revolt was led by Buddho Bhagat in Chhotanagpur area in 1831-32 A.D. This movement continued intermittently later and was finally suppressed.
  • Waghera Revolt in Okha mandal region of Gujarat was against Britishers. It took place in 1818-1819.

The Chronological order of the main revolts in India before 1857 is –

1. Bengal Sepoy Mutiny (1764), in which a group of sepoys in the Army of Hector Munro revolted and went to join the side of Mir Qasim during the battle of Buxar.

2. Vellore Sepoy Mutiny (1806 A.D.)

3. Revolt of Kutch (1816-32 A.D.)

4. Kol Revolt (1831-32 A.D.)

5. Santhal Revolt (1855-56 A.D.)

  • In 1855-56 A.D., Santhal was an important tribal revolt in which we see a lot of tribal anger and hatred against the Britishers. The Revolt took place in the Damin-e-Koh area between Bhagalpur and Rajmahal hills. Moneylenders and Britishers were exploiting them together. Interest ranging from 50 to 500% was charged from the Santhal borrowers. Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav were four brothers who led this revolt. Sidhu once said to officials, “God said to me that this country is not of bosses. God will fight from our side and in

this way, these bosses and soldiers will fight with God.”

The revolt continued till 1856 A.D., at last, Sido (Sidhu) was arrested and hanged and Kanu was killed in action and the revolt was suppressed. In 1855 A.D., Santhals revolted in Bhognadih near Barhait of Sahibganj district. Santhals defeated the Army of Britishers led by Major Burroughs. Finally Commissioner of Bhagalpur Brown and Major General Lloyd ruthlessly suppressed the revolt.

Bhil revolts - Bhils community which lived on the upland basin in the Deccan table land of Khandesh revolted against English in 1818-31 A.D. Officials blamed Peshwa Bajirao II and his representative Trimbakji Dengle for inciting the Bhils to revolt. In reality, the agricultural hardship and the fear of the new English government were the main reasons for this revolt. In 1825 A.D., under the leadership of Sevaram, Bhils revolted again. Britishers ruthlessly suppressed the revolt for the second time with some efforts.

Rampa Rebellion - Rampa hilly area lies north of the Godavari river in Andhra Pradesh. The Tribal revolt was against the exploitation by Moneylenders and the Forest Acts.

  • The second half of 19th Century, Surji Bhagat and Govind Guru named Social reformers tried to bring some reforms in the tribal communities residing in Mewar of Rajasthan, Dungarpur, Banswada, Pratapgarh, Sirohi, Pali, etc. Govind Guru (also called as Lasodhiya) established ‘Samp Sabha’ in 1883 A.D. with an aim to organize Bhils. He is also called as the propounder of Lasodhiya Movement.
  • Birsa Munda led the Revolt of Munda tribes in 1895-1900 A.D. Collective farming prevailed in the Munda community but zamindars, contractors, moneylenders, etc. attacked this tradition to carve out their own interests. Mundas leaders fought for about 30 years to preserve their traditional farming. Sardari fight (Sardari Larai) was the earlier Munda agrarian agitation, while Birsa Munda’s later rebellion is also known as Munda Rebellion or Ulgulan (Great Tumult). In 1895, Birsa declared himself the Messenger of God. The revolt was most famous among the revolts of this time. The revolt started against the attempt to replace the traditional collective farming practices with the Zamindari or Individual ownership practices.
  • Khunt Katti or Mundari was the Customary land tenure/common ownership (Khunt-Katti system) practice of Mundas. But with the passage of time, Birsa transformed this revolt into a religious and political movement. He is called ‘Jagat Pita’ or ‘Dharti Aaba’. He said ‘we will fight with non-tribals and will colour this land red with their blood like a Red Flag’. In February, 1900 A.D., Birsa was arrested and died in prison in June 1900 A.D. The area between (Ranchi Khunt) and Singhbhum side areas (e.g- Chakradharpur) was under his influence. He called for the worship of one god ‘Sing Bonga’ renouncing the worship of other gods.
  • Thakkar Bapa used word ‘Adivasi’ for the tribal population. He was the General Secretary of ‘Harijan Sevak Sangh’.
  • Hauz(Ho) Revolt of 1820-21 A.D. took place in then Santhal subdivision of Bihar (Now Singhbhum district Jharkhand).
  • Khairwar tribal movement in 1874 A.D. was led by Bhagirath Manjhi.
  • Surendra Sai the claimant to throne of Sambalpur led the movement against British. In 1862, he surrendered.
  • Moplah Revolt took place in 1921 A.D. in Malabar area (Tirurangadi) Here the Muslims were the major sharecropper tenants and Hindus were Zamindars. The revolt took place due to exploitation by Zamindars resistance against British Raj and Khilafat movement.
  • Ahom Revolt (1828 A.D.) was led by Gomdhar Kunwar.
  • Tana Bhagat Movement was started in 1914 at Chhotanagpur by Oraon tribes. Jatra Bhagat, Balram Bhagat and Devmenia Bhagat led this revolt.
  • Jadonang was the first tribal leader inspired by Mahatma Gandhi and his philosophy. He was a pioneer freedom fighter for Naga community in Manipur.

Bengal upheaval just after 1857 → Indigo Revolt (1859-60), began at Govindpur, Nadia, led by Digambar and Bishnu Biswas; 'Neel Darpan' by Dinabandhu Mitra. Must know

Don't confuse Sanyasi 1763-1800, Santhal 1855-56 and Pabna 1873-76 are not right after 1857.

Chapter 48

Development of Education in Modern India

35 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (19 points)
  • The Calcutta Madarsa was established by Warren Hastings in 1780 A.D. for the study of Muslim law and related subjects. Mulla Majduddin was the first principal (Najin) of this Madarsa. Farsi, Arabic and Muslim law were taught in this Madarsa and the graduates from here worked as interpreters in the British Raj.
  • The Sanskrit College was established in 1791 by Jonathan Duncan, (the resident at Benaras), for the study of Hindu law, philosophy and literature.
  • Raja Rammohan Roy was granted the membership in the Asiatic Society of Paris (Societe Asiatique).
  • Halhed, in 1778, published Bengali grammars namely – ‘A grammer of the Bengal Language’.
  • Sir William Jones was appointed the Judge of the Supreme Court in Calcutta during the tenure of Warren Hastings. On his initiative, in 1784, Asiatic Society was established and he himself became its first President. This Society, through publication named Asiatick Researches tried to shed light on India’s past. In this order, in 1789, he translated Abhigyan (Abhijnan) Shakuntalam of Kalidas into English.
  • To analyse the educational development after 1854 in India, in 1882, W.W. Hunter led Hunter Commission was established. The report of this commission emphasized on reform and development of the primary education in India.
  • On 8th November, 1905, Rangpur National School was established. It was the first milestone in the National Education Sector.
  • On 16th November 1905, a session was organized in Calcutta and decision was taken to establish National Council of Education, Bengal to provide education related to Science, national literature and technology. Satish Chandra Mukherjee and others constituted the National Council of Education, Bengal on 11 March, 1906; the Bengal National College was inaugurated later on 14 August, 1906.
  • By Charter Act of 1813 an arrangement was made to spend not less than one lakh rupees per year on Education.
  • Sadler Commission was related to education. Government constituted a commission to study the possibilities of Calcutta University in 1917. Dr. M.E. Sadler who was the Vice-Chancellor of Leeds University, was appointed the chiefof the commission. Dr. Ashutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Ziauddin Ahmad were two Indian members of the commission. The commission was asked to inquire into the problems of Calcutta University and to make wider recommendations on secondary, intermediate and university education. The commission suggested that if an improvement is desired in the education system of the university, then the standards of secondary education are required to be listed first.
  • William Bentinck appointed Macaulay (the law member of Governor General Executive Council) as head of Committee of Public Instruction to present a description of the dispute regarding the medium (language) of the Indian education system. Macaulay advocated English as the language of Indian education.
  • The theory of downward filtration is related to education sector in colonial times. According to this theory, education should be firstly granted to a higher section of society which later on percolates slowly downward in the Society.
  • The seed of the modern education system in India was sown by the Lord Macaulay Minute (1835). Lord Macaulay held the view that Indian learning was inferior to European learning, He said. “A single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole literature of India and Arabia”. The proposal of Macaulay was accepted by Lord William Bentinck on 7th March, 1835. During the tenure of William Bentinck, on 7th March, 1835, English was officially accepted as the medium of Indian Education.
  • Considered as the “Magna Carta of English Education in India,” Charles Wood’s Despatch (1854 A.D.) was the first comprehensive plan for the spread of education In India. It proposed three Universities at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay to be established on the patterns of London University. By the efforts of D. K. Karve first Women’s university was established at Pune (1916). ‘Karve’ was a Social worker and reformer in Maharashtra. In 1896 A.D., he established 'Home for Widows' (Now-Maharshi Karve Stree Shikshan Samstha) in Poona. He himself married a Brahmani widow. In 1958 A.D., he was awarded the Bharat Ratna Award.
  • New English school was started by V.K. Chiplumkar, Bal Gangadhar Tilak & G.G. Agarkar in 1880 A.D. in Pune. Later Deccan Education Society was established and Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Mahadeo Ballal Namjoshi, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and Vaman Shivram Apte were the main founders of the Society.
  • Raja Ram Mohan Roy was among the earliest propagators of Modern Education in India. He along with David Hare established famous “Hindu College” in 1817 A.D.
  • Mayo College was established in Ajmer in 1875 A.D. Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College was established in Aligarh in 1875 A.D. Delhi College was established in 1824 A.D.
  • Madan Mohan Malaviya advocated religious teachings in the Indian Universities.
  • In 1916, he established Banaras Hindu University and was the vice-chancellor of BHU from 1919 to 1939 A.D.. He published several magazines and Newspapers in English and Hindi such as Hindustan, India Union, Abhyudaya, Maryada, etc.

Chapter 49

Development of Press in Modern India

62 facts · 13 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (28 points)
  • James Augustus Hicky in 1780 A.D. started the Bengal Gazette, the first newspaper in India. Lord Wellesley enacted Censorship of Press Regulations, 1799. It imposed almost wartime press restrictions including pre-censorship. In 1807 this Act included pamphlets, books and magazines too.
  • Lord Hastings in 1818 abolished the strict pre-censorship of the press in India and dispensed with their submitting their papers to an officer of government previous to publications. Vernacular Press Act, 1878 was passed during the tenure of Lord Lytton (1876-1880 A.D.). The Act empowered the district magistrate to call upon the printer and publisher of any vernacular newspaper to enter into a bond with the government not to cause disaffection against the government or antipathy between persons of different religion, caste, race, through published material.
  • The press and publisher could also be required to deposit security which could be forfeited ifthe regulation were violated, and press equipment could be seized if the offence reoccurred.
  • Under this Act, proceedings were instituted against Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash and Samachar.
  • B. G. Tilak was imprisoned for anti-British journalism in 1882. He was the first Indian to be punished for the performance of his duty in this field.
  • Tilak was arrested after the murder of W.C. Rand and officer Charles Ayerst on the grounds of the publication of a poem, “Shivaji’s utterances” in Kesari, and a speech that Tilak had delivered at the Shivaji festival, justifying Afzal’s Khan murder by Shivaji. Tilak’s defence of Shivaji’s killing of Afzal Khan was portrayed by the prosecution as an incitement to kill British officials. In 1897, he was imprisoned for 18 months for inciting Chapekar brothers for killing W.C. Rand and Charles Ayerst through his articles published in Kesari (he was charged for sedition for writing such articles).
  • 'The Free Hindustan' newspaper was started by Tarak Nath Das in North America (Vancouver).
  • Raja Ram Mohan Roy used the press as a medium to express and publish his views. In 1821 he published ‘Sambad Kaumudi’ Bengali weekly newspaper. After one year he published a newspaper ‘Mirat ul-Akhbar’ in the Persian language. ‘Indian Mirror’ was published from Calcutta (Bengal). Credit for establishment of Indian Mirror (1861) goes to Debendranath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh.
  • Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakana and Kartar Singh Sarabha, etc. founded Hindustan Ghadar Party (Ghadar Party) in USA and Canada to free India from British Rule. ‘Ghadar’ a weekly publication, was a manifesto of the party which was first published on 1st November, 1913 at San Francisco in Urdu. From 9th December, 1913 A.D. its printing in Gurmukhi script also started. It was later on published in Marathi, Hindi, English and Gujarati. Its one edition was also published in Pashto language.
  • Amrit Bazar Patrika, a Bengali (later English) weekly was launched February 20, 1868, in the village of Palua Magura in the Jessore district of Present day Bangladesh, through the efforts of Sishir Kumar and Motilal Ghosh. But later it started being published from Kolkata (West Bengal), but to escape the Vernacular Press Act, it got converted to English format overnight in 1878 A.D.
  • Girish Chandra Ghosh started ‘The Bengalee’ in 1862 A.D. which was transferred to S.N. Banerjee in 1879 A.D. Girish Chandra Ghosh started the Hindoo Patriot. Later on, Harish Chandra Mukherjee became its editor.
  • In 1881 A.D., Tilak published two newspapers Kesari and Mahratta in Poona (now Pune). Kesari in Marathi was the main newspaper of Tilak’s Home Rule Movement. Earlier Gopal Ganesh Agarkar was the first editor of Kesari. The first editor of the Maratta/ Maratha was Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Mahratta was published in English.
  • Bangwasi, Kaal, Kesari etc. Newspaper supported the revolutionary movements and criticized the moderate policies of Congress. Sandhya, Yugantar and Kaal, advocated revolutionary extremism during the freedom struggle.
  • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar in 1858 started publishing ‘Som Prakash’ newspaper, it supported the interests of the Indigo revolutionaries. Vidyasagar mooted the original idea of the newspaper, it was first edited by Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan. The Free Press Journal is an English-language daily newspaper that was established by Swaminathan Sadanand.
  • Indian opinion was started by Mahatma Gandhi in 1903 A.D. in South Africa. Mansukh Lal Hiralal Nazar was its first editor. It was published in Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil and English.
  • Young India was published bi-weekly from Bombay from 7 May 1919 A.D. under supervision of Gandhiji. Jamanadas Dwarakadas and Shankarlal Banker were its foundational member Shankar Lal Banker was its publisher. On 8th October, 1919 A.D. Mahatma Gandhi became the editor of Young India and it was started publishing weekly from Ahmedabad. Jamanadas Dwarakadas and Shankar lal Banker were members of Home Rule Movement of Annie Besant.
  • Indigo Revolt of Bengal was a direct fight against the exploitation of farmers. Harishchandra Mukherjee editor of Hindoo Patriot put a lot of effort in this respect. Girish Chandra Ghosh was the editor of Hindoo Patriot in the first two years (1853-55 A.D.). In 1855 A.D., Harish Chandra Mukherjee became the editor of Hindoo Patriot. He boldly spoke about the exploitation of Indigo farmers by the plantation owners. He helped these farmers in all possible ways. Kristodas Pal in 1861 became the editor of Hindoo Patriot.
  • Aurobindo Ghosh was the editor of English weekly Bande Matram.
  • In 1931 A.D., Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga started The Indian Nation. It was published in Patna.
  • Ram Krishna Pillai was the editor of Swadeshabhamini.
  • Gandhiji started Harijan in English, Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati and Harijan Sewak in Hindi. These were weekly newspapers. First edition of Harijan was published on 11th February, 1933 A.D. from Pune, Maharashtra.
  • On July 1924 A.D., B.R. Ambedkar in Bombay founded an institute called ‘Bahiskrit Hitakarini Sabha’ whose aim was to promote untouchables morally and physically. He started a fortnightly bulletin Bahishkrit Bharat (first published in 1927)
  • Abul Kalam Azad in 1912 A.D. started an Urdu weekly called Al-Hilal. Al-Balagh was published in 1915 A.D. by him. Al-Hilal was banned in 1914 A.D. by Press Act.
  • Lala Lajpat Rai started the Vande Mataram (1905-06) an Urdu daily and The People (1925, Lahore), a weekly in English. Before this, he had already published Young India (1916) in America.
  • George Allen published ‘The Pioneer’ newspaper in 1865 at Allahabad (Prayagraj).
  • Qaumi Awaz an Urdu newspaper was started by Jawaharlal Nehru and Rafi Ahmed Kidwai in 1945 A.D. Its publication was stopped in 2008.
  • Rast Goftar is a newspaper related to Dadabhai Naoroji. Motilal Nehru demanding independence of India (or Home Rule for India) started a newspaper called The Independent in February 1919 at Allahabad.
  • The Commonweal was an English newspaper published in Madras by Annie Besant.

Chapter 50

Socio-Religious Movements

101 facts · 24 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • The dawn of the nineteenth century witnessed the birth of a new vision, a modern vision, among some enlightened sections of the Indian society. This enlightened vision was to shape the course of events for decades to come and even beyond. This process of reawakening, sometimes but not with full justification defined as ‘Renaissance’, did not always follow the intended line and gave rise to some undesirable by-products as well, which have become as much a part of daily existence in the whole of the Indian subcontinent as the fruits of these reform movements.
  • Raja Ram Mohan Roy often called the Father of Indian Renaissance is also known by names like ‘Prophet of Indian Nationalism’, Father of Modern India, ‘First Modern Man’ and ‘Yugdoot’. In 1815 A.D. he set up the Atmiya Sabha in Calcutta to propagate Monotheistic ideals of Hindu religion among his youth followers (mostly rich and influential). In 1828 A.D. he founded Brahmo Sabha, which was later renamed Brahmo Samaj.
  • Devendranath Tagore founded Tattvabodhini Sabha to propagate rational thinking, study ancient texts (like Upanishad) and spread the ideals of Rajaram Mohan Roy in 1839 A.D. Brahmo Samaj was the first reform movement in the Hindu religion which was influenced by modern western liberal ideas and a new reading of ancient Indian texts.
  • Mughal Emperor Akbar II gave Raja Ram Mohan Roy the title of Raja and sent him to the court of British King William IV as his ambassador in 1830. Roy was sent there to discuss about the increment in the pension of Akbar II. On 27th September, 1833 Raja Ram Mohan Roy died at Bristol in England. The mausoleum of Roy is present at Bristol.
  • Raja Ram Mohan Roy advocated English Education in India. According to him, a moderate Western education is necessary to pull us out of the darkness and to provide Indians with partnership in the administration of the country. He opposed idol worship, Child marriage, practice of Sati etc. evil social practices of India.
  • Ramakrishna Paramahamsa emphasized that Hari, Ram, Allah, and Christ are different names for the same God and that there are many ways to God and salvation.
  • Swami Vivekananda spread Ramakrishna’s message and tried to reconcile it to needs of contemporary Indian Society. He emerged as the preacher of Neo-Hinduism. At the Parliament of the World's Religions held at Chicago in 1893, Swami Vivekananda delivered his famous speech. Subhash Chandra Bose said, “So far as Bengal is concerned Vivekananda may be regarded as the spiritual father of Modern nationalist movement.” Swami Vivekananda founded Ram Krishna Mission in 1897 A.D. (it was registered officially in 1909 A.D. under Societies Registration Act 1860). Its headquarter was opened at Belur in Howrah (West Bengal). The objective of Ram Krishna Mission was non-political, non-sectarian spiritual movement, engaged in various forms of humanitarian, social and cultural service activity, but it was highly inspired by the Ancient culture of India. The Theory of Pure Vedanta is the ideal of this mission. Its main aim is the highest spiritual upliftment of Human’s inner self. It also accepted traditional practices of Hindu religion in their original form such as idol worship, rituals, symbols, etc. The second feature of the mission is: ‘Belief in the truth of all religions’. Swami Vivekananda said that all religious beliefs are different ways to reach the same destination that is one God.
  • Mulshankar or Dayanand Saraswati was born in the old Morvi Princely State, Kathiyawara in Gujarat in a Brahmin family. From 1845-60 (for fifteen years) he wandered to different places in search of knowledge. In 1860 he came under swami Virajananda Saraswati at Mathura and started preaching in 1864. In November, 1869, he engaged in a mighty Shastrartha with leaders of Hindu orthodoxy at Kashi. In 1867 A.D., he hoisted “Pakhand Khandini Pataka”. In 1875 A.D., he founded ‘Arya Samaj’ in Bombay. His views are inscribed in his famous book Satyartha Prakash. Rigvedadibhashya bhumika, Rigveda Bhashya, Advaitmat Khandan, Panch Mahayajya Vidhi and Ved-Viruddh-mat-Khandanam were important works of Dayanand Saraswati. The Arya Samaj was spreading rapidly as a reaction against the western influences. In 1877 A.D., its headquarter was shifted to Lahore which helped in accelerating the spread of this movement. Dayananda’s slogan of “Go Back to Vedas” was a call for a revival of Vedic learning and purity of religion. He rejected the religious practices like idol worship, incarnations, tantra-mantra, etc. His aim was the oneness of all religions, society, and of the nation itself. He is also called as “The (Martin) Luther of India” for his efforts in religious reforms. Arya Samaj got divided into two groups, one supported western education and other one opposed western education. Swami Sraddhanand (Mahatma Munshi Ram Vij), Lekhraj etc. were opposed to western education. They established ‘Gurukul’ in 1902. Lala Lajpat Rai and Hansraj were supporters of western education. They established Dayanand Anglo Vedic College. Dayanand Saraswati was the first to use word Swaraj and advocated Hindi as the official language of India. He was the first to suggest renunciation of foreign goods and the adoption of country-made indigenous goods.
  • After being inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen, Atmaram Pandurang founded Prarthana Samaj in 1867 A.D.
  • Mahadev Govind Ranade in 1869 A.D. joined this organization. The main aim of this organization was to oppose the caste system, increment in the age of men and women for marriage, promotion of widow remarriage and women education. Ranade is also called as “Precursor of cultural Renaissance of Western India”.
  • Shiv Narayan Agnihotri at Lahore in 1887 A.D. founded ‘Dev Samaj’. The Preaching of this Samaj is mentioned in a book, Dev Shastra.
  • Jyotirao Phule in 1873 A.D. founded Satya Shodhak Samaj. He was born to a gardener family in 1827 A.D. With his book Gulamgiri and his Samaj, he criticised the opportunistic Vedas of the Brahmans and called for the need for protection of lower castes from exploitation.
  • Radhakant Deb opposed Socio-Religious reforms and supported orthodox elements by founding Dharma Sabha in 1830 A.D. at Culcutta (Bengal).
  • Radhasoami (Radhaswami) Satsang movement began in Agra in 1861. The first and founding member of this movement was Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji) or Swamiji Maharaj originally he was ‘Persian Language translator’ later joined his father’s moneylending business. His followers believed in one god, the greatness of teacher, Satsang and ordinary social life.
  • Social reformer of Maharashtra Gopal Hari Deshmukh (1823-92 A.D.) was famous as Lokahitwadi. He was also a member of Governor-General Council in 1880.
  • Vishnu Shastri Pandit was a social reformer and advocate of widow remarriage during 19th century. (specifically in Maharashtra). In 1850’she founded ‘Punarvivahottejak Mandali to promote the practice of widow remarriages. Vishnu Shastri published a Marathi translation of Vidyasagar’s book in Indu Prakash in 1868.
  • Behramji M. Malabari, a Parsi social reformer, was born in 1853 A.D. at Baroda. The Age of Consent Act, 1891 was passed through his efforts.
  • M.G. Ranade and Raghunath Rao in 1887 A.D. founded Indian National Social Conference. The main aim of the Conference was to abolish social evils like Polygamy, Child marriage, and Patriarchy.
  • The widow remarriage got legal backing By Hindu Widows Remarriage Act of 1856. The Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829 was passed by then Governor General Lord William Bentinck, making the practice of Sati illegal.
  • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, principal of Sanskrit College, struggled a lot for the Widow Remarriage. He tried to prove the affiliation of widow remarriage through spiritual sactions by Hindu Shastras/Dharmashastras. By his efforts, The Hindu Widows Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) was passed on 25 July, 1856.
  • Raja Ram Mohan Roy opposed Sati Practice strongly. Sati Practice was abolished (by Regulation XVII (1829) passed by the Governor-General in Council) by his efforts in 1829 A.D. Slavery became illegal in 1843 A.D. by an Act passed by Lord Ellenborough.
  • Keshab Chandra Sen in 1872 played an important role in the passing of Native Marriage Act (Act III of 1872 commonly referenced as the Special Marriage Act, 1872) according to which the minimum age of girls and boys for marriage was fixed at 14 years and 18 years respectively. This is also called as Brahmo Marriage Act of1872. The Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 was enacted through the efforts of Indian Judge Dr. Har Bilas Sharda. On his name, it was called Sharda Act. By this Act, the minimum legal age of girls for marriage was 14 years and for boys, it was 18 years. This act was amended in 1978 and later repealed substituted by ‘Prohibition of Child Marriage Act’, 2006. At present marriage age is 18 years for girls and 21 years for boys.
  • Theosophical Society was founded by Madame H.P. Blavatsky, Colonel H.S. Olcott (American army officer) and others in 1875 A.D. It was founded in New York. They shifted their Headquarters from New York to Adyar in 1882 on the outskirts of Madras which later on became its International Office. In 1889 A.D. Annie Besant became a member of the Society and in 1893 A.D. she arrived in India and played the most active role for the Society. She believed Hinduism as the most spiritual and esoteric religion.
  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale, in 1905, founded Servants of India Society. He chaired the 21st Session of Congress in 1905 A.D. He was the political guru of Gandhi.
  • In 1910 A.D., Mukund Rao Patil and Shankar Rao Jadhav in the influence of Jyotiba Phule founded Bahujan Samaj.
  • The demand of rights to enter the temple by Nadars led to several riots in Tirunelvelli. In a conference organized on the abolition of untouchability, Tilak said, “If God tolerates the untouchability then I do not believe in God”. Tilak is often called as Lokmanya or Betaj Badshah.
  • The founding members of Darul Uloom Deoband, was Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi, Haji Syed Muhammad Abid Deobandi, Mahtab Ali Deobandi, Zulfiqar Ali Deobandi, Fazlur Rahman Usmani Deobandi, Haji Fazle Haq Deobandi, Shaikh Nihal Deobandi and others; and the foundation was laid on 31 May 1866.

UP1 paper question

Chapter 51

Political Organisations Established Before Congress

26 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (9 points)
  • Raja Ram Mohan Roy was the guide of social reforms and political movements in Modern India. His associates in 1836 for the first time started an association called Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha. Raja Ram Mohan Roy was the earliest individual to struggle for political reforms in India.
  • Zamindari Association or Landholders Society was established at Calcutta in 1838. This society marked the beginning of an organized political activity and use of methods of constitutional agitation for the redressal of grievances. The aim of the Society was to safeguard the rights of Zamindars. This Society was founded by Dwarkanath Tagore and his fellow Zamindars.
  • The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was one of the strongest political organisation of 19th century India. It was launched on 2 April 1870 in the Pune district of Maharashtra. It was the result of the labour of many great men like G.V. Joshi, S.H. Sathe and S.H. Chiplonkar. Fresh vigour and energy were infused into the Sabha in November 1871 A.D. with the entry of M.G. Ranade. M.G. Ranade provided fantastic leadership to this Sabha. In 1875 this Sabha presented a petition in British House of Commons. The petition consisted of the demands of representatives of India.
  • Indian Association was founded on 26th July, 1876 A.D. by Surendranath Banerjee with the help of Anand Mohan Bose in Calcutta. This was the most important political association before Congress with the tag of an All India Nationalist Organisation. Surendranath Banerjee passed the Civil Services exam in 1869, but as there was some trouble over his exact age he was declared disqualified. He published 'The Bengalee' newspaper for the promotion of mass consciousness. He was Congress President twice.
  • British Indian Association was started on October, 1851 A.D. in Calcutta whose founders were, Radhakant Deb (President) and Debendra Nath Tagore (General Secretary) etc.
  • Syed Ameer Ali in 1877 A.D. founded Central National Muhammadan Association at Calcutta.
  • Getting inspired by Rajnarayan Basu, Nabagopal Mitra in 1867 founded a Society named ‘Hindu Mela’. The main aim of this society was to promote the nationalist feelings and use of indigenous goods amongst the masses.
  • In 1843 A.D., George Thompson founded Bengal British India Society.
  • Bombay Presidency Association was founded in 1885 A.D. by Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang and Badruddin Tyabji. These three are known as Trimurti of Bombay.

Zamindari Association (Landholders' Society), Calcutta, 1838 → first political organisation in India; Dwarkanath Tagore and landlords; protected landlords' interests by constitutional means.

2 papers question

Chapter 52

Indian National Congress

45 facts · 14 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • Allan Octavian Hume was a retired British officer of Indian Civil Service.
  • In 1884 A.D., he established Indian National Union which was the precursor of Indian National Congress.
  • Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 A.D. by A.O. Hume and its first session was held on 28-30 December, 1885 A.D. at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College at Bombay. In this session, Dadabhai Naoroji suggested that the name Indian National Union should be changed to Indian National Congress.
  • A total of 72 delegates took part in this session. It was presided over by W.C. Banerjee, and its first General Secretary was A.O. Hume.
  • Lord Dufferin (1884-88 A.D.) was the Viceroy of India during the establishment of Congress. He mocked and described Congress as a microscopic minority of the Indian people. The second session of Congress was held in 1886 at Calcutta presided by Dadabhai Naoroji.
  • Badruddin Tyabji is recognized as the first Muslim president of Indian National Congress. He presided over the 3rd session of Indian National Congress held at Madras on 27-30th December, 1887 A.D. A total of 607 delegates took part in this Session. For the first time in this session, working operations of Congress was handed to a committee of delegates. A subject’s Committee was appointed for the first time in this session.
  • ‘George Yule’ was the first elected European President of Indian National Congress. He presided over the 4th Session of Congress held at Allahabad (Prayagraj) in 1888 AD. British Committee of the Indian National Congress was founded under the Presidency of Sir W. Wedderburn in London in 1889 to gather support for Congress and its cause. It was a committee of Indian National Congress. It started a monthly journal called ‘India’ to spread awareness among Britishers about the matters relating to India (which became weekly later).
  • Lala Lajpat Rai often called ‘Sher-e-Panjab’, in 1920 A.D. presided over the Congress special session and resolution on the non-cooperation movement was passed by Congress in this session.
  • Mrs. Annie Besant having Anglo-Ireland origin, was the President of Theosophical Society from 1907 to 1933 A.D. In 1916 A.D., she founded Home Rule League and in 1917 A.D. she became the first women president of Congress by presiding over Indian National Congress Session of 1917 A.D.
  • 27th Session of Indian National Congress (INC) was held at Bankipore (Patna, Bihar) in December, 1912 A.D. This session was presided over by R.N. Mudholkar.
  • A.O. Hume was called the Father of Congress in this session.
  • The Indian National Congress held its session at Lucknow in 1916 and the muslim League also held its session at Lucknow in the same year. In this session, a pact was signed between INC and Muslim League is known as Lucknow Pact. The extremist leaders of INC who were excluded 9 years ago were again included. Ambica Charan Mazumdar was the President of the Lucknow Session of INC.
  • At the session of 1916 A.D. Tilak said, “Swaraj mera janma sidhha adhikar hai, aur mai ise lekar rahunga.” (Swaraj is my birthright, I shall have it).”
  • In 1888 AD, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Shiv Prasad Singh (King of Banaras) founded United Indian Patriotic Association the aim of which was to restrict Congress from spreading its ideals to masses and to keep people away from Congress.
  • In 1900 A.D., Curzon said that “the Congress is tottering to its fall, and one of my greatest ambitions while in India is to assist it to a peaceful demise.”
  • Gandhiji recommended dissolution of Congress after Independence of India.
  • Lord Wellingdon took part in 30th session of INC (held in Bombay in 1915 and it was presided over by Sir Satyendra Prasanna Sinha). He was then Governor of Bombay.
  • Mahatma Gandhi was president for one time in 1924 A.D. at Belgaun (Belagavi) Session of INC.
  • Sarojini Naidu (1879-1949 A.D.) was a famous poet and national leader. In 1925 A.D. after presiding over 40th annual session of INC she became the first Indian female president of INC. During 1947-49 AD, she was the Governor of U.P.
  • Jawahar Lal Nehru was the president of INC in 1929 A.D. at Lahore, April 1936 A.D. at Lucknow and in December 1936 A.D. at Faizpur Sessions.
  • 51st session of INC was held at Haripura of Gujarat presided by Subhas Chandra Bose on 19-21st February, 1938 A.D.
  • National Planning Committee was established with Jawahar Lal Nehru as its Chairman. The committee was set up in 1938 by Subhas Chandra Bose, as the president of Congress (INC), K.T. Shah was its secratary.
  • Abul Kalam Azad was president of Congress from 1940-46 AD.
  • J.B. Kripalani was elected president at 54th session of Congress. He was also President of Congress during Independence.
  • Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramaiyyah presided over the 55th session (December 1948 Jaipur).
  • ‘Jan-Gan-Man’ composed by Rabindranath Tagore was adopted as the National Anthem of India on 24th January, 1950 A.D. It was first sung at Calcutta session on 27th December, 1911 A.D.
  • Bal Gangadhar Tilak was present for the last time at Amritsar session in 1919 A.D..

Chapter 53

Moderates and Extremists in Congress

29 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (14 points)
  • The first two decades of INC are often described in history as a moderate era. Some of the prominent moderate leaders were Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendra Nath Banerjee, Mahadev Govind Ranade, Pherozeshah Mehta, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Anand Mohan Bose. They had a sense of confidence in British justice and their generosity. They never aimed at aggressive nationalism for attaining independence. Leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, raised extremist ideology.
  • Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha, Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee and Surendra Nath Banerjee were leaders of Moderate group. They all belonged to urban areas, in fact most of the Moderate leaders who believed in moderate politics belonged to Urban areas. The Congress during moderate phase was dominated by people having professions like Advocates, Doctors, Engineers, Journalists and Person related to Literature works. the Connection to common masses was missing in Congress during Moderate domination.
  • Pherozeshah Mehta once said, that the voice of Congress is not of Masses, but it is the responsibility of citizens in contact with Congress to understand these emotions and propagate these to the Nation.
  • GopalKrishnaGokhalewasamoderateleader. Hebelievedinthe purity of Means and Ends. He was the political mentor (Guru) of Mahatma Gandhi. For the first time, he tookpart in politics in 1889.
  • In 1897 A.D., Gokhale and Dinshaw Wacha were asked to present proofs of Indian expenditure in front of ‘Welby Commission’. In 1899 A.D., Gokhale was elected to Bombay legislative council and in 1901 A.D. was elected to Imperial council of the Governor general of India.
  • In early 1900s Extremist leaders of Congress emerged in Indian Political Scenario. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghose were four important extremist leaders. Their main objective was ‘Swaraj’. They didn’t believe in the agitation through constitutional means of the Moderates. They blamed the Congress for politics of Petition, Prayers and Protest. Under their leadership, the policy of petition and prayers was criticised/challenged.
  • Moderates believed in constitutional agitation, annual sessions, speeches, sending petitions to British Parliament, etc. but extremists believed in self-sacrifice, mass movement, aggressive resistance and strong determination.
  • Extremists wanted ‘Swaraj’; as Congress presidential address, Calcutta, 1906 defines Swaraj as – self government like that of the United Kingdom or the Colonies on the other hand moderates believed in “Selfrule under the colonial empire”.
  • Lala Lajpat Rai also known as Sher-e-Panjab, was the representative from Punjab and an extremist leader. He is also known as Punjab Kesari.
  • Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Bal Gangadhar Tilak are together called Lal-Bal-Pal. During a protest against Simon Commission Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in lathi charge due to which he died on 17 November, 1928 A.D. After reading the Biography of Mazzini Lala Lajpat Rai accepted him as his political mentor.
  • He translated a work of Mazzini ‘The Duties of Man’ into Urdu.
  • During the Partition of Bengal, Aurobindo Ghosh was one of the prominent leader of the Swadeshi Movement. Other important leaders of this movement were Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. Tilak believed in sacrifice and had courage to challenge British establishment. He was called the “Father of Indian unrest” by Sir Valentine Chirol. After Bal Gangadhar Tilak’s 1897 sedition conviction and the rejection of his Privy Council appeal, Professor Max Muller and Sir William Hunter led an influential petition to the Queen, asking mercy for Tilak on the ground that he was a great Sanskrit scholar.
  • Later in 1908 A.D., Tilak was jailed for 6 Years in Mandalay (Myanmar then Burma) on the charges of sedition initiated against him for printing an anti-British Article in his Newspaper ‘Kesari’.
  • Tilak wrote ‘Gita Rahasya’ from ‘Mandalay’ prison. Starting Shivaji Mahotsav and Ganpati festival, he tried to grow the feeling of Nationalism amongst the masses. He died on 1st August, 1920 A.D., and his funeral bier was lifted by Mahatma Gandhi, Maulana Shaukat Ali and Saiffudin Kichlew. Maulana Hasrat Mohani read the eulogy after his death.

All four shaped the pre-Gandhi national movement: Italian-Abyssinian War, Boxer movement (China), Irish revolutionaries, Japan's 1905 win over Russia (greatest impact).

Memory aid Japan beating Russia broke the myth that the white race was invincible.

Chapter 54

Revolutionary Movements in India

58 facts · 14 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (20 points)
  • ‘Mitra Mela’ was an organization founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar in 1899 AD. It was later converted into a secret organization 'Abhinav Bharat Society' in 1904 A.D. Besides Maharashtra, its branches were opened in Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka.
  • On 27th September, 1925 A.D., Rashtriya Swayam Sevak Sangha was founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar. Its headquarter is located in Nagpur, Maharashtra.
  • Jatindranath Mukherjee (1879-1915) was a Bengali Revolutionary. He was a heartened follower of Vivekananda and Aurobindo Ghosh. He was an active member in Revolutionary Committees such as Yugantar, Anushilan Samiti, Gadar Party etc. He was also known as Bagha Jatin.
  • Vyayam Mandal was founded by Chapekar Brothers - Damodar Hari Chapekar and Bal Krishna Hari Chapekar and Vasudeo Hari Chapekar in 1896-97 A.D. at Poona. It was founded with clear political intentions. In June 1897 A.D., Chapekar Brothers killed President of Poona plague committee Rand and Lieutenant Ayerst. Damodar Hari Chapekar including his other brothers was hanged in this crime. They were arrested on the information given by Dravid Brothers. Britishers charged/arrested Tilak for inciting murders through writings (sedition) but they got no evidence to prove that.
  • In July 1897 A.D., Tilak was charged with sedition as per Section 124-A of IPC and was sentenced for 18 months. It made Tilak an All India leader and people gave him the title of Lokmanya.
  • In December 1909 A.D., Anant Laxman Kanhere a member of Karve Group shot and killed District Collector of Nasik ‘Jackson’. Kanhere, Krishnaji Gopal Karve and Vinayak Deshpande were hanged in Jackson murder case.
  • V.D. Savarkar was arrested in London and brought to India with some other people who were charged in Nasik conspiracy case and was sentenced to life imprisonment.
  • The place of Barra Dacoity 1908 A.D. was located in East Bengal. The group which executed Barra Dacoity was led by Pulin Bihary Das.
  • On April 30th, 1908 A.D., Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chandra Chaki threw a bomb at Kingsford, but he escaped and unfortunately wife and daughter of Mr. Kennedy who was a sympathizer of National movement were killed. Prafulla Chandra Chaki committed suicide and Khudiram Bose was caught and hanged.
  • In Alipore Conspiracy Case (1908 AD), Aurobindo Ghose, his brother Barindra Kumar Ghose all together 49 persons were accused for waging war/conspirary etc. 19 people were sentenced, but Aurobindo Ghosh was released. Chittaranjan Das putting a lot of efforts saved Aurobindo Ghosh. Kanhai Lal Dutt and Satyendra Bose shot and killed Narendra Gousai (a government witness in Alipore conspiracy case) in the prison. They were sentenced to death. For operating Revolutionary movements in India, a conference of Young revolutionaries was organised at Kanpur in October 1924 A.D., and Hindustan Republican Association was founded in that conference. Its founding members were Sachindra Sanyal (President), Ram Prasad Bismil, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Chandra Shekhar Azad. The organization executed robbery on 9th August, 1925 A.D. at Kakori and looted Government treasure from the train “Eight down Saharanpur - Lucknow passenger train” of North railway’s Lucknow - Saharanpur Zone. Approx 40 revolutionaries were arrested among which Ram Prasad Bismil,Asfaqullah, Roshan Lal and Rajendra Lahiri were hanged. Chandra Shekhar Azad was the key member of Hindustan Republican Association who escaped. Keshab Chakravarthy and Murari Lal Gupta also escaped earlier. Asfaqullah Khan was the first recorded Muslim to be hanged for the struggle of India’s Independence. He was sentenced to death in Kakori case (Kakori Train Action) and was hanged on 19th December, 1927 A.D. at the age of 27 in Faizabad Jail (Now Ayodhya Jail).
  • Famous revolutionary Ram Prasad Bismil refused to drink milk when it was offered to him two days before hanging. He said, “I will drink only my mother’s milk”.
  • Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was founded at Feroz Shah Kotla (New Delhi) in 1928 A.D. by Chandra Shekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and others. Two members of this organization Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt on 8 April, 1929 A.D. threw Bomb at Central Legislative Assembly. The Lahore Conspiracy Case (1929-1930) was a pivotal trial where British authorities prosecuted Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) revolutionaries namely Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru and others for killing ASP J.P. Saunders to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death. After this incident, 18 members of Hindustan Socialist Republican Association were arrested and charged with cases in Lahore conspiracy. Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were hanged and secretly cremated on the bank of river Sutlej at Hussainiwala in Firozpur district on 23rd March, 1931 A.D., becoming a major turning point in India's freedom struggle.
  • Chittagong Armoury Raid was an attempt to raid the armoury of the police and auxiliary forces at Chattagaon in Bengal. It was organized by Surya Sen who was also famous by the name of "Master Da".
  • The Indian Republican Army (IRA) was established by Surya Sen in Bengal with the Cooperation of namely Ganesh Ghosh, Loknath, Nirmal Sen, Ambika Chakraborty, Naresh Roy, Kalpana Dutt, Ananda Gupta, Tegra, etc. On 18th April 1930 A.D., Surya Sen raided the Chittagong Armoury. Struggle took place on 22nd April, 1930 A.D. between Government forces and IRA in which 80 soldiers and 12 revolutionaries were killed. On 16th February, 1933 A.D., Surya Sen was arrested and faced legal proceedings and ultimately hanged on 12th January, 1934 A.D.
  • On 14th June, 1929 A.D. Jatin was arrested on such type of charges under the supplementary Lahore Conspiracy Case. He started a hunger strike for Jail reforms, and due to this long hunger strike which lasted 63 days, Jatin died on 13th September, 1929 A.D.
  • The theory of Passive resistance was formulated by Aurobindo Ghosh in newspaper Bande Mataram.
  • Subhash Chandra Bose founded Forward Bloc on 3rd May, 1939 after resigning from Presidentship of Congress.
  • In December 1931 AD, Shanti Ghosh and Suniti Chowdhury two school students killed district magistrate.
  • Bina Das fired gun-shots at governor sir Stanley Jackson at point-blank range at a convocation in 1932 A.D.
  • Bhagat Singh once said, “Criticism and independent thinking are the two indispensable qualities of a revolutionary".

Chapter 55

Revolutionary Activities Outside India

20 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (10 points)
  • In February 1905 AD, Shyamji Krishna Verma established the Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS) at London. IHRS established nationalist student hosted, named as 'India House' (1905-10) to foster radical Indian nationalist thoughts. The aim of this society was to establish self-rule by promoting nationalistic ideas/propaganda among Indians in Britain. From here a monthly journal ‘The Indian Sociologist’ was started in Jan 1905.
  • The Ghadar Party was founded on 21st April, 1913 (at Oregon) with its headquarters at San Francisco (USA) with an objective to free India from British rule. Indians residing in Canada and the USA founded this party.
  • In 1913, Sohan Singh Bhakna founded a society named ‘Hindustan Association of the Pacific Coast’. This society published a newspaper named Ghadar, that is why this party became famous as Ghadar Party. Lala Hardayal was the torchbearer of this party.
  • Barakatullah, Rash Behari Bose, Raja Mahendra Pratap, Abdul Rahman, Madam Bhikaji Cama, Bhai Parmanand, Kartar Singh Sarabha and Pt. Kashiram were prominent members of the party.
  • Raja Mahendra Pratap with Barakatullah Khan founded the first provincial government of India in Afghanistan (Kabul) during the first world war on December 1, 1915. Raja Mahendra Pratap himself became President and Baraktullah Khan was the Prime Minister.
  • Madam Cama was born on 24th September, 1861. Her parents were Parsi. She served as the personal secretary of Dadabhai Naoroji in Indian Nationalist Movements. She was married to Rustomji who was an advocate and a social worker.
  • Bhikaiji Rustom Cama was a supporter of Revolutionary Nationalism. She operated revolutionary activities from Europe and America. She participated in International Socialist Congress held at Stuttgart (Germany) where she was the first person to hoist Indian Flag on foreign land, which was designed jointly by V.D. Savarkar, Shyamji Krishna Verma and Bhikaiji Rustom. She is famous as the ‘Mother of the Indian Revolution’.
  • Madanlal Dhingra and Udham Singh were hanged for the assassination of British officials in England. Madanlal Dhingra on 1st July, 1909 A.D., shot and killed Curzon Wyllie who was the political aide-de-camp to the Secretary of State for India and Cowasji Lalkaka during a meeting of National Indian Association. Udham Singh killed Michael O' Dwyer (Former Lieutenant Governor of Punjab) in London in March 1940 who was responsible for endorsing and upholding the actions taken during Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. The Kamagata Maru was a Japanese steamliner chartered by an affluent Punjabi businessman, Gurdit Singh to bring Indian immigrants to Canada. The ship departed in 1914, taking 376 Indians for Canada’s Vancouver port, but the Canadian authorities refused their entry in Canada. A Shore Committee was constituted to protect the rights of Indian travellers under the leadership of Hussain Rahim, Balwant Singh, and Sohan Lal Pathak. Indian, Bhagwan Singh, Baraktullah, Ramchand and Sohan Singh also carried out a movement in favour of Indian emigrants. When Kamagatamaru reached Budge Budge port at Calcutta, a clash occurred between angered passengers and British Police. In firing by the Police, 20 of the passenger were killed, one drowned and 202 passengers were sent to Jail.
  • Rash Bihari Bose was an Indian National living in Japan. He organized a conference in Tokyo on 28th-30th March 1942 A.D. to discuss political problems of India.
  • This conference was given an organized form in June, 1942 A.D. and Subhas Chandra Bose was invited. Ras Bihari Bose founded Indian Independence league in this conference and unanimously elected as President of the league.

Chapter 56

Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi Movement

26 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • British Government announced the partition of Bengal on 20 July, 1905 A.D. (Resolution date was July 19, 1905) On 7 August 1905 A.D., a historic meeting took place at the town hall of Calcutta and the Swadeshi movement was started. The historic Boycott resolution was passed here. After this anti partition movements started in various parts of Bengal.
  • On 16 October 1905 AD, the partition formally came into force and Bengal was divided. The day was observed as the 'Mourning day' in the whole Bengal. On the suggestion of Rabindranath Tagore the day was celebrated as ‘Rakhi Diwas’ amongst the people of Bengal.
  • After its partition, the Bengal was divided into East and West Bengal. East Bengal was merged into Assam, and a new province was formed (named as Eastern Bengal and Assam) which included Rajshahi, Chatgaon (Chittagong), Dhaka etc. Decca (now Dhaka) was the capital of this province.
  • Its second part included Bengal province, Orissa and Bihar.
  • Bengal was divided during the tenure of Lord Curzon (1899- 1905 A.D.).
  • Sir Andrew Henderson Leith Fraser was an officer of Indian Civil Service. He served as the lieutenant governor of Bengal from 1903-1908 A.D. He played an important role in the planning of Bengal Partition.
  • Rabindranath Tagore was a critic of certain aspects of Swadeshi movements like aggressive and exclusive nationalism and reliance solely on boycotts etc., and he emphasised on better relation between the East and West cultures. He believed that the West had committed some mistake in understanding the East, this doesn't mean East do the same with the West.
  • Krishna Kumar Mitra the editor of ‘Sanjivani’, published a special edition on 13 July 1905 A.D., and for the first time suggested that people should boycott British goods, and mourn against the partition and should break all linkages from British officers and offices. All of this should be done as a protest against the partition of Bengal.
  • A public gathering on 16 July 1905 A.D., at Bagerhat (then in Khulna district, Bengal Presidency, British India) supported the suggestion of Krishna Kumar Mitra.
  • British Government called partition a necessity for the administrative purposes but the real reason was to weaken the growth of nationalism in Bengal. According to then viceroy Lord Curzon, “Calcutta is the centre from which the Congress Party is manipulated throughout the whole of Bengal and indeed the whole of India ..... The whole of their activity is directed to creating an agency so powerful that they may one day be able to force a weak government to give them what they desire.”
  • The announcement of Partition of Bengal was the immediate cause of Swadeshi movement. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai were the prominent leaders of this idea. They wanted a country wide Swadeshi movement but the moderates wanted to keep movement limited to Bengal & preferring constitutional methods.
  • The Swadeshi Movement that started in Bengal was spread to throughout the country and Tilak was prominent leader in Maharashtra region. Ajit Singh and Lala Lajpat Rai led the movement in Punjab and U.P., Syed Haider Raja led this movement at Delhi and V.O. Chidambaram Pillai led the Swadeshi movement in Madras Presidency.
  • To organise masses for this movement Ashwini Kumar Dutt founded “Swadesh Bandhav Samiti”. Women played an active role in this movement. However, farmers and Muslims showed limited participation in Swadeshi and Boycott movements.
  • Vande Mataram became the anthem/ralley cry song of Indian National movement during the Swadeshi movement.
  • British journalist H.W. Nevinson was related to Swadeshi Movement. He travelled for four months across India and he reported for Manchester Guardian, Glasgow Herald and Daily Chronicle. Later on, he compiled his reports in a Book titled ‘The New Spirit in India’.
  • In the atmosphere of increasing National Movement Abnindranath Tagore and his brother Gaganendranath Tagore founded Indian Society of Oriental Art in 1907 AD (which was initiated by E.B. Havell) to reconstruct the precious Indian Arts and Culture and to develop new consciousness among the masses.

Last of these: Partition of Bengal (1905). Earlier: Permanent Settlement (Cornwallis, 1793); Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley); annexation policy/Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie, 1848-56).

  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale chaired the 1905 A.D. Benaras session of Congress. He founded the 'Servants of India Society' the same year.   • Dadabhai Naoroji also remembered as 'Grand Old Man of India' was the first Indian who got elected to British Parliament in 1892 from central Finsbury constituency on a ticket of Liberal Party.   • A split took place in Congress at Surat in 1907 when the dispute again arose for the Presidentship of 23rd Session of Congress. Moderates wanted Rash Behari Ghosh as President while Lala Lajpat Rai was the choice of Extremists. The extremists wanted a guarantee that all four resolution would be accepted. Therefore, to pressurise the moderates, they even decided to oppose the duly elected president Rash Behari Ghosh. Both sides had come to the session prepared for the conflict. At the session the members started to fight with each other and the congress finally split into Moderates and Extremists.

Chapter 58

Formation of Muslim League (1906)

8 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (9 points)
  • In October 1906 A.D., Muslim representatives gathered at Shimla under the leadership of Aga Khan III decided to form a gathered separate muslim representation with an aim to protect the interests of Muslims.
  • All India Mohammadan Educational Conference was organized at Dhaka in December 1906 A.D. President of Welcome Committee and organizers of Political meetings, Nawab of Dhaka Salimullah Khan, proposed establishment of an All India Muslim League. A 60 member temporary committee was established with Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Waqar ul-Mulk as joint secretaries. Aga Khan III became its first President. It was headquartered at Lucknow.
  • Three main objectives of the organization were -

1. To promote among the Muslims of India feelings of loyalty to the British government, and to remove any misconception that may arise as to the intention of government with regard to any of its measures.

2. To profit and advance the political rights and interests of the Muslims of India, and to respectfully represent their needs and aspirations to the government.

3. To prevent the rise, among the Muslims of India, of any feeling of hostility toward other communities, without prejudice to the aforementioned objects of the League.

  • Sessions of Muslim League were held at Karachi in 1907 A.D. and at Amritsar in 1908 A.D. The clear and formal demand for the separate electorates by Muslim League was demanded in Amritsar Session (30-31 December, 1908). In this session the league denounce the idea of joint electorates and insisted on separate electorates for Muslims.
  • On 1st October, 1906 A.D., a delegation of Muslims (Simla Delegation having a gathering of35 prominent muslim leaders) led by Aga Khan III met Minto and demanded separate electorate for elections at all levels of governance. Morley-Minto reform (1909 A.D.) accepted the provision of separate electorate for Muslims.
  • In 1908 A.D., the London Muslim League was established by Syed Ameer Ali.

Chapter 59

Morley-Minto Reforms

5 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (1 points)
  • In 1905, Lord Curzon was replaced by Lord Minto as Viceroy of India and John Morley was secretary of state for India then. Morley-Minto Reforms are related to the reforms initiated by these two. These constitutional reforms were passed as an act by British Parliament and officially they were called Indian Councils Acts, 1909. It is generally known as Morley-Minto Reforms. The biggest blunder of this reform was the separate electorate given to Muslim community under the Communal representation system. According to this system, the Muslim members of the council were not elected by general electorate but were elected by the Muslim voters only. This system accepted Muslims as a separate community in India. This created many fundamental issues in India. The unity of India was attacked and demolished in just a stroke. Gandhiji said - " The Morley – Minto Reforms have been our undoing. Had it not been for the separate electorates then established then we should have settled our differences by now."

1911 (Delhi Durbar, 12 December) → annulment of 1905 Bengal Partition announced and capital transfer Calcutta to Delhi; Lucknow Pact was not in 1911.

Chapter 61

Lucknow Session of Congress (The Lucknow Pact)

7 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (4 points)
  • In December 1916 AD, both Indian National Congress and Muslim League held their sessions at Lucknow.
  • Both parties passed separate resolutions on demands for constitutional reforms and agreed on a pact to work together in the political field on a common programme. This is known as Lucknow Pact or Congress-League Scheme.
  • Ambika Charan Majumdar was president of Congress in this session. As a result, they together released 19 bulletins to give a positive direction to the contemporary political scenario.
  • Lucknow session was very significant due to two reasons, first, the Extremists who were separated from Congress nine years ago (in 1907 A.D.) were again merged to Congress and, secondly there was a pact between Congress and League. Annie Besant and Tilak played a significant role in the return of Extremists to Congress. On the other hand, the efforts of Jinnah and Tilak were responsible for Congress-League Pact. The period from 1916 A.D. to 1922 A.D. was the time of consensus between Congress and League (although the rupture in their relation stated in 1920, as Jinnah resigned from Congress in 1920 due to his disagreements with Mahatma Gandhi's approach). Lucknow Pact wasjust a temporary arrangement. Muslim League, besides this pact had its own identity and it advocated for the interests of Muslims where ever possible. Both League and Congress were together until 1922 A.D.

Home Rule League Movement

Key facts from the book (9 points)
  • Tilak started Home Rule League in April, 1916 A.D. Annie Besant started the Home Rule League in September, 1916 A.D.
  • Besant through The Commonweal (weekly) and New India and Tilak through Mahratta and Kesari promoted their league to masses.
  • Joseph Baptista was the first president of Tilak’s Home Rule League and N.C. Kelkar was its secretary.

Both leagues never merged because in Annie Besant'swords, “Some of Tilak’s supporters dislike me and some of mine dislike him. We however, had no quarrel with each other".
  • In Home Rule League movement both Tilak and Annie Besant had same meaning of ‘Swaraj’ i.e. to get a responsible government and administration at central and provincial levels under the British Empire and to have treatment like white ruled states like Canada and Australia which were dominion states of British. Annie Besant described Home Rule Movement in her newspaper 'The Common Weal' on 2nd January, 1914 A.D. Under this a programme was made for Religious freedom, National Education, Social and Political reforms keeping in mind the objective of Selfgovernment under the British Commonwealth.
  • The movement was very famous in India during the first World War. Lucknow session of 1916 A.D. was an excellent occasion for Home Rule League’s members to show their might.

George Arundale, organizing secretary of Besant’s League asked their supporters to show their presence at Lucknow in huge numbers.
