Chapter 91

Constitutional Development of India

53 facts · 12 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (37 points)
  • British Parliament passed Regulating Act, 1773 to curb rampant corruption and misgovernance. According to this act, Madras and Bombay Presidencies came under the Calcutta Presidency. Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (under Governor General and Council of Fort William in Bengal in specified matters). Warren Hastings was appointed the first Governor-General of Bengal. The aim of the Regulating Act was to put the activities of East India Company in India under the supervision of the British Government.
  • By the Regulating Act of 1773 a Supreme Court was established at Calcutta with a Chief Justice and three other judges. The Supreme Court was established in 1774 AD with Elijah Impey as its Chief Justice, and Robert Chambers, Le Maistre and John Hyde as its other justices.
  • In the year 1786 AD, a bill was presented and passed before the British Parliament for amending measures, enabling the Governor General to act against/overrule the council. According to the new rule, the Governor-General was given power to overrule the decision of its council in some special cases. Cornwallis didn’t want the District Magistrate to be very powerful so he adopted the principle of separation of power (separating financial/revenues from judicial functions).
  • Monopoly of trade of East India Company (except trade in tea and trade with China) came to an end by 1813 Charter Act. With this Act of 1813 for the next 20 years the Company was granted the control of revenue of the British territorial acquisitions in India under company government.
  • By the Charter Act of 1833, the company's monopoly of trade/commercial privileges were abolished; it ceased to be a mercantile corporation and the company was given only political works. By this Act, the Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor General of India. By this act a law member was added as the 4th member to the Governor-General's executive council this law member should not belongs to company itself, Also, he was not entitled to sit or vote in executive meetings. The Law member will be of English origin.
  • Macaulay became the first law member of the Governor-General's executive council.
  • By the Charter Act of 1853, the salaries of Members of Board of Control started to be decided by the Crown (His majesty) by Warrant but was paid by the East India Company. The number of directors were decreased 18 out of24, and 6 out of those were to be nominated by crown. There was a provision in this act that recruitment to the service would be done by competitive exams set to regulations/qualifications without any discrimination as per the non-discrimination clause mentioned in 1833 Act.
  • British Government by the Government of India Act, 1858, took away the control of Administration of India from the Company. Now all the powers of the Board of Control and Court of directors was handed over to Secretary of State for India.
  • Governor General of India was granted right to issue ordinance in Emergency Period by the Indian Councils Act, 1861. These ordinances had a maximum life of 6 months. By this Act, the executive council of viceroy was given law-making powers.
  • Lord Canning started Portfolio system, Lord Canning gave departments to other members of his council this way he prepared the base of Ministerial government system in India. By this system, each department of administration was assigned to one member. On the recommendation of Montagu Chelmsford reforms, Civil Services exam started to be held together in India and England from the year 1922 AD.
  • Aitchison Commission in its report in 1887 stated that the Indian Civil Services Exam should not be held in India and England together.
  • The reforms announced on 20 August 1917 AD are also known as Montagu declaration on the name of the then Secretary of State for India Montagu.
  • The report of then Viceroy Lord Chelmsford and Secretary of State for India Montagu became the base of Government of India Act, 1919.
  • The Dyarchy at provinces was introduced by Mont-ford reforms, 1919. It is also called as Government of India Act 1919. By this Act, the subjects of provinces were divided into two categories reserved and transferred subjects. Transferred subjects were given to the governor acting with ministers appointed under the act; whereas the reserved subjects were looked on by the Governor in Council.
  • In 1926 AD, India’s Public Service Commission was constituted. By the Indian Councils Act 1861, the council of viceroy was expanded and additional members minimum 6 and maximum 12 were added to this council, for lawmaking processes. They were nominated by Viceroy and had a tenure of two years. In this council, at least halfofthe persons so nominated were to be non-officials.
  • By this act the Madras and Bombay Presidencies were restored of their lawmaking power and were allowed to make amendments to the existing law. But the laws made by these Presidencies would be valid only after the assent of the Governor-General.
  • High Courts at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were established by Indian High Courts Act, 1861.
  • By the Indian Councils Act, 1892, the rights of the Members of Legislative Councils were increased in two aspects -

(i) They were given the right to discuss the budget without the right to vote or to move any amendment to the budget.

(ii) After giving the advance notice of6 days, they were allowed to asks questions on Public interests.

  • Indian Councils Act, 1909 was of the shortest duration amongst the constitutional experiments of Britain in India. In words of Ramsay MacDonald, “This reform is incomplete and momentarily deal between democracy and bureaucracy”.
  • Montagu-Chelmsford reforms in its report in 1918 stated that the Indians participation in administration should be increased. It was also proposed in the report that the exam of Indian Civil Services should be held simultaneously in India and Britain and one-third of the posts (at least) should be held by Indians.
  • By the 1935 Act, the Public Service Commission became the Federal Public Service Commission (it was set up on April 1, 1937).
  • From 1937 AD, Federal Public Service Commission and The Civil Service Commission (UK) started conducting their exams separately. In 1950, after the enactment of constitution, the Federal Public Service Commission was renamed as Union Public Service Commission.
  • By this Act Dyarchy at Provinces were abolished and Dyarchy was introduced at the centre. Provinces were given autonomy and the dual governance came to an end. With this the distinction between the reserved and transferred was abolished. The reserved seats under a joint electorate was expanded and now it included Scheduled Castes, Muslims, Sikh, Europeans, Anglo Indians, Indian Christians etc. The present Constitution of India is very similar to the 1935 Act.

The Main Provisions of 1935 Act are-

(1) Provision for establishment of a federation.

(2) Dyarchy at Centre

(3) Autonomy of provinces was restored and Dyarchy at provinces abolished.

(4) Bicameral central legislative

(5) System of Provincial government

(6) Provincial Legislative Assembly

(7) Division of Power between centre and provinces

(8) Establishment of federal court, etc.

  • Jawaharlal Nehru said, "1935 Act is a Machine (Car) with strong brakes but no Engine". He was the Prime Minister of India from 1947 to 1964 AD. He was the proponent and architect of'Five Principle of Peaceful Coexistence' (Panchsheel) and a believer of Non-aligned Movement. Nehru in his address to Congress in Lucknow Session, 1936 AD rejected Government of India Act 1935, he termed this Act as Charter of slavery and offered some severe criticism. Lucknow Session (1936) was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Act of 1935 was the lengthiest enactment in the history of laws made by Britain for British India. It included 14 parts, 321 sections and 10 schedules.
  • The “Instrument of Instructions” of the Government of India Act,1935 was included as Directive Principles of State Policy in India’s Constitution in 1950.

Chapter 92

Modern History : Miscellaneous

279 facts · 11 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (47 points)
  • In 19th century the fear of Russian expansion towards India became the basis of Anglo-Afghan relationships. The Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828 AD) created fear among the British due to the increasing influence of Russians. Experts in England called this ‘The Crisis in India.”
  • North Western passes were the key to entering India. Then it was thought that Afghanistan should be under a friendly government or a government which is in congruence with Britishers. The British "Forward Policy" in 19th century Afghanistan was a proactive, aggressive strategy designed to establish a buffer state against Russian expansion towards India, particularly during the first Anglo-Afghan War (1839- 42). It was advocated by Lord Auckland. This became the basis of Anglo-Afghan relations.
  • In 19th century Odisha was hit by a severe famine in 1866-67 AD. An estimated one million deaths took place in Odisha. This famine was described as ‘Sea of Calamity’. Odisha famine emerged decisively in the history of Indian famines because after this a Famine Commission under George Campbell was constituted to look into Famines.
  • Lord Hastings suppressed the Pindaris. Pindaris were first mentioned at the time of the Mughal attack on Maharashtra in 1689 AD. In the beginning of 19th century, Pindaris had three main leaders - Chittu, Wasil Muhammad and Karim Khan.
  • Gandhi and Tilak both toured throughout India and worked for social upliftment. Tilak was the first nationalist leader who worked for establishing close relations with masses at the root level.
  • G.V. Mavalankar who became the last President of Central Legislative Assembly in 1946 AD was the first speaker to enter the office wearing a Gandhi cap and not the ‘wig’.
  • Famous constitutionalist B.R. Ambedkar was born on 14 April, 1891 AD at Mhow (now Dr. Ambedkar Nagar) in M.P. and died on 6 December 1956 AD. He was awarded Bharat Ratna posthumously.
  • Rabindranath Tagore, also known as Gurudev won a Nobel Prize in literature and was a famous author. He was born on 7 May 1861 AD at Calcutta as son of Debendranath Tagore and Sharada Devi. In 1901 AD, he started a school at Shantiniketan which was later converted into a University named as Vishva Bharti in 1921 AD. In 1913 A.D. Tagore was awarded with Nobel Prize for literature for his literacy works like - 'Song Offerings', the English translation of his collection of poems ‘Gitanjali’. He was called as the Great sentinel by Gandhiji. Gandhiji believed that Rabindranath Tagore emphasized on moral forces for the freedom struggle.
  • The famous slogan of Jai Jawan Jai Kisan was given by former P.M. of India Lal Bahadur Shastri.
  • During Quit India Movement which was started on 9 August 1942 AD Gandhiji said that Freedom is within our reach and we should hold it very tight. Gandhi gave the mantra- 'Do or Die' We shall either free India or die in the attempt.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru post-Independence said that everything could wait but not the agriculture.
  • Mountbatten blamed Jinnah for India’s partition.
  • In August 1923 AD, the session of All India Hindu Mahasabha at Banaras was chaired by Madan Mohan Malviya. It was attended by 1500 delegates from various religions such as Hindu, Sikhs, Parsis, etc.
  • Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Frontier Gandhi) born at Utmanzai (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan), Frontier Tribal area of early British India is also known as Bacha Khan, Fakhr-e-Afghan etc. He was awarded Bharat Ratna in 1987 AD.
  • Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya a nationalist and Indian historian of Indian National Congress, was a doctor by profession. He lost the election for the president of Congress in 1939 to Subhas Chandra Bose.
  • In 1929 AD, a Royal commission was formed to inquire about labour conditions in India with J.H. Whitley as its chairman. Thejob of this council was to recommend reforms in the fields of health of workers, efficiency and conditions such as the condition of plantation labourers, industrial labourers, relation between employees and employed,
  • 1943 AD is the year of Bengal famine in which nearly 3.0 million people died.
  • During the cold war, J.L. Nehru was one of the founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) to maintain the peace and coordination in the world. The policy of Nehru and India was mostly focused on peace, disarmament and equality of races so that worldly conflicts can be resolved calmly.
  • P.M. Jawaharlal Nehru with President of Egypt Gamal Abdel Nasser, President of Yugoslavia Marshal Tito, President of Ghana Kwame Nkrumah and Indonesia President Sukarno founded a third front of the world as "Non-Alignment Movement" in the capital of Yugoslavia. The first session of the Non-Aligned Movement countries was held in Belgrade in 1961.
  • At the time of India's Independence Goa was still under Portuguese rule. After keeping patience for 14 years, India freed Goa from Portuguese using force in 1961.
  • Jawahar Lal Nehru, the first P.M. of India, was influenced by the ideas of socialism, British liberals and Gandhiji. He never supported German nationalism. In his famous book Glimpses of World History, the ideas of socialism are clearly visible in his articles and speeches.
  • Calcutta Female School (Now known as Bethune School) was established by John Elliot Drink- water Bethune. It is one of the earliest school for girls in Calcutta opened with the help of Raja Dakshinaranjan Mukhopadhyay, Ramgopal Ghosh etc. Pandit Ishwar Chand Vidya Sagar was the first secretary of Bethune school. He established 35 female schools in Bengal Presidency.
  • Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay was one of the first two graduates of Calcutta University.
  • Abul Kalam Azad was related to Deoband. His writing/articles were later compiled as Mazameen al-Nadwa. He was president of Congress from 1940 AD to 1946 AD. He wrote India Wins Freedom.
  • For the first time in India, a Communist government was established in Kerala in 1957 AD.
  • Nehru was the follower of ideals of Gandhiji such as Truth, Non-Violence and transparency but on economic policies, both had various differences. Gandhiji focused on small and cottage industries but Nehru focused on heavy Industrialization for Economic development after the Second World War.
  • Clement Attlee said that the imperialism has extinct as the Dodo Bird.
  • America dropped first Atom Bomb on Hiroshima city of Japan on 6 August 1945 AD and second Atom Bomb on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945 AD in the Second World War. After these two blasts Japan on 15 August 1945 AD announced to surrender (and formal surrender took place on 2nd September, 1945) to the Allied Forces.
  • French Revolution began in 1789 AD. The Revolution was a revolt of the third Estate (including peasants, artisans/urban workers and bourgeois groups) against Feudalism, privileges by birth/estate-based privileges corrupt bureaucracy and incapable or uncontrolled monarchy.
  • Jawahar Lal Nehru died during his 4th term on (1947-52, 1952-1957, 1957-1962, 1962-1964) 27 May 1964. Nehru represented the Phulpur constituency of Allahabad (Prayagraj) in Parliament.
  • Morarji Desai was India’s first non-Congress leader who became the prime minister on 24 March 1977 AD. He represented Surat constituency of Gujarat.
  • Bankim Chandra Chatterjee composed ‘Vande Mataram’ song. It is mentioned in his novel Anandamath.
  • Shimla Agreement was signed between Indira Gandhi (Prime Minister of India) and Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto (President of Pakistan) after the Indo-Pak war of 1971 AD.
  • Operation Vijay was the successful military operation against Pakistan during Kargil war in 1999 AD.
  • 23 December every year is celebrated as Kisan Diwas to remember former P.M. Late Chaudhary Charan Singh.
  • First meeting of All India Socialist Youth Congress was held at Calcutta on 27 December 1928 AD chaired by Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Alipore Central Jail is situated in Calcutta (now Kolkata) (West Bengal). It was established in the year 1906. Political prisoners during British Rule were kept here.
  • Operation Polo was initiated as a military operation in Hyderabad state between 13-18 September 1948 AD.
  • Karl Marx explained the class struggle with the theory of Dialectical Materialism.
  • According to Marx, the basis of society in ancient time was slavery, Land is the basis of feudal society and capital is the basis ofbourgeoisie/capitalist. This is his materialistic explanation of history. According to him, the history of Society is determined by economic factors into which lies the elements of class struggle.
  • Gregorian Calendar is the most famous Calendar of the present time. It is used in the most of the countries.
  • Mother Teresa was born in Skopje (now in North Macedonia; of Albanian origin) in 1910 AD and at the age of 18 she joined the institute of the "Blessed Virgin Mary (Sisters of Loreto)". She came to India in 1929 and taught at the St. Mary's School for Girls Calcutta. At the time of her death on 5 September 1997 AD, she was an Indian citizen.
  • Fateh Singh Rathore was also known by the nickname of Tiger man.
  • Sirimavo Bandaranaike is the first woman Prime Minister of any country in the World. She was the Prime Minister of Sri Lanka.
  • 10 Downing Street is the official residence of British P.M. which is situated in the Westminster, City of Westminster, London. The People's Liberation Army (PLA) invaded Tibet in October 1950. Through Seventeen Point Agreement (1951) hold its control over Tibet (Internal affairs was managed by Tibet government). In 1959 AD, the sovereignty of Tibet ended as the rebellion/uprising was crushed by PLA. Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) also referred to as the Soviet Union was dissolved into 15 independent republics on 26 December 1991 AD.
  • After the Second World War Germany was divided into United States of America British & French zones influenced West Germany and Soviet influenced East Germany and finally on 3 October 1990 AD Germany was again united.
  • Cai-Lun is credited for the invention/improvement of paper making in China. He was a resident of Leiyang, Hunan province of China and he made paper in 105 A.D.

UP1 paper question

Chapter 93

Magazines, Books and Their Authors

186 facts · 31 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (35 points)
  • Annie Besant founded Central Hindu College in 1898 AD and was elected as the President (International) of the Theosophical Society in 1907 AD. She founded a weekly newspaper 'Commonweal' in January 1914 for her political work. In June 1914 she purchased the 'Madras Standard' and renamed it 'New India', which thereafter became her chosen organ for her tempestuous propaganda for India's freedom.
  • Lieutenant Colonel James Tod in his book 'Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan' wrote about the feudal system of Rajasthan.
  • Shyamji Krishna Verma was an Indian revolutionary andjournalist who published journal ‘The Indian Sociologist'.
  • Amar Sonar Bangla was composed in 1905 during the partition of Bengal by Rabindranath Tagore. The melody (tune) of this song were inspired by Harkara's ‘Ami Kothay Pabo Tare’ song of Gagan Harkara. First ten lines of the song Amar Sonar Bangla were adopted as National Anthem of Bangladesh officially in 1972 AD. This song was translated into English by ‘Syed Ali Ahsan’. Rabindranath Tagore composed Jan-Gan-Mana too. He is the only poet credited with authoring the national anthems of two countries. The Bengali edition of Gitanjali was published on 14 August 1910 (31 Shravan 1317). Its English edition was published for the first time in November 1912 AD. Rabindranath Tagore won the 1913 Nobel Prize in literature; Gitanjali: Song Offerings was the english book chiefly associated with the award, and it was Tagore'sown English selection/recasting of the Bengali Gitanjali (version) alone (not direct translation of the book only). Deliberative book “Hind Swaraj” was firstly published in Gujarati in 1909 AD. British Government censored this book. In March 1910, the Bombay Government proscribed its circulation; Gandhi then published his own English rendering, Indian Home Rule, in reply. In this book, Gandhiji compared British Parliament to a sterile women and a prostitute and commented on working processes of the British Government. "Gokhale: My Political Guru, a book was first published in February, 1955 by Navajivan Publishing House, Ahmedabad. The book is an English compilation of Gandhi's earlier writings and speeches on Gokhale".
  • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820-1891 AD) was a great social reformer and educationist of the 19th century. Primarily by his efforts the Hindu Widows Remarriage Act, 1856 was passed. He wrote ‘Bahuvivah’ and ‘Balya Vivaher Dosh’.
  • ‘Das Kapital’ was written by famous German socialist Karl Marx. In this book he straight away criticized the capitalism and presented his Socialist principles which are also known as Marxism (like inquiry into the laws of motion of modern society). First part of the book was published during the lifetime of Marx whereas the second and third part of the book was edited and published by his friend and associate Friedrich Engels.
  • ‘Anand Math’ of Bankimchandra Chatterjee is considered as the Bible of Bengali patriotism. This Book is based on the Sanyasi Revolt (1763-1800 AD).
  • Kesari Singh Barhath was poet and freedom fighter of Rajasthan. In 1903, he wrote ‘Chetavani-Ra-Chungatya’ having 13 soratha/couplets.
  • Maithili Sharan Gupta is a famous poet adorned with the title of‘National Poet’. He is the writer of'Bharat Bharti'. His other works include Panchavati, Saket, Yashodhara, Jayadrath Vadh etc.
  • 'Ae Mere Watan ke logo' a patriotic song is written by Pradeep. Born in a small town Badnagar with in the Ujjain district, Madhya Pradesh the real name of Pradeep was Ram Chandra Narayanji Dwivedi. He wrote a condolence song on the martyrs of 1962 AD Indo-China war. The music of this song was composed by C. Ramchandra.
  • Md. Iqbal was born on 9 November 1877 AD at Sialkot in Punjab of British India. The famous poet of Urdu and advocate by profession Iqbal was a nationalist from the beginning. He wrote - ‘Sare Jahan se Accha Hindostan Hamara’ but later on he joined Muslim League. ‘Majhab Nahi Sikhata apas me bair Rakhna’ is a line from the Song Sare Jahan se Accha by Iqbal.
  • ‘Landmarks in Indian Constitutional and National Development’was written by writer Gurumukh Nihal Singh. He was the Governor of Rajasthan from 1956 to 1962 AD.
  • G.A. Natesan was the editor of the book 'Congress Presidential Addresses' (1934-35 AD). This book was published in two parts. The first one contained the congress Presidential Addresses from 1885 to 1910, and the other one contained the same from 1911 AD to 1934 AD.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru when he was jailed at Ahmednagar Fort (1942-1945 AD) wrote a book named The Discovery of India. Also, in his jail term, Nehru wrote an Autobiography (also known as Toward Freedom) and Glimpses of World History (in 1930s).
  • Sachindranath Sanyal wrote ‘Bandi Jeevan’.
  • ‘A Journey through the Kingdom of Oude in 1849-50’ report was written by W.H. Sleeman and published in two volumes in London.
  • ‘JP Movement-Emergency and India' Second Freedom' was a book written by M.G. Devasahayam.
  • Lieutenant General Brij Mohan Kaul wrote the book ‘The Untold Story’. This book was published in 1967 AD and throws light on India-China war of 1962 AD.
  • Hans Christian Andersen in his writings wrote about fairy tales. His important works are:

The Steadfast Tin Soldier, The Snow Queen, The Little Mermaid, Thumbelina etc.

  • 'The Golden Gate' published in 1986 AD is the first novel by Vikram Seth.
  • Rachel Carson wrote ‘Silent Spring’. She was a famous American Biologist. In this book, questions are raised about the use ofpesticides.
  • ‘The Satanic Verses’ is the fourth novel of Salman Rushdie. Its first publication took place in 1988 AD. This book was in the news for some time regarding various controversies. Rushdie's first published novel 'Grimus', appeared in 1975.
  • 'The Namesake' was the first novel of Jhumpa Lahiri. Jhumpa Lahiri is a Pulitzer Prize winner. She received this award for the “Interpreter of Maladies” which she published in 1999 AD.
  • 'Manas ka Hans' is a prestigious novel by Amritlal Nagar. Generally, the story is written around the life of Tulsidas who wrote Ramcharitmanas.
  • Sumitra Nandan Pant is one of the prominent poets of modern India. He was a Chhayavaadi poet. His famous works are Chidambara, Lokayatan, Veena, Yugvani, Pallav, Bharat Mata Gram Wasini and Kala aur Boodha Chand.
  • J.K. Rowling written/created Harry Potter in which Cornelius Fudge is a Minister for magic.
  • ‘Mrignayani’ is a novel written by Vrindavan Lal Verma. His main novels are - Jhansi Ki Rani, BhuvanVikram, Sangam, Lagan, Ahilyabai, etc.
  • ‘Bikhre Moti’ is a story collection published by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan in 1932 AD. Besides this, she wrote 'Unmadini' and 'Seedhe-Sadhe Chitra'.
  • Charles Dickens wrote the novel ‘David Copperfield’ published serially in 1849-50 AD (and in book form in 1850 A.D.). The novel is based on the life of Charles Dickens semi autobiographical.
  • ‘The Proudest Day’ was written by Anthony Read and David Fisher. The story of the book is related to the freedom of India.
  • ‘Kamayani’ was written by famous Hindi poet Jaishankar Prasad. In this epic, the episode of Manu and Shraddha is narrated. His famous works are - Aansu, Lahar, Ajatashatru, Titli and Kankal.
  • Verrier Elwin studied Baiga Tribe and wrote a book named ‘The Baiga’. He suggested making national parks for the tribes.
  • ‘Ignited Minds’ is written by former President of India Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam who is also known as the Missile Man of India. He also wrote 'Wings of Fire' (An autobiography: APJ Abdul Kalam with Arun Tiwari).
  • ‘The Story of the Integration of the Indian States’ was written by V.P. Menon.

1 paper question

First Bharat Ratna → 1954 (instituted 2 Jan 1954): Dr. S. Radhakrishnan, C. Rajagopalachari and C.V. Raman. Nehru was not among the first. Must know

Memory aid First trio = three Rs: Radhakrishnan, Rajagopalachari, Raman.
